docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Set up Boilerplate and its Python development environment on Windows, macOS, or Linux. Choose your operating system below and follow the steps appropriate to your platform.

Overview

  • Windows 11: Recommended path with a fully automated installer.
  • Windows 10: Older builds, and machines without App Installer, have no winget. Install PowerShell 7, Git, and VS Code first and then run the installer, or use the manual path.
  • macOS / Linux: Manual setup.
  • Python installation is handled by uv; no preinstallation is required.

Do not run bare pip install boilerplate

That name is already taken on PyPI by an unrelated, same-niche package — pip install boilerplate silently installs that package, not this one. Boilerplate is not published to PyPI; use one of the install commands below. See adr-008 for the full mis-install hazard.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Python: nothing to preinstall — uv provisions Python for you.
  • Admin rights: needed only for the winget installs — PowerShell 7 when missing, Git, and VS Code.
  • -ExecutionPolicy Bypass: scoped to that one PowerShell process; it does not change your machine's execution policy.

docs.title: Setup options
docs.text:
WindowsmacOS / Linux Automated Setup (Recommended)Manual Setup

Run the installer (no repo clone required) — it works from the stock Windows PowerShell 5.1: it installs PowerShell 7 via winget (if needed) and relaunches itself under it.

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TheRealBillSiegler/boilerplate/v0.4.0/scripts/install.ps1 | iex"

The script sets up the full Python development environment and installs the Boilerplate CLI. It:

  • Installs Git and Visual Studio Code using winget, skipping either one that is already installed. Without winget, it continues when the code and git commands are already on PATH, and stops with an error at the first one that is not.
  • Installs the recommended set of VS Code extensions.
  • Installs uv, which will install Python and manage the virtual environment.
  • Installs the boilerplate CLI using uv tool install git+https://github.com/TheRealBillSiegler/boilerplate.git@v0.4.0.

No manual PATH edits needed

The script refreshes PATH for this terminal so you can use uv and boilerplate immediately.

Already have the repo cloned? Run the local script instead. 
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\scripts\install.ps1

  1. Install PowerShell 7+

    PowerShell 7+ required

    Boilerplate assumes you are using PowerShell 7+. The automated path above installs this for you — this step is only needed here, in Manual Setup.

    Verify InstallationInstall PowerShell 7

    Verify your PowerShell installation:

    $PSVersionTable.PSVersion

    The Major version should be >= 7.

    Follow the official PowerShell docs, or install via winget:

    winget install --id Microsoft.PowerShell -e --source winget --accept-source-agreements

  2. Install Git — download for Windows and accept the defaults, or install via winget:

    winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget --accept-source-agreements

  3. Install Visual Studio Code — download and install, or install via winget:

    winget install --id Microsoft.VisualStudioCode -e --source winget --accept-source-agreements --override '/VERYSILENT /NORESTART /MERGETASKS="!runcode,desktopicon,addcontextmenufiles,addcontextmenufolders,associatewithfiles,addtopath"'

  4. Install VS Code extensions Ensure the code CLI is on your PATH, then:

    $exts = @(
    'ms-python.python',
    'ms-toolsai.jupyter',
    'charliermarsh.ruff',
    'esbenp.prettier-vscode',
    'tamasfe.even-better-toml'
)
foreach ($e in $exts) {
    code --install-extension $e
}

  5. Install uv Install using the Windows instructions.

  6. Install the Boilerplate CLI

    uv tool install git+https://github.com/TheRealBillSiegler/boilerplate.git@v0.4.0

Using a private package feed? See the Customization guide for the org-adoption pattern.

Under active verification

These macOS/Linux steps are under active verification — please report any issues.

Manual Setup

  1. Install Git

    # macOS
brew install git
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt-get install -y git

  2. Install Visual Studio Code Download and install from code.visualstudio.com.

  3. Install VS Code extensions Ensure the code CLI is installed (via "Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH" in VS Code), then:

    for e in \
    ms-python.python \
    ms-toolsai.jupyter \
    charliermarsh.ruff \
    esbenp.prettier-vscode \
    tamasfe.even-better-toml; do
    code --install-extension "$e"
done

  4. Install uv Install using the macOS and Linux instructions.

  5. Install the Boilerplate CLI

    uv tool install git+https://github.com/TheRealBillSiegler/boilerplate.git@v0.4.0

Using a private package feed? See the Customization guide for the org-adoption pattern.

Install the development version instead

The commands above install a release. To try unreleased changes, install the CLI from the develop branch:

uv tool install git+https://github.com/TheRealBillSiegler/boilerplate.git@develop

See Troubleshooting if you hit errors during installation.

docs.title: Organization adoption
docs.text: Boilerplate itself ships with public defaults. Organizations customize in two places, both after the canonical install: point uv at the org feed (machine configuration), and drop a profile.toml with the org's generation defaults. See the Customization guide for the pattern and a reference script.

docs.title: Verify installation
docs.text:
Test your boilerplate installation by getting the version.

boilerplate --version

Expected: prints a semantic version and exits 0.

Verify the PATH is correct.

PowerShellbash 
Get-Command boilerplate

Prints a path (often %USERPROFILE%\.local\bin\boilerplate) if PATH is correct.

command -v boilerplate

Prints a path (often ~/.local/bin/boilerplate) if PATH is correct.

Command not found? See Troubleshooting or the FAQ.

docs.title: Update the CLI
docs.text:
To update, pick the newest version in the docs' version selector and run its install command again; uv replaces the installed CLI with that release. uv tool upgrade boilerplate does not move a release install, because the install names a fixed tag.

An install from develop follows the branch instead: uv tool upgrade boilerplate moves it to the branch's latest commit.

Next steps

  • Read the Quickstart Guide — Create your first project and run it.
  • Explore Boilerplate CLI Usage — Learn commands and workflows.
  • Review the Environment Overview — Understand the toolchain.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Less yak. More stack. Scaffold fully configured, dependency-locked Python projects with Boilerplate.

This guide shows you how to:

  1. Scaffold your first project
  2. Run the dev loop

This guide scaffolds your first project and runs its tests. Install Boilerplate first — Setup options and Verify installation — and skim the toolchain it standardizes.

docs.title: Scaffold a new project
docs.text:
Generate a clean, opinionated project structure, accepting every default in one shot:

boilerplate new project my-first-project --non-interactive

Expected: creates my-first-project/ with:

  • src/my_first_project/module.py (with an add(a, b) function)
  • tests/my_first_project/test_module.py (with tests for add)
  • pyproject.toml, README.md, .vscode/, and notebooks/
  • __init__.py with a version string
  • additional files

Want to set the project name, description, dependencies, and author yourself? Drop --non-interactive and answer the 9 prompts interactively (each has a sensible default — press Enter to accept it):

boilerplate new project my-first-project

Building a Streamlit app? Use the Streamlit template:

boilerplate new streamlit my-streamlit-app

Pin to an exact template version when needed (check the current version with boilerplate list; the bundled project template is currently at 0.3.0):

boilerplate new project@0.3.0 my-versioned-project

Planned

boilerplate update — moving a generated project to a newer template version — is planned; see the roadmap for sequencing and the update model design for the approach.

Non-interactive (accept defaults) and overwrite a non-empty destination:

boilerplate new project --non-interactive -f my-first-project

--force / -f overwrites without confirmation

If my-first-project already exists, --force silently overwrites any files the template writes there, without asking first. It does not delete files the template doesn't manage. There is no undo — make sure any file the template will touch doesn't hold work you want to keep.

docs.title: Available templates
docs.text: Boilerplate ships two first-party templates today — see Choose a template for what each one adds and when to reach for it.

docs.title: The dev loop
docs.text:
The dev loop is the cycle you repeat inside a project; the Development Environment guide covers it in full.

  1. Enter the project directory

    cd my-first-project

  2. Add a dependency

    uv add pandas pydantic

    Tip

    Add --dev for a development-only dependency.

  3. Open the project in VS Code

    code .

    Or: VS Code → File → Open Folder → select my-first-project

  4. Run tests

    uv run pytest

    Tip

    Use -q for quiet; Use -vv for detailed diagnostics.

    Expected: tests run; all passed; exit 0.

docs.title: Project layout at a glance
docs.text: See Project structure for the generated tree and what each part is for.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Installation Guide — platform-specific installation details
  • Templates Hub — pick a starting point
  • Commands — every command and option explained
  • VS Code Guide — tips for a friction-free experience in your IDE (code editor)

Enjoy building with Boilerplate! ✨

docs.title: Build-out roadmap
docs.text:
The design specification suite describes the target contract, Implementation status tracks what exists today, and this page sequences the path between them — phases ordered by dependency, not by design-document numbering, with effort labels that are scope-based (small / medium / large by scope and files touched), never clock time.

How to read this page

Each phase lists what ships, why it sits where it does, and which design documents govern it. The CI pipeline reference describes the repository's own CI, and phase completion is recorded by releases — one minor version per completed phase — in the changelog. When a sequencing decision here no longer reflects reality, update this page in the same PR.

docs.title: Sequencing principle
docs.text:
Primitives-first, just-in-time. The design suite's slice numbering is not the build order. Operational primitives — atomic staged write, the lock file, checksums — are prerequisites of the lifecycle slices, so they ship first; bulk hardening that nothing yet depends on defers.

The design documents are well-factored, but two seams cross document boundaries and must be re-cut into the work:

  1. Artifact fetching (design 06 Part 3) is lifecycle-document content but federation-track work. It belongs to Phase 4, and Phase 3 declares an interface dependency on it.
  2. Per-operation invariants in design 07 ship inside the phase that introduces the operation needing them — they are not deferred hardening. The advisory lock attaches to every mutating operation. The intent journal attaches to in-place mutation, where a crash can strand partial state that the staging pattern cannot undo: it ships with Phase 3's update commit window, not with new, whose crash recovery is deleting the stale staging directory.

docs.title: Phase summary
docs.text: Phase Theme Depends on Effort 0 Release gate: CI, error codes, YAML hardening, determinism, content audit — Small–medium per item 1 Provenance and atomicity for new (lock file, atomic render) 0 Large 2 Read-side lock tooling (lock verify, local-only) 1 Medium 3 update + add + adopt + eject — the longest pole 1 (interface dep on 4 for remote) Large 4 Catalog federation and remote sources 1; parallel with 3 Large 5 Environment provisioning 0 (topology contract), 1 (primitives); parallel with 3 and 4 Large 6 Observability track (cross-cutting) Any time after 0 Medium

docs.title: Phase 0 — Release gate
docs.text:
Most of this is cheap now and is good launch hygiene. The CLI ships via the bootstrap installer (scripts/install.ps1 on Windows), which installs uv and boilerplate from git and uses no PyPI name, so cutting the first public tag without a PyPI publish freezes nothing. The distribution name becomes genuinely irreversible only once published to PyPI (re-publishing under a different name orphans every prior PyPI install and silently mis-routes pip install boilerplate to the unrelated package — see adr-008). The legal / no-leak items (LICENSE, NOTICE, a clean history) gate public exposure regardless of version. Everything else here (error-code rename, CI) is reversible during 0.x per SemVer, so doing it now is good hygiene rather than a hard pre-tag deadline.

The gate's criteria:

  1. CI — the full test suite runs from the repo root across the OS × Python matrix, with the src/ doctests collected by an explicit step rather than silently omitted.
  2. Error codes — every shipped code follows BP_{PHASE}_{DESCRIPTOR} and is registered in design 07's Error Code Registry, so codes match the target scheme before anyone scripts against them.
  3. Hardened YAML loading — all boilerplate-owned parse sites load through a shared helper with duplicate-key errors and capped alias expansion per design 03, while copier.yml parsing is delegated to Copier's own loader.
  4. Topology determinism — sibling order follows extends declaration order per design 04 Stage 2, with lexicographic order only across independent roots, held by fixed-order regression tests.
  5. INT-007 content audit — the license stance lives in RELEASING.md: all direct dependencies permissive, and vendored docs assets, all credited in NOTICE. Re-verify NOTICE against what the tree actually vendors whenever vendored content changes — it is an acceptance criterion, not a settled fact. The history criterion is satisfied by publishing from a fresh repository — see the INT-007 acceptance criteria.
  6. ADR-003 decision recorded (small) — going public under the documented permissive-execution posture is sanctioned by ADR-003 while template sources are local and deliberately chosen. The hard deadline for trust-gated execution is Phase 4 entry — before remote/Git/community sources ship. Optionally, land a minimal tier-less consent gate early via Copier's native trust setting.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Provenance and atomicity for new (the spine)
docs.text:
Every later lifecycle feature stands on these two units. They are sequential, not parallel — both restructure the new render pipeline.

  • 1b — Atomic staged-write render (large): stage → verify → commit, with temp-then-rename semantics and the Windows non-atomic fallback. Crash recovery for new is deletion of the stale staging directory (timestamped staging names plus an age check) — the destination is untouched by construction, so no intent journal is needed here; the journal ships with Phase 3, whose in-place commit window is what it actually protects. Standalone value: a crash mid-render can no longer leave partial output.
  • 1a — Lock emission on new (large): the BoilerplateLock model plus checksums, written by new, with a provenance-complete schema from day one — per-layer name / version / source / commit / checksum and a trust-tier field, per design 02 — so Phase 4 does not have to reshape it. Provenance-complete means exactly this verified core plus schema_version and copier_version. The source_bundle / subdirectory fields, and the bundle_uri and bundle_checksum fields, are reserved/optional and deferred with the wheel_bundle seed cache (ADR-006) — recorded by external catalog or enterprise-infra tooling for air-gap restoration; they carry no logic today, are never consulted by lock verify, and must not be required by any shipped command. The cut fields answers_hash and answers_preset_path are not written to the lock file at all — no command reads them, and including them would calcify unconsumed surface in user-owned files. Attribution fields (invoked_by, hostname, flags_used) are fully cut from the schema. Each first-party template already declares _answers_file: and ships its answers-file stub ({{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}.jinja), per ADR-015; this phase adds copier_answers_file_hashes recorded in the lock against those per-layer files, so locks are born update-ready; otherwise every project created during Phases 1–2 mints a legacy lock that Phase 3 must migrate. Also ships the .boilerplate/migrations.yml created record and the advisory-lock primitive for mutating operations. Standalone value: every new project carries verifiable provenance.

Order: 1b, then 1a. Landing the lock-write first would mean relocating it when 1b restructures the render pipeline.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Read-side lock tooling
docs.text: lock verify only, explicitly scoped local-only: checksum recompute and answers-file hash compare against the lock written in Phase 1 (medium). status is deferred to Phase 3 — it must report drift, which requires the fetch layer (Phase 4) or at minimum the update machinery to have meaningful output; shipping it in Phase 2 would imply guarantees it cannot yet check. Source-reachability checks arrive with Phase 4's fetch layer; environment-state reporting arrives with Phase 5.

docs.title: Phase 3 — update + add + adopt (longest pole)
docs.text:
Ship local-source update first; remote-source update has a declared interface dependency on Phase 4's fetch layer (large overall).

Prerequisites inside the composition engine, in order:

  1. The rest of the CopierWorker abstraction (design 04, Copier Worker Interface): the Worker subclass ships, so what remains is the run_worker / WorkerResult contract and the startup BP_COPIER_COMPAT_FAILED check.
  2. Per-layer answers-file consumption (the per-layer answers files projects already carry).
  3. Version-conflict detection and graph size/depth limits.

Then the three-way merge envelope — UpdatePlan, the staging worktree, and the restore marker that keeps an interrupted copy back in git (new's staging pattern needs neither, so Phase 1 defers it) — then add, which stages and copies back through the same worktree and restore marker to add a layer to a managed project, and finally adopt, which reuses the same machinery to bring an existing project under lock management. The conflict-pause / safe-orphan / never-auto-delete semantics governing this envelope are specified in ADR-007.

status ships here rather than in Phase 2: reporting drift requires the update machinery to have a meaningful reference point, and source-reachability checks require Phase 4's fetch layer. A Phase 2 status would silently omit the most useful signals.

eject also ships here: a guarded delete (requires the advisory mutex) that removes boilerplate.lock and the .boilerplate/ directory, releasing a project from lock management — the inverse of adopt, reusing the same mutex and idempotency contract.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Catalog federation and remote sources
docs.text:
Runs in parallel with Phase 3 after Phase 1, under the parallelism contract below (large).

  • boilerplate-sources.yml plus the CatalogSource / trust model (design 09, design 03).
  • Git source — build a Git-backed TemplateRepository — then archive sources and the local catalog cache. The wheel-bundle source stays deferred per ADR-006; build it only on demonstrated demand for an offline seed cache.
  • TOFU pinning, the git credential helper, and the revoked-templates read protocol (Reserved for Phase 4 / remote sources) (design 10).
  • Owns artifact fetching (design 06 Part 3): the fetch layer lives here exclusively.
  • Carries the ADR-003 expiry: full trust-tier consent gating must land at Phase 4 entry, together with the superseding ADR that ADR-003's expiry clause requires.

Open sequencing question — the git source became a first-party dependency

The same amendment moves the git source out of "Phase 4 nicety" and into the update spine's prerequisites: a project is only updatable if its answers files record a resolvable git source, so new must render first-party layers from a published repo (or a local clone) rather than the wheel's plain directories. Implementing the Git-backed TemplateRepository therefore gates the updatable-project outcome, not just catalog federation. Resolve before Phase 3 begins: either move the git source into Phase 1/early Phase 3, or accept that projects created before it lands are copy-only and rehome via a one-line _src_path edit.

docs.title: Phase 5 — Environment provisioning
docs.text:
Runs in parallel with Phases 3 and 4 (large). The build order within the phase, per design 08:

profile models → ProfileCatalog and scanner → extends resolution → .prototools generation → ProtoWorker → env apply and env status (the env command group thin core).

Gated on the pinned topology-ordering contract from Phase 0: the profile extends resolution mirrors the composition topology, so the ordering semantics must be frozen before this phase consumes them.

docs.title: Phase 6 — Observability track
docs.text:
The genuinely cross-cutting work (medium): a single JSON-to-stderr structured log stream (no file rotation or aggregation), redaction plus a non-serializing secret type, subprocess-output capture at DEBUG, correlation IDs, the retry policy, and performance budgets per design 07.

What is not in this phase

Advisory locks and intent journals are not here — locks ship inside Phases 1–5 attached to each mutating operation, and the journal, which identifies a staging folder for stale cleanup, ships with Phase 3's staged update, whose interrupted copy back the restore marker covers, per design 07 and the sequencing principle above. Placing them in a trailing hardening phase would mean retrofitting every command shipped before it.

docs.title: Backlog
docs.text:
Unsequenced planned scope — an item leaves the backlog once a phase adopts it into the sequencing above.

  • Merge strategy annotations — per-field merge behavior (append, unique, deep-merge) instead of today's fixed strategy set.
  • Conflict reporting — compose --conflicts flags file-level composition conflicts instead of silent overwrites.
  • Version specifiers in extends — PEP 440 constraints (e.g. parent@>=1.2) pin a layer to a compatible parent version range instead of today's exact-version-only match.
  • File overlay preview — graph --files shows which files each layer would touch before rendering.
  • Author lint — fails the build when a layer's delta unnecessarily repeats a base default.
  • Generated-project CI scaffolding — templates ship CI configuration for the generated project itself, not just the three quality-check commands you wire into your own CI provider.
  • A deploy-time and runtime guardrail layer — checks that run after generation, not only at scaffold time.
  • Design 05's confirmation contracts — plan-then-prompt for mutating commands: update, add, env apply, and eject show their plan before acting.
  • A backward-compatibility test suite — pins the public surfaces (CLI, template contract, lock schema) and fails CI on an accidental break.

docs.title: Release workstream
docs.text:
Independent of the feature phases, sequenced against the go-public decision:

  • Day-one distribution: the bootstrap installer — scripts/install.ps1 on Windows installs uv + boilerplate from git, needs no PyPI name.
  • Cross-platform bootstrap: a macOS/Linux equivalent of install.ps1 (e.g. install.sh), so the bootstrap-first install is canonical on every platform.
  • Publish pipeline (fallback / parallel, non-gating): a GitHub Actions release pipeline — PyPI via an OpenID Connect (OIDC) trusted publisher, tag-driven — per INT-010 in the intentions register; deferred until the PyPI distribution name (boilerplate-cli, adr-008) is final.
  • Template publishing: deterministic per-template extraction (git subtree split) from the authoring monorepo, publishing the resulting repositories with tags kept in sync with each template's boilerplate.yml version — the canonical first-party distribution channel per ADR-006. The wheel-bundled seed cache is an optional, deferred item, built only on demonstrated demand.
  • Version checkpoints: wired to the release checklist in RELEASING.md. Proposal: 0.3.0 = Phase 0 complete, cut at go-public; one minor version per completed phase after that.
  • Dormant ci/ content: the Azure Pipelines templates under ci/ are first-party template substrate per PROD-001 — shipped product material, not this repository's own CI. Standing decision: relocate them into template material when the catalog work lands; never delete them, and exclude them from the repo's own CI concerns.

docs.title: Parallelism contract
docs.text:
Tracks 3, 4, and 5 may proceed in parallel after Phase 1 only under three conditions:

  1. The lock schema ships provenance-complete in Phase 1a (source, commit, checksum, trust-tier field), so Phase 4 extends values rather than reshaping the model Phase 3 is consuming.
  2. The fetch/Git layer belongs exclusively to Phase 4, and Phase 3 declares an explicit interface dependency on it for remote-source update, shipping local-source update first.
  3. The shared merge points — command registration in cli/cli.py, common/exceptions.py, and constants.py — are treated as append-only. They are coordination points, not evidence of independence.

If any condition fails, the affected tracks serialize.

docs.title: Tracking
docs.text:
• One milestone per phase.
  • One epic per phase — a parent issue with native sub-issues — linking the phase's governing design documents.
  • area:* labels per component, doubling as a spec-coverage map.
  • Optionally a GitHub Projects v2 board with Status / Area / Size / Priority fields and Board / Table / Roadmap views.

All tracker scaffolding is created once the repository is public (see INT-007 in the intentions register).

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Implementation status — what exists today, the ground truth under this sequencing.
  • Contributing — how to pick up work aligned with the current phase.

docs.title: Implementation Status
docs.text:
This page tracks how much of Boilerplate's design specification is actually implemented in code today. It is maintained by hand: a feature is marked Implemented only when code backs it, and usually tests too.

The design docs describe the full target system; this page lists which parts are Implemented, Partial or Planned.

Legend: Implemented · Partial · Planned (design-only)

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
The implemented core is local template composition: discover templates from local directories, resolve an extends graph, merge their configuration and question schemas, and render through Copier. That pipeline ships end to end and is covered by the test suite, but several of design 04's contracts are still open (graph limits, the run_worker contract), so the area is rated Partial below. Beyond the core, two customization mechanisms ship: an env/.env-driven Settings object (three of design 09's ten Settings fields, plus two code-only extras) and the per-user profile (profile.toml); the earlier typed Profile model, its resolution chain, and the boilerplate config command were retired in favor of the profile. Reproducibility and lifecycle are partial: new writes boilerplate.lock, and the per-layer update and add engines (three-way merge, migration records) are implemented but driven only by tests, with no command wired to them. Catalog federation (remote/Git sources, trust tiers, search) and the environment-provisioning subsystem are design-only.

Design area Status 01 — Overview / architecture Partial 02 — Data models Partial 03 — Template system Partial 04 — Composition engine Partial 05 — CLI reference Partial 06 — Project lifecycle Partial 07 — Operational quality Partial 08 — Environment provisioning Planned 09 — Settings & configuration Partial 10 — Security Partial

docs.title: 01 — Overview / architecture  Partial
docs.text:
• Implemented: Service split: resolver / composer / render engine as independent, wired classes
  • Partial: Atomic / no-partial-output rendering — render is a sequential per-layer overlay with no transactional rollback, so a mid-render failure can leave partial output
  • Partial: Pluggable repository abstraction — the ABC exists, but only the directory repository is implemented

docs.title: 02 — Data models  Partial
docs.text:
• Implemented: TemplateMeta, TemplateInfo, TemplateSpecifier, SerializableVersion, TemplateCatalog
  • Partial: BoilerplateLock, LockLayer and MigrationRecord (models/) — implemented; new writes the lock, and the update and add engines append migration records, driven only by tests

docs.title: 03 — Template system  Partial
docs.text:
• Implemented: Local template discovery across multiple directory roots (catalog/, repository/directory_repository.py)
  • Implemented: extends-based layering and topological composition
  • Implemented: Bundled Jinja extensions and the project / streamlit scaffold templates
  • Planned: Catalog federation, remote/Git sources, classification, and trust/verification levels — catalog is local-only; a Git-backed repository remains unimplemented, with no stub in code — build_template_catalog (cli/utils.py) constructs only the directory repository

docs.title: 04 — Composition engine  Partial
docs.text:
The most mature area. The resolution → graph → merge → render pipeline works end to end and is heavily tested; the gaps are specific design 04 contracts, not missing pipeline stages.

  • Implemented: Resolution, graph ordering, and composition (composition/resolution/, composition/graph/, composition/composer.py) — ordering is deterministic: siblings follow extends declaration order, with lexicographic order only across independent roots (design 04 Stage 2)
  • Implemented: Config & question-schema merging — deep-merge of questions, dicts, and tasks, with dedicated strategies for _jinja_extensions (union) and _min_copier_version (highest wins) (composition/merging/). Note: this is configuration-layer merging, not file-level three-way merge.
  • Implemented: Composition serialization to YAML/JSON (composition/serialization/)
  • Implemented: Cycle detection and merge-conflict errors (composition/graph/exceptions.py, composition/merging/exceptions.py)
  • Implemented: Version-conflict detection — an extends diamond that pins the same template name at two different versions is rejected during resolution, raising VersionConflictError with error code BP_RESOLVE_VERSION_CONFLICT (design 04 Stage 1) (composition/resolution/resolver.py, composition/graph/exceptions.py)
  • Planned: Graph size/depth limits — BP_GRAPH_* covers cycles only
  • Partial: CopierWorker abstraction — the Worker subclass ships as ScopedWorker, and composition renders and updates through it (composition/rendering/scoped_worker.py); the run_worker / WorkerResult contract and the startup BP_COPIER_COMPAT_FAILED check are not built
  • Implemented: Per-layer answers files — each bundled template declares _answers_file: .copier-answers.<layer>.yml and ships the answers-file stub; Copier writes one per layer natively during that layer's render, and no canonical .copier-answers.yml is written (design 04's per-layer _answers_file: contract, the foundation for per-layer update)
  • Implemented: Scoped rendering — boilerplate new asks the merged questionnaire once, then renders each layer under its scoped view (the questions and extensions of that layer and its ancestors), so each answers file records only its own scope; ancestors' file-path extensions load for the descendants that use them (composition/rendering/engine.py, composition/views/)

The questionnaire pass sees the merged _jinja_extensions union (see What gets merged), so a question default can use any layer's filter instead of crashing; the merged tasks run once, on the last layer.

docs.title: 05 — CLI reference  Partial
docs.text:
See the command table below for the specified-vs-implemented command areas.

  • Implemented: Global options (--verbose/--quiet/--color/--ci/--version) and Typer's own did-you-mean on a mistyped command
  • Implemented: The banner above the top-level help — the braille logo beside the name, the name alone where the logo can't show, and its opt-outs (cli/display/banner.py, cli/display/terminal_probe.py)
  • Planned: Design 05's confirmation contracts (plan-then-prompt for mutating commands) — no code; sequencing in the backlog

docs.title: 06 — Project lifecycle  Partial
docs.text:
• Partial: Project creation (new) — resolves, composes, and renders with --dry-run, --force, --non-interactive, --no-tasks, --data/--data-file, --format json (the flag names match design 05's Answer Presets contract except the missing -d short flag; new rejects _-prefixed keys in --data-file where the design warns and skips them, and update and add take no --data or --data-file yet). It ends by writing boilerplate.lock (composition/rendering/creation_lock.py).
  • Partial: Lock-file generation (boilerplate.lock) — new writes it after a successful render: each layer's name, version, source, commit (null for a bundled folder), checksum, and a hash of each answers file. No command reads it yet
  • Partial: Project update and layer add — the per-layer update and add engines are implemented (composition/updating/, composition/adding/) and driven only by tests; the update and add commands are planned

docs.title: 07 — Operational quality  Partial
docs.text:
• Implemented: Logging via stdlib logging — Rich console on TTY; non-TTY / --ci stderr gets one strict-JSON object per event with phase, operation, request_id, success, and error_code on failure, plus BOILERPLATE_REQUEST_ID passthrough (logging_config.py). Redaction and duration_ms terminal events are not implemented.
  • Partial: Error attribution — a uniform CLI error boundary, exception hierarchy, phase-tagged BP_{PHASE}_{DESCRIPTOR} codes, and per-exception remediation hints exist (cli/utils.py, common/exceptions.py); the severity / retryable fields are declared but hardcoded ("error" / False) on every exception and read by nothing yet, and attribution labels and the --verbose diagnostic block are not emitted
  • Implemented: Exit codes — the design's canonical six-value set defined (constants.py), with ACTION_REQUIRED=4 routed in the CLI error boundary (no shipped operation produces exit 4 yet; its first producer is the update conflict pause) and USER_CANCELLED=130 shipped: Ctrl+C at a prompt exits 130 as clean cancellation
  • Partial: Advisory locks and the intent journal — implemented (common/file_lock.py, composition/staging/) and used by the update and add engines, driven only by tests
  • Planned: Metrics, performance budgets, retry policy, automation gates, and atomic staged writes for new

docs.title: 08 — Environment provisioning  Planned
docs.text: Design-only. There is no proto/toolchain code, no .prototools/.protolock generation, and no env command group. (The profile covers package index and container registry values — not toolchain versions or provisioning.)

docs.title: 09 — Settings & configuration  Partial
docs.text:
Two mechanisms ship, both tested: an env-driven Settings object and the per-user profile (profile.toml). The rest of design 09's surface (the full Settings field set, catalog source config, revocation file) is not yet built. The typed Profile model, its resolution chain, and the boilerplate config command group were retired in the template-customization redesign; named default sets and a repurposed config command are designed but deferred.

  • Implemented: Settings object loaded at every CLI startup — BOILERPLATE_-prefixed env vars and .env; ships five fields: three of design 09's ten (default_templates_dir and extra_template_dirs drive template-directory resolution, debug drives logging) plus log_dir and file_logging_enabled, which sit outside design 09's field set and are not consumed yet (settings/settings.py)
  • Implemented: Profile loader: [defaults] + [templates.<name>] merged from profile.toml (settings/profile.py)
  • Implemented: Platform-aware config-root resolution for profile.toml (settings/paths.py)
  • Planned: The seven remaining design-09 Settings fields (four operation timeouts, allowed_extension_packages, request_id, accessible) and catalog source config (boilerplate-sources.yml) — design-only (the revocation file is reserved for Phase 4, not a pending surface)
  • Planned: Named default sets + a repurposed config command to switch between them — designed, deferred
  • Retired — the strict Profile model, the CLI/env/profile/defaults resolution chain, config show/use/validate, and the pre-profile migration hint (replaced by profile.toml)

docs.title: 10 — Security  Partial
docs.text:
• Partial: YAML safety — boilerplate-owned files load through the shared hardened loader (common/yaml_loading.py): safe-load semantics plus duplicate mapping keys as errors and capped alias expansion, per design 03's YAML parsing rules; copier.yml parsing is delegated to Copier's own loader; validate warns on custom YAML tags in boilerplate.yml
  • Partial: Execution posture — template tasks and Jinja extensions run under Copier's unsafe grant, scoped per layer to what that layer's Worker invocation loads (for extensions that is the layer's scoped view, its own and its ancestors' union, and the composition-wide union for the questionnaire pass — see design area 04 above), per the accepted permissive posture in ADR-003; trust-gated execution is deferred until remote sources ship
  • Planned: Checksums, signatures, trust verification, and Jinja2 sandbox enforcement — no code exists

docs.title: CLI: specified vs implemented
docs.text: Command Status Notes new Partial Renders projects (incl. answers supplied with --data/--data-file) and writes boilerplate.lock (cli/commands/new.py) list Implemented cli/commands/templates.py compose Implemented cli/commands/compose.py graph Implemented cli/commands/graph.py validate Implemented Template-dir well-formedness (cli/commands/validate.py) config Planned Retired with the Profile system; a repurposed config for the profile is designed, deferred update Planned Planned; the per-layer update engine is implemented and driven only by tests add Planned Planned; the add engine is implemented and driven only by tests status Planned Not implemented adopt Planned Not implemented eject Planned Not implemented doctor Planned Not implemented test Planned Not implemented init-template Planned Not implemented search Planned Discovery is list only — no search/filter/trust env (apply/status/diff/rollback/…) Planned No env command group lock (migrate/verify) Planned No lock command; new writes the lock and nothing reads it cache warm Planned No cache layer shell completions Partial Typer's built-in completion only

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
These are specified in the design docs but no shipped command exercises them — listed here so expectations are clear. Items 2 to 4 have engines implemented and driven only by tests, so they are partial; their commands are not yet wired. The rest are design-only:

  1. Using the lock (boilerplate.lock) — new writes it, but no command reads it: there is no lock verify, status or update.
  2. Project update lifecycle — the per-layer update engine is implemented and driven only by tests; the update command is not yet wired, so no shipped command diffs versions or applies an update.
  3. Three-way merge / conflict resolution — the update engine merges through Copier and pauses on a conflict, driven only by tests; the only merge a shipped command performs is configuration-schema merging. The target semantics (conflict-pause, safe-orphan, never-auto-delete) are specified in ADR-007.
  4. Migration records & rollback — the update and add engines append migration records, driven only by tests; no shipped command writes them or exposes a rollback.
  5. Environment provisioning — the entire proto toolchain subsystem and env * commands.
  6. Catalog federation & discovery — remote/Git sources, search, trust tiers, classification.
  7. Security verification pipeline — checksums, signatures, trust verification, Jinja sandbox.
  8. Operational quality remainder — metrics, performance budgets, retry policy, and automation gates (advisory locks and the intent journal are partial, above; the phase-tagged error codes and six-value exit taxonomy are shipped; see design area 07 above).
  9. Lifecycle/quality commands — status, adopt, eject, doctor, test, init-template, cache warm.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Roadmap — the sequencing these states feed.
  • Design specifications — the target being built toward.
  • Commands — the shipped command surface in detail.

This page reflects the state of the develop line. Please update it in the same PR whenever a feature moves between states.

docs.title: Error: boilerplate command not found
docs.text:
The installer places the boilerplate executable in a user-local bin directory that may not be on your PATH (the list of folders your shell searches for commands) yet.

WindowsmacOS / Linux
  • Problem: boilerplate (or uv) is not recognized.
  • Cause: PATH not refreshed in the current terminal, or %USERPROFILE%\.local\bin is not on PATH.
  • Solution:
    1. Close and reopen PowerShell (or the VS Code terminal) to pick up PATH changes written by the installer.
    2. If still not found, open Start → Edit the system environment variables → Environment Variables and check or add %USERPROFILE%\.local\bin to Path under User variables.
  • Verify: 
    boilerplate --version
Get-Command boilerplate
  • Problem: boilerplate (or uv) is not found.
  • Cause: Shell session hasn't reloaded PATH, or ~/.local/bin is not on PATH.
  • Solution:
    1. Reload your login shell (exec "$SHELL" -l) or open a new terminal.
    2. If still not found, confirm ~/.local/bin is on PATH: echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | grep local. If missing, add export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" to your shell profile (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, etc.) and reload.
  • Verify: 
    command -v boilerplate
boilerplate --version

docs.title: Error: Template not found
docs.text:
Verify available templates:

boilerplate list

docs.title: Error: Permission denied
docs.text: Ensure you have write permissions to the destination directory.

docs.title: VS Code not detecting the Python interpreter
docs.text: Symptoms include a missing interpreter right after cloning or generating a project, and lint or type errors that persist after a fix. See VS Code setup: interpreter not detected for the fix.

docs.title: Ruff not formatting automatically
docs.text: Symptoms include Python files saving without Ruff's formatting or fixes applied. See VS Code setup: Ruff not formatting automatically for the fix.

docs.title: Tests not discovered or not running in VS Code
docs.text: Symptoms include the Test Explorer showing no tests, or uv run pytest passing while VS Code reports none. See VS Code setup: tests not discovered for the fix.

docs.title: Profile and render errors
docs.text:
Boilerplate's render pipeline emits phase-tagged error codes (BP_RENDER_*, BP_INPUT_*) for problems around destination state, required answers, and interactive-prompt failures. The code appears as a bracketed suffix on the Error: line alongside a remediation hint; see Error codes for the fix for each.

  • BP_INPUT_DEST_REQUIRED — non-interactive render names no destination.
  • BP_INPUT_ANSWERS_MISSING — non-interactive render cannot proceed: a question has no default and no supplied value.
  • BP_INPUT_DATA_INVALID — --data/--data-file could not be parsed.
  • BP_INPUT_TTY_REQUIRED — interactive render without a terminal.
  • BP_RENDER_PROMPT_FAILED — environment cannot show interactive prompts.
  • BP_RENDER_USER_CANCELLED — cancelled at a prompt.
  • BP_CONFIG_PROFILE_INVALID — profile.toml isn't valid TOML or a section isn't a table.

docs.title: General troubleshooting
docs.text:
For persistent issues:

  1. Restart your development environment (VS Code, terminal session)
  2. Check for conflicting settings in VS Code workspace or user settings
  3. Run commands via uv run (e.g., uv run pytest) rather than relying on a manually activated virtual environment
  4. Review the logs — re-run with --verbose (or set BOILERPLATE_DEBUG) for debug-level output.
  5. Check file permissions for the project directory

If problems persist, see the FAQ or report a bug.

docs.title: Why Boilerplate?
docs.text:
Boilerplate takes care of the parts around writing code — a working toolchain and a configured project — so a new Python project starts on one golden path and you start at the work. A golden path is the supported, opinionated way to build one kind of project.

Boilerplate is an ethos made executable: engineering judgment — which tools, how they're configured, how a project is laid out — encoded as software that runs, so a new project inherits the discipline instead of being advised toward it. It is two things at once: a particular Python development environment, and the scaffolder that stamps out projects configured for it.

docs.title: Yak shaving
docs.text:
You need one package for the task at hand. That package needs a newer Python. The newer Python needs a PATH fix before it will even run. Three side quests deep, and the actual work hasn't started. The chain has a name — yak shaving: a prerequisite that hides another prerequisite until the original task is buried under toil that isn't the task.

No single link in that chain is hard. The damage is the pattern — individually tolerable incidents that quietly become an operating model:

  • "I'll just copy the last project." "Works on my machine."
  • Tool choice debated again for every repository — Ruff or Black, uv or Poetry.
  • Onboarding that takes a day before the first test runs.
  • A setup README that drifted from what the tooling actually does.

Python itself raises the stakes. The ecosystem ships no equivalent of npm create or dotnet new — no official starting point for a working project — and the tooling underneath keeps moving: packaging and environment managers compete, get replaced, and leave layers of guidance behind them. Much of what a search turns up teaches techniques the current PEPs have already superseded, and there is no canonical, up-to-date reference project to copy from. Every project works out "modern" for itself, or keeps whichever year's answer its oldest tutorial gave.

Less yak. More stack. is the promise to cut that chain down: the environment arrives working, the project arrives configured, and you start at the task itself.

docs.title: The ethos
docs.text:
Three opinions the tool executes rather than recommends:

  • Opinionated defaults, visible overrides. Every pick — uv, Ruff, Pyright strict, pytest — is a default rather than a mandate: template questions, profile.toml, and plain config edits are the sanctioned escape hatches.
  • Automation over documentation. When a practice matters, it is encoded — in the installer, the template, or the generated config — instead of written into instructions that drift.
  • Legibility before trust. You can inspect what generation will do before believing it: boilerplate new --dry-run shows the render plan — layer order and destination — without writing anything, boilerplate graph shows the layers, boilerplate compose shows the merged configuration.

docs.title: A whole environment, one pick per slot
docs.text:
A development environment is a set of slots — shell, runtime and package manager, linter, type checker, test runner, editor — and most projects fill them one tool at a time, as each need comes up. Boilerplate fills each slot with one opinionated, overridable pick, at three layers:

  • Machine — the installer bootstraps the baseline itself: PowerShell 7 (installed first when missing), Git, VS Code with extensions, uv, and the boilerplate CLI. There is no prerequisites section that quietly assumes an hour of setup.
  • Project — every generated project arrives with a uv-managed, locked environment and Ruff, Pyright strict, and pytest configured in pyproject.toml; its example module and test pass those checks on the first run.
  • Editor — templates ship .vscode/ settings and extension recommendations, so the editor and the toolchain agree on interpreter, linting, and formatting.

The environment overview walks the full toolchain and how the pieces fit. Environment validation is deliberately thin today (Implementation Status).

docs.title: One path, not a repeated conversation
docs.text:
Boilerplate started in 2024 inside a small enablement team, as a way to stop re-explaining the same project setup to every new project. It was research before it was software: a systematic pass over the landscape — package and environment managers, scaffolders, type checkers, test runners — judged against one brief, the most modern and lightweight in each, and against what current PEPs actually prescribe. The stack settled late that year, and the tool was built for colleagues from its first mention. The leverage is structural: the judgment gets absorbed once, upstream, and one maintained path replaces the recurring setup conversation.

The tool holds itself to the standard it hands out: this repository's own CI runs the same checks it configures in every generated project — Ruff, Pyright strict, pytest — plus a strict docs build. See the local check.

One early user described the before-and-after: "before, it was like having your laundry folded — but on the floor. After, it's like sliding the drawer into the dresser: the clothes go in, and it slides friction-free." Another summed up the install as ending in "a fully suped-up Python environment."

docs.title: Built on Copier
docs.text:
Boilerplate stands on Copier rather than reinventing it: Copier does the rendering, prompting, and answers-file bookkeeping, and templates stay standard Copier templates. Composition metadata lives in a separate boilerplate.yml beside copier.yml; Boilerplate never modifies or replaces your copier.yml, and a template becomes a layer by adding that one file.

Boilerplate adds two things on top. The first is the opinions: Copier is deliberately a general-purpose engine — any language, any layout, bring your own templates and your own judgment — while Boilerplate ships the ethos and the environment above as maintained templates and an installer that keep pace with the toolchain and with current standards. Adopting it with a single template and no composition at all still gets you that.

The second is a layer Copier does not provide natively: declared template composition. Copier's open issue on updatable template hierarchies and reuse shows the demand, and a member of the Copier project wrote there that a native composition feature might address updating a project whose parent template is applied from a task, where that template's migrations never run, but would need more thinking and probably an actual implementation. Copier's own multi-template pattern works well when templates touch disjoint files; its practical boundary is overlap. When two templates render the same file — pyproject.toml is the recurring example (discussion #1485) — there is no merge: Copier prompts per conflicting file, or the last-applied template wins. With Boilerplate, the template author declares composition once — extends: [project] in the template's boilerplate.yml — and boilerplate new renders the full layer stack in one command, with one merged question set and deterministic precedence when layers overlap; the composition guide covers the mechanics in depth. A profile.toml pre-fills org answers (your package index, your registry) across the whole catalog without forking templates.

Already using Copier? Your templates keep working unchanged; composition and the curated environment are what's new.

Use case Recommended tool Your own templates, any language, no opinions wanted Copier An opinionated, maintained Python environment and scaffold Boilerplate Single custom template, no composition Copier Multiple templates touching disjoint files Copier's multi-template pattern Layered templates with extends, overlapping files Boilerplate One merged question set across layers Boilerplate Org-wide default answers without forking templates Boilerplate

docs.title: Who it's for
docs.text: Platform teams and template maintainers who own more than one template and want the common foundation defined once — and individuals who want an opinionated, preconfigured Python scaffold without assembling the toolchain themselves.

docs.text:

  • Implementation status — what is implemented, partial, or planned.
  • Quickstart — install and scaffold your first project.
  • Template composition — the extends mechanics in depth.
  • Environment overview — the toolchain, slot by slot.

docs.title: Design Specifications
docs.text:
The canonical target architecture spec for Boilerplate. See 01-overview.md for the principles, glossary, and architecture overview.

This corpus describes the target only — no implementation status appears here. For what exists in code today, see Implementation status.

Single-owner rule. Every normative fact has exactly one owning document; other documents cross-reference it, never restate it.

The ancillary documents in this directory:

  • adr-001-build-vs-adopt.md — build-vs-adopt: orchestrate Copier/proto rather than reimplement them.
  • adr-002-copier-internals-shim.md — depend on Copier's private Template/Worker through one audited shim.
  • adr-003-permissive-execution.md — renders with template tasks/extensions enabled (current posture, ahead of the trust model).
  • adr-004-exit-code-taxonomy.md — six-value exit-code taxonomy with BP* codes for detail.
  • adr-005-integrity-model.md — integrity today: filesystem-permission-based for the lock file; cryptographic signing and a revocation list deferred.
  • adr-006-template-distribution.md — git-backed template distribution: monorepo authoring → release-time extraction into published per-template repos, whose URLs and tags the answers files and lock record (the wheel bundle is a deferred offline seed cache).
  • adr-007-update-model.md — safe update: conflict is a pause (exit 4; resolve, commit, rerun update); structural change is migration-driven; updatability is per-layer.
  • adr-008-distribution-name.md — distribution name: PyPI boilerplate is taken by a same-niche tool; publish the dist as boilerplate-cli, keep boilerplate as the command/repo/brand (Pending — may become boilerplate if the name is acquired).
  • adr-009-environment-provider-protocol.md — target: generalize Environment Provisioning into a provider protocol (proto is one kind, optional).
  • adr-010-profile.md — profiles are plain default-answer files (profile.toml riding Copier's overridable user_defaults= channel).
  • adr-011-structured-overlay-merge.md — proposed and deferred: deep-merge structured overlay fragments (<file>.overlay.toml) for downstream file customization; the 0.x releases ship without it.
  • adr-012-positioning.md — docs framing relative to Copier: foundation framing (pixi/hatch pattern), the public-signal evidence behind it, and its pre-launch, proxy-only epistemic status.
  • adr-013-interactivity-contract.md — stdin-TTY-gated prompting, fail-closed with named substitute flags, two-layer enforcement, no CI-env-var input-mode switching.
  • adr-014-deferred-task-execution.md — _tasks accumulate across layers and run once on the final layer against the completed project, in Copier's native task shapes.
  • adr-015-idiomatic-artifacts.md — idiomatic artifacts, orchestrated engine: a composed project is Copier on disk (per-layer answers files); compose and boilerplate update both run each layer through its scoped view (the layer plus its ancestors), and a hand-run vanilla copier update per layer is the escape hatch.
  • adr-016-project-vocabulary.md — proposed: the vocabulary is one ontology in CONTEXT.md, in modules with namespaces, each entry with the same relation lines and each concept kept apart from the file that stores it; concept files and automated checks follow when sweeps keep finding drift.
  • adr-017-build-backend.md — build backend: the project template offers uv_build (default, its version range moved with the streamlit Dockerfile's uv tag) and hatchling; a before-update migration keeps existing projects on hatchling; the full when-to-choose table covers nine backends.
  • dev-environment-landscape.md — the reference taxonomy of development-environment slots, and the slots a first-party template fills for its dev loop, one opinionated pick per slot.
  • Intentions register — the tracked outcomes (INT-XXX) that design decisions and roadmap items cite by ID. The product definition those documents cite as PROD-001 (enforcement_layers, shipped_gating_scaffolding, candidate_scope) has no rendered page; it is the YAML source docs/products/PROD-001.yaml, linked from the register's "Source of truth" section.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Every passage is either a normative requirement — it constrains observable behavior or a persisted artifact, stated as a testable MUST — or an implementation note explicitly marked non-normative ("a conforming implementation MAY…").
  • Rationale prose survives only where it guards a correctness trap (e.g. PEP 440 pre-release ordering). Justification of arbitrary-but-fine choices was deliberately removed: a missing "why" is intentional — argumentation belongs in an ADR, not the spec body.
  • Scope boundaries are negative requirements ("Reserved for Phase 4" = MUST NOT do now). They are load-bearing, not stubs.
  • An ADR states the current decision. When the decision changes, the ADR is rewritten in place under the same number, and its history lives in git. An ADR carries no dates in its header, no superseded markers, no amendment sections and no record of earlier positions.
  • Rules were once labeled with INV_* identifiers; the labels were stripped (verified unreferenced in code, tests, and the PRD) and every rule survives in place as a plain MUST. Do not reintroduce an invariant-naming scheme; historical INV_* citations refer to rules that still exist. The §03 create-path lock rule and §06 update-path lock rule are deliberately separate requirements, not duplicates to merge.

This directory is served as part of the boilerplate documentation site (mkdocs) and is also the authoritative source for the implementer-facing spec — see 01-overview.md.

docs.title: What Boilerplate solves
docs.text:
Python projects accumulate friction at four points:

  • Environment drift — tools, versions, and configurations diverge across machines and contributors.
  • Configuration sprawl — every new project re-discovers and re-wires linter, formatter, type-checker, and test-runner settings.
  • Onboarding friction — new contributors spend hours on setup before their first commit.
  • Inconsistent toolchains — no team-level authority decides which tools and versions win.

These problems compound at organizational scale, where dozens of repositories each accumulate their own configuration debt.

docs.title: What Boilerplate is
docs.text:
A catalog of golden paths, Python first. Each derived template is one kind of project done the textbook way — a Typer CLI, a Streamlit or React web app, an MCP server — on a base layer its ecosystem shares, which carries the common standards. A template brings the toolchain its kind of project needs, secondary ones included (a containerized app declares Docker); patterns with a marked place for your code; and its ecosystem's published standards, the PEPs for Python. The environment installs and verifies what the template declares, so a secondary toolchain needs no setup script of its own. Templates compose by extends, and a project created from them updates layer by layer as the templates move.

Start fast. Stay consistent. Reproduce anywhere.

Boilerplate has two surfaces:

  • Managed development environment — the toolchain each template's profile declares (for Python: uv, ruff, pyright, pytest, and VS Code workspace settings), installed and version-pinned via boilerplate env apply.
  • CLI and template system — boilerplate new scaffolds a project from a curated template; boilerplate update applies upstream template changes to existing projects safely; boilerplate list and boilerplate compose make the catalog navigable.

The slot model. A development environment decomposes into recurring roles — slots — catalogued in The Development Environment Landscape. Each first-party template declares, through its required profile, the slots its kind of project needs, with one opinionated, preconfigured tool per slot:

  • Declared slots — the slots its ecosystem's dev loop uses, plus any secondary toolchain.
  • Slots within those slots — the template pre-wires each tool's per-project configuration (rule sets, strictness, markers, workspace settings).

The environment installs and verifies what the profile declares. Slots no first-party template requires are out of scope; the landscape page states the rule.

Principle enforcement spans two substrates: Boilerplate's runtime enforces its own invariants, and the artifacts it ships preconfigure principles as machine-checkable defaults. Per-layer assignments are specified in PROD-001 enforcement_layers; shipped vs planned gating content lives in PROD-001 shipped_gating_scaffolding.

Python first, with an extensible template system. The reference implementation is written in Python; most of the first-party catalog is Python, and first-party templates for other ecosystems (a React web app) follow their own ecosystem's standards the way the Python ones follow PEPs. The template system, composition engine, and CLI impose no language requirements on template content. Teams may author templates for any language or framework. PEP 440 is the default versioning standard; SemVer-compatible versions (e.g., 1.2.3) are valid PEP 440 and work without modification.

docs.title: When to use Copier directly
docs.text:
Boilerplate orchestrates Copier — it does not replace it. For some use cases, Copier alone is the right choice:

Use case Recommended tool Single template, no composition Copier Single-template projects — copier update covers their updates Copier Layered templates with extends chains Boilerplate Reproducible project creation with lock files Boilerplate Multi-layer template updates with three-way merge Boilerplate CI/CD drift detection (lock verify) Boilerplate Environment provisioning (env apply) Boilerplate

Existing Copier templates work with boilerplate new without modification — Boilerplate adds a boilerplate.yml metadata file alongside copier.yml but does not modify or replace it. The boilerplate.lock file is informational; if you stop using Boilerplate, your projects and their Copier answers files are untouched.

docs.title: Core Principles
docs.text: These principles are non-negotiable. Every implementation decision MUST honor them.

docs.title: Reproducibility is mandatory
docs.text:
Every created or managed project MUST be reproducible across machines and time. Lock files, pinned tool versions, and deterministic configuration are required at every stage. Changes that reduce determinism MUST be rejected.

Scope: Reproducibility is guaranteed at the project level via lock files — a locked project can be reconstructed identically. At the template declaration level, unversioned extends references (e.g., extends: [project]) resolve to the latest available version at resolution time, which may differ across invocations. The lock file captures the exact resolution, ensuring reproducibility from the point of creation forward.

docs.title: Templates and environments are both first-class surfaces
docs.text:
The template system is the primary surface; the managed development environment is a real companion surface, scoped to installing and verifying what templates declare. A change to one MUST keep the other aligned: a new CLI behavior that affects scaffolding MUST be reflected in template guidance; a new toolchain capability MUST be reflected in environment profiles; documentation MUST update alongside both.

In practice: boilerplate new and boilerplate env apply are independent operations, not phases of one workflow. Templates declare what gets rendered; profiles declare what tools render and run it. The first-party project template ships with both a boilerplate.yml (template surface) and a corresponding boilerplate-env.yml (environment surface).

docs.title: Safety-first operations
docs.text:
Operations that modify or remove existing managed state (update, add, env apply, eject) MUST preview the planned changes and require explicit user confirmation before applying. Operations that create or advance managed state MUST record provenance: project operations write a MigrationRecord, and env apply writes the EnvironmentProvisionRecord. eject removes that managed state and records nothing; recovery is to re-adopt.

Forward-looking (no current referent): Bulk operations MUST require confirmation.

In practice: boilerplate update, boilerplate add and boilerplate env apply display a plan and prompt for confirmation before applying changes. boilerplate new writes directly because creating a project into a new directory is not destructive. Provenance is recorded across two domains: MigrationRecord entries in .boilerplate/migrations.yml cover project-domain operations (create / update / add / adopt), and the EnvironmentProvisionRecord in .boilerplate/environment.yml records the last applied environment state (env apply).

docs.title: Atomic Staged Write Pattern and lock ownership
docs.text:
Template rendering MUST follow the Atomic Staged Write Pattern: render to a staging area, validate, then commit with no partial state left behind. On failure, the staging area MUST be cleaned up and the destination MUST remain untouched. The boilerplate.lock file is owned by Boilerplate and MUST be written only after a successful commit.

Platform caveat: Windows directory rename is not atomic; Boilerplate provides best-effort crash recovery (see 06-project-lifecycle.md).

docs.title: Environment lifecycle is managed
docs.text:
Boilerplate manages the toolchain across its full lifecycle — installation, version verification, updates, and cleanup — not just initial scaffolding. Environment setup operations MUST be idempotent (safe to re-run) and fail-fast (halt with diagnostic on error before partial work persists). Tools MUST be verified to exist and meet declared version requirements before any operation that depends on them proceeds.

In practice: boilerplate env apply re-runs deterministically — applying the same profile twice produces the same .protolock state. Tool-version checks happen before invocation, not lazily during; missing or mismatched tools fail with BP_ENV_* codes and remediation guidance, not with downstream subprocess errors.

docs.title: Orchestrate tools, do not replace them
docs.text:
Boilerplate MUST orchestrate established external tools (Copier, package managers, version checkers) instead of reimplementing their responsibilities. Ownership boundaries between Boilerplate and integrated tools MUST be explicit in every operation.

Boilerplate MUST use all of its underlying technologies idiomatically, as each technology's own documentation describes, and set the example of doing so. Where the design departs from a technology's idiom, it MUST name the departure and the reason. ADR-015 is the principle's worked instance.

docs.title: Versioning and compatibility
docs.text:
The Boilerplate tool itself follows Semantic Versioning 2.0.0. Breaking changes MUST be accompanied by a major version bump and documented migration path. Templates use PEP 440 — a SemVer-compatible superset that PEP 440 itself endorses for the MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (clauses 1-8) public-version part. Templates carry versions in this scheme and declare their compatibility constraints.

In practice: PEP 440 is the wire format (see §02 Version). Plain X.Y.Z versions are valid in both grammars and order identically; PEP 440 adds Python-ecosystem-specific syntax for pre-release (1.0a1), post-release (1.0.post1), dev (1.0.dev1), and epoch (1!2.0) identifiers — those identifiers MUST be expressed in PEP 440 form (not SemVer's 1.0.0-alpha.1 / 1.0.0+abc forms) because the two grammars order incompatibly outside the X.Y.Z subset. Lock files record exact resolved versions so updates are explicit, never silent.

docs.title: Standards compliance in first-party templates
docs.text: First-party (official) Python templates MUST conform to the relevant Python Enhancement Proposals for every pattern they implement. This includes but is not limited to: PEP 440 (versioning), PEP 508 (dependency specifiers), PEP 517/518 (build system), PEP 621 (project metadata in pyproject.toml), PEP 660 (editable installs), and PEP 723 (inline script metadata). When a PEP defines the canonical way to do something, the template MUST use it — no custom conventions that duplicate or contradict a PEP. A first-party template for another ecosystem MUST conform to that ecosystem's published standards and MUST name them in its template guide. Third-party templates are not bound by this requirement, though they are encouraged to follow it.

docs.title: Trust-gated catalog federation
docs.text: Templates are sourced from a federated catalog. Trust is binary — a source is either trusted or untrusted — and behavioral, not cosmetic: it gates what a template MAY do (execute tasks, load Jinja2 extensions, install plugins), default-deny for untrusted code. Untrusted code requires explicit per-operation consent. The full model — the trusted/untrusted boundary, default-deny task gating, and consent gates — is specified in 03-template-system.md §Trust and Verification Levels.

docs.title: Security and privacy defaults
docs.text:
• No secrets in code, configuration, or logs. Use environment variables or a vault.
  • Validate and sanitize all external inputs at trust boundaries.
  • Redact personal data in logs.
  • Fail closed: errors MUST not leak sensitive internal details to the user.

See 10-security.md for the full security specification.

docs.title: Platform Portability
docs.text:
Boilerplate supports Windows, macOS, and Linux. See 07-operational-quality.md §Platform Portability for platform-specific rules and constraints.

Precedence policies: Boilerplate uses two distinct precedence rules in different contexts. Catalog registration uses first-wins: the first source to register a template name+version owns it — see 02-data-models.md §TemplateCatalog. Composition merging uses last-wins: later layers override earlier layers' values — see 04-composition-engine.md §Merge Rules.

Persisted artifacts (data models, the lock schema, merge and checksum semantics) are specified most carefully because they outlive any single implementation.

docs.title: System Boundaries and External Dependencies
docs.text:
This table covers cross-system boundaries — which tool owns which concern across Boilerplate's external integrations. For per-domain state-file inventories, see 06 §Project State Files (project domain) and 08 §State Files (environment domain).

Concern Owner Notes Template file rendering Copier Boilerplate orchestrates; Copier renders. See 04-composition-engine.md. Answer collection Copier Interactive or defaults mode Copier answers files (per-layer .copier-answers.<layer>.yml; singular .copier-answers.yml for legacy projects) Copier Boilerplate MUST NOT write or mutate these files boilerplate.lock Boilerplate Written after successful render commit Git submodule initialization Boilerplate Initialized recursively before Copier invocation Package / dependency resolution External package manager Out of scope for the core tool Environment toolchain management proto Boilerplate orchestrates; proto installs tools. See ADR-001. .prototools proto proto's native toolchain declaration; Boilerplate generates from merged profiles .protolock proto proto's native lock file recording exact tool versions and checksums; enabled by Boilerplate .boilerplate/environment.yml Boilerplate Records which profile was applied and the resolved extends chain Git initialization Git Boilerplate MAY invoke; does not own

docs.title: Feature Slices
docs.text:
The product is organized into five vertical slices, each independently deliverable.

Slice Name Acceptance Criteria CLI Commands Design Docs 001 Template Discovery list, graph, validate return correct results for first-party and filesystem templates list, graph, validate, test, cache warm 03, 05 002 Project Creation new renders multi-layer compositions atomically with lock file generation new, compose, init-template 02, 03, 04, 05, 06 003 Project Update & Adoption update performs three-way merge; add applies one more template layer to a managed project; adopt imports Copier-only projects; eject stops Boilerplate management (inverse of adopt) update, add, adopt, eject, status, lock verify 05, 06 004 Environment Profiles env apply provisions tools via proto and records the applied state; re-running env apply is the recovery path env apply, env status 08 005 Operational Quality doctor validates system health; structured logging and error codes operational doctor 07 — Developer Experience — — 05

See Implementation Status.

docs.title: Environment Profiles
docs.text: Declarative profiles (boilerplate-env.yml) pin the development toolchain per project and compose via extends. Boilerplate resolves the chain and writes .prototools (proto's native input); proto installs tools and writes .protolock (exact versions + checksums). Boilerplate writes .boilerplate/environment.yml for profile provenance. Same "orchestrate, don't replace" pattern as Copier — see ADR-001. Operational contract: §08 Environment Provisioning.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                CLI                                   │
│  Project:  new | update | add | status | adopt | eject               │
│  Template: list | compose | graph | validate | test | init-template  │
│  System:   doctor | env | lock | cache                               │
└───────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                │ commands invoke
               ┌────────────────▼────────────────┐
               │        Application Layer         │
               │  Resolver  Composer  Render       │
               │  Updater   Profiler               │
               └───────┬────────────────┬─────────┘
                       │                │
          Templates                Environment Provisioning
                       │                │
    ┌──────────────────▼───────┐  ┌─────▼──────────────────┐
    │      Template Catalog    │  │    ProfileCatalog       │
    │  TemplateCatalog         │  │  (profile index)        │
    │  (in-memory index)       │  └─────┬──────────────────┘
    └──────────────────┬───────┘        │ delegates to
                       │          ┌─────▼──────────────────┐
                       │          │      ProtoWorker        │
         populated by  │          │  (orchestrates proto)   │
                       │          └─────┬──────────────────┘
    ┌──────────────────▼───────┐        │ invokes
    │    Template Repository   │  ┌─────▼──────────────────┐
    │  DirectoryTemplateRepository │  │    proto (external)     │
    │  RemoteSource            │  │  tool install & manage  │
    └──────────────────┬───────┘  └────────────────────────┘
                       │ reads
    ┌──────────────────▼───────┐
    │   Template Files on Disk │
    │  boilerplate.yml         │
    │  copier.yml | src        │
    └──────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Layer responsibilities
docs.text:
CLI — Parses user input, bootstraps the runtime context (settings, logging, display), dispatches to application services, and renders output. The CLI MUST NOT contain business logic.

Application Layer — Contains all domain logic: resolving dependency graphs, merging configurations, orchestrating renders, computing update plans, and managing profiles.

Template Catalog — An in-memory index populated at startup from one or more repositories. Provides lookup by canonical tag (name@version) and by name (resolves to latest).

Template Repository — Discovers and loads templates from a source (local directory, remote registry). Produces TemplateInfo records for catalog registration.

Template Files — The on-disk artifacts. Each template MUST contain a boilerplate.yml (Boilerplate metadata) and a copier.yml (Copier questionnaire). Templates MAY extend other templates via boilerplate.yml.

docs.title: Runtime Configuration (Settings)
docs.text: The runtime is configured by a Settings object loaded from environment variables and an optional .env file. See 09-settings-and-configuration.md for the complete Settings specification, including all fields, env var names, types, and defaults, and for the boilerplate-sources.yml configuration file.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Core terms used throughout this document suite. For data model details see 02-data-models.md; for composition details see 04-composition-engine.md. Canonical definitions live in CONTEXT.md at the repository root.

Target-state vocabulary

These definitions describe the design. Implementation status records which parts exist today.

docs.title: core
docs.text:
Concepts every module uses.

Copier · core:Copier The external tool (Copier) responsible for file rendering, answer collection, and task execution. Boilerplate orchestrates Copier without replacing it.

  • Related: core:Template, core:Question, composition:AnswersFile, composition:RenderEngine, customization:Task
  • Defined in: src/boilerplate/integrations/copier_types.py (the single audited import point for the Copier internals Boilerplate uses)
  • See: docs/design/adr-001-build-vs-adopt.md; docs/design/adr-002-copier-internals-shim.md

Template · core:Template A directory containing boilerplate.yml (name, version, extends) and copier.yml that boilerplate renders into a project — a Copier scaffold. Its filesystem location is the template root.

  • Related: core:Copier, core:Question, core:TemplateSpecifier, composition:Layer, customization:Task, model:StarterTemplates, model:GoldenPath
  • Stored in: boilerplate.yml, Boilerplate-specific metadata (name, version, and dependencies through extends), and copier.yml, Copier's questionnaire (questions and tasks), both at the template root, for example src/boilerplate/templates/project/boilerplate.yml and src/boilerplate/templates/project/copier.yml. Copier owns copier.yml; Boilerplate reads it and MUST NOT write to it.
  • Defined in: src/boilerplate/models/template_meta.py (TemplateMeta, the boilerplate.yml schema), src/boilerplate/models/template_info.py
  • See: design 02 §TemplateMeta; design 03 §boilerplate.yml Schema
  • Avoid: generator, skeleton, blueprint
  • Carve-out: "template skeleton" names the init-template command's scaffold output, not this term.
  • Matches: template, in Copier's documentation (close: Copier's template is a directory, usually a Git repository's root, with an optional copier.yml; a Template here also carries boilerplate.yml)
