Reads the project's Copier answers file(s) — either Copier's default singular .copier-answers.yml (legacy projects) or per-layer .copier-answers.<layer>.yml files (projects scaffolded from Boilerplate-enabled templates that declare _answers_file:) — resolves the template in the catalog, writes boilerplate.lock, and initializes .boilerplate/migrations.yml. The project's files are not modified — only Boilerplate state files are added.

Arguments:

Argument Required Description project-dir No Path to the project directory (defaults to .)

Options:

Option Short Type Default Description --dry-run -n flag false Show what would be written without making changes. Default: false. --format — enum table Output format: table, json. Default: table.

Preconditions:

  • The project directory MUST contain at least one Copier answers file — either Copier's default singular .copier-answers.yml or one or more per-layer .copier-answers.<layer>.yml files (Copier-managed project)
  • The project directory MUST NOT contain a boilerplate.lock file (not already adopted). If boilerplate.lock already exists, exit with code 3 and the message: 'Project already managed by Boilerplate. Use boilerplate update instead.'
  • The template referenced by the discovered answers file(s) MUST be resolvable in the catalog. If the template has a boilerplate.yml (Boilerplate-compatible), the full composition chain is resolved. If it is a Copier-only template, a minimal lock file is written with a single layer.

Behavior: Reads the project's Copier answers file(s) (singular or per-layer; see 06-project-lifecycle.md §Project Adoption), resolves the template in the catalog, writes boilerplate.lock and .boilerplate/migrations.yml (with adopted status), and prints adoption summary with next steps.

Exit codes: 0 on success, 1 on failure (template not found, copier-answers unreadable), 3 on validation error (already adopted, no copier-answers found).

docs.title: eject
docs.text:
Usage: boilerplate eject [path] [options]

Stop Boilerplate lifecycle management of a project. This is the exact inverse of adopt: it removes the Boilerplate-owned management state and leaves all rendered project files in place. After ejecting, the directory is a plain Copier project (or plain files) — update, status, and lock verify no longer apply, but the project is otherwise untouched.

Arguments:

Argument Required Description path No Path to the project directory (defaults to .)

Options:

Option Short Type Default Description --yes -y flag false Skip the confirmation prompt. Default: false. --dry-run -n flag false List what would be removed without changing anything. Default: false. --format — enum table Output format: table, json. Default: table.

What is removed (Boilerplate-owned artifacts only):

  • boilerplate.lock
  • The entire .boilerplate/ directory (e.g., migrations.yml, and environment.yml if present)

What is kept (not owned by Boilerplate):

  • The Copier answers files (.copier-answers.<layer>.yml, or the legacy singular .copier-answers.yml) — these are Copier-owned, so an ejected project can still be managed as a plain Copier project.
  • All rendered project files.
  • .prototools and any proto-installed tools. eject NEVER touches proto state. Tool teardown is proto's job: the proto install store is shared across projects, so removing it on one project's behalf is unsafe. Use proto directly to remove tools.

Behavior:

  • Confirmation: Because it deletes management state, the default (interactive) invocation prints a summary of what will be removed and prompts Proceed? [y/N] (see Confirmation Contracts). --yes/-y (or the global --ci, which implies --yes) skips the prompt; the summary is still printed to the operator log.
  • Idempotent: eject is a no-op only when neither boilerplate.lock nor .boilerplate/ is present (env apply can create .boilerplate/environment.yml with no lock, so the check keys on both). When the project has neither, eject emits a warning ("No Boilerplate management state found; nothing to eject.") and exits 0. When either is present, it removes both boilerplate.lock (if any) and the entire .boilerplate/ directory.
  • Mutating operation: eject acquires the standard advisory mutex on the project before removing state (same rule as new, update, add, adopt, and env apply; see 06-project-lifecycle.md §Concurrency).
  • No recovery to stage: eject is a delete, not a staged write — there is nothing to roll back or resume. A user who ejected by mistake can re-adopt the project to regenerate boilerplate.lock and .boilerplate/migrations.yml from the existing Copier answers. eject reuses none of update's merge or backup machinery.

--dry-run: Prints the list of artifacts that would be removed and exits 0 without deleting anything or prompting.

Example:

$ boilerplate eject
This will stop Boilerplate management of ./my-service and remove:
  boilerplate.lock
  .boilerplate/ (migrations.yml)

Rendered files and .copier-answers.<layer>.yml are kept. proto tools are not touched.
Proceed? [y/N] y
Ejected my-service. To resume management later: boilerplate adopt .

Exit codes: 0 on success (including the idempotent no-op when neither boilerplate.lock nor .boilerplate/ is present), 1 on a filesystem or permission failure during removal (BP_FILESYSTEM_PERMISSION).

docs.title: test
docs.text:
Usage: boilerplate test <template-path> [options]

Run automated regression tests for a template using fixture directories. See §03 Template Testing for the fixture layout specification.

Arguments:

Argument Required Description template-path Yes Path to the template directory to test

Options:

Flag Short Description --fixture <name> — Run only the named fixture; also scopes --update-snapshots to the named fixture. Default: run all discovered fixtures. --update-snapshots — Overwrite expected/ directories with current render output. Default: false. See --update-snapshots notes below. --match <glob> — Only diff files matching the glob pattern against expected output (e.g., --match "pyproject.toml"). Non-matching files are ignored. --format {text\|json} — Output format. Default: text.

--update-snapshots notes: Use to create initial fixtures or update after intentional template changes. When combined with --fixture, only the named fixture's expected output is updated.

--match notes: Useful for large templates where only specific files need assertion (e.g., --match "src/**/*.py").

Fixture discovery: Scans {template-path}/tests/*/ for directories containing answers.yml. Each such directory is a fixture; the directory name is the fixture name.

Composition behavior: boilerplate test resolves the full composition chain (including extends dependencies) and renders the complete merged output. Base templates are resolved from configured sources. Use --templates-dir to include local base templates during development (e.g., boilerplate test ./my-template --templates-dir ./).

Test execution:

  1. For each fixture, resolve the full extends chain and render the composed template to a temp directory using answers.yml as pre-seeded answers (non-interactive, no tasks)
  2. Diff the rendered output against {template-path}/tests/{name}/expected/
  3. Report pass (no diff) or fail (unified diff per differing file)

Output: Per-fixture pass/fail with unified diff on failure. Summary line: N fixtures passed, M failed.

Exit codes: 0 = all fixtures passed; 1 = one or more fixtures failed; 2 = configuration error (template not found, fixture malformed).

Tip: Use boilerplate validate to check template structure before running tests. Use boilerplate new --render-to <dir> to inspect rendered output without creating a project.

docs.title: doctor
docs.text:
Usage: boilerplate doctor

Runs health checks and reports issues with remediation guidance.

Checks: Settings loadable, template directories exist, Copier available, Git available, catalog sources reachable, environment profiles valid, Windows core.longpaths enabled (Windows only), WSL2 proto binary not from Windows host (WSL2 only). In a project, doctor also reports each disagreement between a layer's answers file and boilerplate.lock (04 §Safe Update) and each layer whose answers file lacks the key of a question of its scoped view at the recorded versions that is neither secret nor hidden (04 §Safe Update defines hidden), as a hand-run update of the layer leaves it, and each such key that no layer records, naming the layer and the keys.

Output (unified check-result format):

Boilerplate Doctor

  PASS  Configuration loaded
  PASS  Default templates dir exists (14 templates)
  PASS  Extra templates dir /opt/team-templates exists (8 templates)
  PASS  Git available (2.44.0)
  PASS  Copier available (9.4.1)
  FAIL  Extra templates dir /opt/legacy-templates does not exist
        -> Check BOILERPLATE_EXTRA_TEMPLATE_DIRS in your configuration

6 checks: 5 passed, 0 warnings, 1 error

Uses the same PASS/WARN/FAIL format as validate and lock verify.

Exit codes: 0 all checks pass (warnings OK), 1 any check fails.

docs.title: init-template
docs.text:
Usage: boilerplate init-template <name> [directory]

Create a minimal template skeleton in the target directory. This is the template authoring entry point.

Arguments:

Argument Required Description name Yes Template name (must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_\-]+$) directory No Target directory (defaults to ./<name>/)

Behavior: Creates the target directory (if it does not exist) containing:

  • boilerplate.yml — minimal manifest with the provided name and version 0.1.0
  • copier.yml — minimal Copier configuration with a project_name question
  • {{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}.jinja — answer persistence file for Copier
  • A sample template file demonstrating variable substitution
  • tests/defaults/answers.yml — sample answer file for the default test fixture, pre-populated with project_name: "test-project" and a comment: # Run 'boilerplate test . --update-snapshots' to populate expected output.
  • tests/defaults/expected/ — empty directory for snapshot output (populated by --update-snapshots)

The generated skeleton provides a minimum viable template that renders successfully out of the box. Each generated file MUST include explanatory inline comments.

If the target directory already exists and contains a boilerplate.yml, the CLI MUST exit with code 3.

Exit codes: 0 on success, 3 on validation error (invalid name, directory already contains template).

docs.title: env
docs.text:
Manage environment profiles. The env group has one mutating subcommand (env apply, whose pipeline is owned by §08 Provisioning Pipeline) and one read-only inspector (env status). Each subcommand is documented below.

The <profile-spec> argument used by env apply follows the same name or name@version syntax as other template references. See Template Argument Resolution.

To recover from a failed or partial provisioning, re-run boilerplate env apply; provisioning is idempotent and converges to the profile's declared tool set.

For background on environment profiles as a concept, see Product overview (Environment Profiles).

docs.title: env apply
docs.text:
Apply an environment profile to the current project or directory.

boilerplate env apply [options] <profile-spec>

Arguments:

  • <profile-spec>: Profile name from the project's boilerplate.yml or a path to a standalone profile YAML file.

Options:

Flag Short Description --dry-run -n Display the provisioning plan without applying changes. Default: false. --yes -y Skip confirmation prompt. Default: false. --force -f Re-install tools even if the correct version is already present. Default: false.

Behavior: The full provisioning pipeline (resolve, plan, confirm, lock, stage, install, commit, record) is specified in §08 Provisioning Pipeline. env apply invokes that pipeline; the CLI surface adds only argument parsing, plan display, and confirmation handling on top.

Exit codes: 0 (success), 1 (provisioning failure), 3 (validation error). env apply does NOT produce exit code 4: per §08 Part 4 Stage 4, any installation failure triggers a full pipeline rollback to the pre-apply state, so there is no partial-install pause that requires user resolution. (For the resumable user-intervention pattern, see the update conflict pause: resolve, commit, rerun.)

docs.title: env status
docs.text:
Usage: boilerplate env status

Reports the current environment state by reading .boilerplate/environment.yml and .protolock.

Reports the current profile, applied timestamp, tool versions, and protolock integrity. If proto_lock_hash does not match the current .protolock, emits a WARNING.

Exit codes: 0 (informational, including warnings), 1 (error reading state files).

docs.title: lock verify
docs.text:
Usage: boilerplate lock verify

Verify that the current project state matches the lock file. Checks that template source checksums, commit hashes, and answer hashes are consistent. Intended for CI gates enforcing "no drift from template."

Checks:

Check Description Lock file parseable boilerplate.lock exists and parses correctly Schema version supported Lock file schema version is recognized. A lock whose major schema_version is newer than the tool supports is refused (fail closed). Template sources accessible Source paths/URLs for all layers are reachable Checksums match Template content checksums match lock file values Commits match Git commit hashes match lock file values (when source is a git repo) Answers hash match Each .copier-answers.<layer>.yml hash matches its entry in copier_answers_file_hashes

Checksum comparisons are computed in git's content sense (line endings normalized before hashing), not on raw bytes: Copier's git-based update rewrites line endings of otherwise-untouched files under core.autocrlf=true (ADR-015 §Verification), so a raw-byte comparison would report false drift.

Output (unified check-result format):

Verifying lock file integrity...

  PASS  Lock file parseable
  PASS  Schema version supported (boilerplate/lock@1)
  PASS  Template sources accessible
  PASS  Checksums match
  PASS  Commit hashes match
  FAIL  Answers hash mismatch
        -> A .copier-answers.<layer>.yml file has been modified since last update.
        -> Run: boilerplate update to reconcile.

6 checks: 5 passed, 0 warnings, 1 error

Uses the same PASS/WARN/FAIL format as validate and doctor.

Exit codes: 0 all checks pass, 1 any check fails (drift detected or verification error).

docs.title: cache warm
docs.text:
Usage: boilerplate cache warm [source-name]...

Pre-populate the local template cache from configured remote and archive sources. Useful for seeding CI build agents; the broader air-gapped story is an org-local clone or mirror of the published first-party repositories (ADR-006), not this command. A wheel-bundled seed cache remains deferred pending demonstrated demand.

Arguments:

Argument Required Description source-name No One or more source names to warm. If none provided, warms all configured remote and archive sources.

Options:

Option Short Type Default Description --force — flag false Re-download even if the cache is current. Default: false.

Behavior: For each targeted source, fetches the current template catalog and downloads template contents into the local cache. Already-cached and up-to-date sources are skipped unless --force is active. On completion, reports per-source status (cached templates count, time taken).

Exit codes: 0 = all sources warmed successfully; 1 = one or more sources failed (errors logged per source).

docs.title: config
docs.text: Reserved for surfacing the per-user profile (09 §Profile); no command surface is specified.

docs.title: Shell Completions
docs.text:
Shell completions are handled by Typer's built-in --install-completion and --show-completion flags. No custom completions command is provided.

boilerplate --install-completion    # Install completion for current shell
boilerplate --show-completion       # Show completion script

Completion targets:

Context Completions offered Top-level Command names new <TAB> Template names from the catalog new <template> <TAB> Directory paths add <TAB> Template names from the catalog compose <TAB>, graph <TAB>, validate <TAB> Template names from the catalog --format <TAB> table, json, yaml, tree, wide (context-dependent) --trust <TAB> trusted, untrusted --type <TAB> boilerplate-enabled, copier-only --section <TAB> final, layers, states, deltas, stats --category <TAB> Known category values from the cached catalog env apply <TAB> Profile names from the catalog

Template name completions are loaded from the cached catalog. If the cache is empty or stale, completions fall back to an empty list (no network calls during completion).

docs.title: Developer Experience Contracts
docs.text: The following contracts are cross-cutting. They apply to every command and workflow.

docs.title: Pipeline Narration
docs.text:
Boilerplate operations are multi-phase pipelines. Operations can take seconds to minutes. The user MUST see the pipeline progressing, not silence.

When stdout is a TTY:

Phase Output Resolution Resolving {template-ref}... followed by Resolved {n} layers Composition Composing {n} layers... Rendering Rendering layer {i}/{n}: {name}@{version}... per layer Lock Writing lock file... Post-tasks Running post-creation tasks...

Each phase line replaces the previous (single-line progress). On completion, a summary line:

Created my-project in 3.2s (2 layers, 47 files)

For updates:

Updated my-project in 5.1s (project 0.1.0 -> 0.2.0, streamlit 0.1.0 -> 0.1.1, 12 files changed)

When stdout is piped or --quiet is active: No progress output. The completion summary is still written to stderr unless --quiet is active.

docs.title: Confirmation Contracts
docs.text:
Destructive or high-impact operations MUST require confirmation.

Prompt format: The CLI MUST:

  1. Print a summary of what will happen (files modified, versions changed)
  2. Print the prompt: Proceed? [y/N]
  3. Default to No (capital N) — pressing Enter without input cancels
  4. Accept y, yes (case-insensitive) as confirmation; anything else cancels

--yes / -y flag: All commands that require confirmation MUST accept --yes / -y to bypass the prompt. When --yes is active, the summary is still printed (to the operator log), but the prompt is skipped.

When confirmation is required:

Trigger Command Summary content Any update (default behavior) update Update plan with version deltas and file impact Adding a layer (default behavior) add Add plan with the layer, its version, file impact, the layer's own tasks, the Jinja extensions its scoped view loads and what undo can and cannot reverse Environment provisioning env apply Tools to install/upgrade Stop management (state removal) eject Artifacts to remove (boilerplate.lock, .boilerplate/)

Note: --force on new does NOT trigger confirmation — force implies consent. The --yes flag bypasses confirmation on update, add, env apply, and eject.

All update, add, env apply, and eject invocations show a plan and prompt for confirmation by default. --dry-run suppresses the prompt (plan only). --yes suppresses the prompt (plan + apply).

docs.title: Post-Action Guidance
docs.text:
After completing an operation, the CLI MUST print contextual next steps. Guidance sources, in display order:

  1. Default: Always cd {destination}. uv sync follows it only when the template's setup tasks were skipped (--no-tasks); otherwise the tasks already installed dependencies and Next steps lists only what is left to do.
  2. Profile-derived: If the template declares requires_profile, include boilerplate env apply.
  3. Template-declared (printed after new only, per 03 §post_create_message): post_create_message from boilerplate.yml, accumulated from all layers in topological order, labeled "From the template author:".
  4. Tip: block: Hint that the template's answers file is a ready-made answer preset for CI reproducibility. Printed only when the root template's .copier-answers.<template>.yml exists in the destination, and suppressed when --data-file or --ci was used.

Template-declared guidance is informational only — MUST NOT execute automatically.

Example (new):

Created my-project in 3.2s (2 layers, 47 files)

Next steps:
  cd my-project

From the template author:
  This template uses FastAPI. Start the dev server with:
  uvicorn src.main:app --reload

Tip: Reuse these answers in CI:
  boilerplate new fastapi my-other-project --data-file my-project/.copier-answers.fastapi.yml --non-interactive

After add: Show the layer added and the changed files list, then "Next steps:" (git diff, review, commit). The result is uncommitted. When the layer runs no tasks, or --no-tasks is active, Next steps also lists uv sync.

After update: Show changed files list, then "Next steps:" (git diff, uv sync, uv run pytest). uv sync is always listed, because the project template's setup task runs only when Copier copies, so an update does not install dependencies. When conflicts are present, "Action required:" replaces "Next steps:" with resolution instructions (resolve and commit, then rerun boilerplate update, or set the partial update aside).

docs.title: Answer Presets
docs.text:
An answer preset is a YAML file, passed to --data-file, that supplies answers to template questions declaratively, enabling reproducible project creation in CI/CD pipelines and scripts.

CLI flags (available on new, update, and add), Copier's own names and short flag:

Option Short Type Description --data <key=value> -d string Forced answer for one question (repeatable) --data-file <path> — path YAML file mapping question name to forced answer

Both flags feed Copier's data channel: a forced answer is never prompted for.

Precedence: --data > --data-file > profile pre-fills (new), the recorded answer (update) or an ancestor layer's recorded answer (add) > template default. Prefer --data-file for structured, multi-field, or cross-platform scenarios; use --data for simple scalar overrides.

Answer preset format:

# answers.yml
project_name: "my-service"
description: "Order processing microservice"
dependencies:
  - fastapi
  - pydantic
author_name: "Platform Team"

Behavior:

  • If --data-file or --data is provided without --non-interactive, the user is prompted for questions NOT supplied (partial answers)
  • If --data-file or --data is provided WITH --non-interactive, questions not supplied take the next source in the precedence order (a profile pre-fill on new, or the recorded answer on update and add, then the declared default); a question with none of these stops the run with BP_INPUT_ANSWERS_MISSING
  • --data-file skips underscore-prefixed keys (Copier directives) with a one-line warning that names the skipped keys, so a Copier answers file is accepted as a preset; an underscore-prefixed key in --data is an error
  • A key that is not a string, or is empty, fails fast
  • Answer presets MUST be pure data (YAML maps). No Jinja2 expressions, no executable content.

The template's answers file is a preset: new takes one template, and that template's .copier-answers.<template>.yml records its own and every ancestor's answers (ADR-015 point 4), so when the template ships the answers-file stub (04 §Render Behavior), the root template's file (the template named on new, not any layer's file) that a finished new leaves in the project is a complete preset. Answers to questions marked secret: true are the exception: Copier does not record them, so supply them again as 10 §Privacy describes.

docs.title: Interactive Prompting Contract
docs.text:
Boilerplate delegates prompting to Copier, but composition means the user faces a merged questionnaire from multiple layers.

Principles:

  1. One pass: The user answers all questions once, on the first layer. Subsequent layers reuse answers silently.
  2. No surprises: The merged questionnaire is the union of all layers' questions. The user sees one flat list, not a per-layer interrogation.
  3. Validation is immediate: If a question declares choices, Copier validates the answer before moving to the next question. Invalid input is re-prompted.
  4. Partial answers merge cleanly: When --data-file or --data provides some values and the mode is interactive, only unanswered questions are prompted. Answered questions are shown as a summary before prompting begins:
Using supplied answers:
  project_name: "my-service"
  author_name: "Platform Team"

Remaining questions:
  description [A new Python project.]: _

Questionnaire ordering: Questions from base templates first (in topological order, dependencies before dependents), then questions contributed by the root template. Within each group, declaration order from copier.yml is preserved.

docs.title: Output Display
docs.text:
Message type When used info Informational progress and results success Confirmation of a completed operation error Failure condition; always to stderr warning Non-fatal issue the user should know about

Errors MUST be printed to stderr. All other output MUST go to stdout. This ensures shell pipelines work correctly.

docs.title: Terminal vs. Pipe Detection
docs.text:
The CLI MUST detect whether stdout is a terminal. When outputting to a pipe or file:

  • No color codes
  • No progress spinners
  • Plain text only

When outputting to a terminal, rich formatting (color, tables, tree) is permitted.

docs.title: Quiet Mode
docs.text:
When --quiet is active, the command MUST produce no output to stdout under any normal condition. Only error messages (to stderr) are permitted. Help still prints for --help, or when no command is given, but without the banner; --version still prints the version.

Interaction with --format json: --quiet and --format json are mutually exclusive. If both are provided, the CLI MUST exit with code 3 (VALIDATION_ERROR) and the message: Cannot combine --quiet (suppress output) with --format json (structured output). Use --format json without --quiet for machine-readable output, or --quiet without --format for silent operation.

docs.title: Verbose Mode
docs.text:
When --verbose is active:

  • Debug-level log messages are printed
  • Debug info about resolution, composition, and rendering steps is logged

--verbose controls log verbosity only. To expand the list output columns, use --format wide.

docs.title: Terminal Accessibility
docs.text:
This section defines the universal accessibility contract for all CLI output. Individual command sections inherit these rules; per-command accessibility notes (e.g., graph tree rendering) supplement but do not override them.

  1. NO_COLOR contract: When the NO_COLOR environment variable is set (to any value), the CLI MUST NOT emit ANSI escape codes or Unicode characters outside the printable ASCII range (U+0020–U+007E). This applies to all output: errors, progress, check results, tree rendering, and table formatting. The --color never flag has the same effect.

  2. Color is never the sole differentiator: All status indicators MUST use text labels (PASS, WARN, FAIL, Modified, Added, Removed, Conflict) that carry meaning independently of color. Color is a supplementary enhancement in TTY mode, not the primary signal. This ensures usability for users with color vision deficiencies (e.g., deuteranopia).

  3. Progress output: When stdout is not a TTY, or when NO_COLOR is set, progress output MUST use append mode (newline-terminated lines). Carriage-return overwrite (\r) MUST NOT be used in these contexts, as it is hostile to screen readers and log file consumers.

  4. --color flag: The --color auto|always|never global flag provides explicit control over color output. auto (default) uses TTY detection and respects NO_COLOR. always forces color on (useful when piping to less -R). never forces color off. When --color is provided, it takes precedence over NO_COLOR.

  5. BOILERPLATE_ACCESSIBLE environment variable: When enabled, activates all accessibility accommodations as a single toggle. It follows the same truthiness rule as the other BOILERPLATE_* boolean env vars (see the environment variable equivalents note in Global Options): the value is trimmed of surrounding whitespace, then enabled when the trimmed value is non-empty and not 0 or false (case-insensitive). Equivalent to setting NO_COLOR=1 plus: append-mode progress (no carriage-return overwrite), PASS/WARN/FAIL text labels (no Unicode symbols), no banner, and TERM=dumb-compatible output. This variable exists so that screen reader users and accessibility-focused workflows can enable the full suite of accommodations without remembering individual settings. When BOILERPLATE_ACCESSIBLE is active, --color auto resolves to never.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
All CLI commands MUST handle BoilerplateError subclasses by:

  1. Printing a human-readable error message to stderr
  2. Exiting with the appropriate exit code per 02-data-models.md §Error Hierarchy

Each exception type maps to one or more stable BP_* error codes defined in Operational quality. The exception hierarchy is the implementation mechanism; the BP_* codes are the stable public contract surfaced to the user. Unrecognized exceptions outside the BoilerplateError hierarchy MUST exit with code 1 (FAILURE).

Errors MUST NOT leak internal stack traces to the user by default. When --verbose is active, additional context MAY be shown.

docs.title: Exit Code Reference
docs.text: Exit codes are defined in Data models. Scripts SHOULD treat exit code 4 (ACTION_REQUIRED) as distinct from failure — it means user intervention is needed (e.g., merge conflict resolution).

docs.title: Flag Reference Summary
docs.text:
The following table summarizes flag availability across commands. Global flags (--verbose, --quiet, --help, --version, --templates-dir, --format, --offline) apply to all commands and are omitted from this table.

Flag new update add adopt eject list compose graph validate status doctor init-template test env lock cache --force X X X --non-interactive X X X --skip-answered X --dry-run / -n X X X X X X --data / -d (repeatable) X X X --data-file X X X --no-tasks X X X --allow-extensions X X X --allow-tasks X X X --allow-untrusted X X X --template-source X X --yes / -y X X X X X --git-init X --render-to X --target-version / -t X --category X --tag (repeatable) X --trust X --type X --all-versions X --include-archived X --source X --refresh X --questions / -Q X --section (repeatable) X --all X --stats X --output / -o X --tree X --strict X --fixture X --match X --update-snapshots X

Short flag assignment: -f is assigned to --force (on new and env apply), matching universal CLI convention (rm -f, cp -f, docker rm -f). --format uses long-form only.

docs.title: Constraints and Invariants
docs.text:
1. Every command that runs longer than 1 second MUST show progress when stdout is a TTY.
  2. Every command MUST support --format json for machine-readable output.
  3. Every destructive or high-impact action MUST support --yes / -y to bypass confirmation.
  4. Post-action guidance MUST be informational only — never auto-execute commands on the user's behalf.
  5. Shell completions MUST NOT make network calls.
  6. doctor and status MUST NOT modify any state.
  7. validate MUST work without a project context (it validates a template directory, not a project).
  8. Answer presets MUST be pure data (YAML maps). No Jinja2 expressions, no executable content.
  9. --force and --non-interactive are independent. Neither implies the other.
  10. Destination for new MUST be explicit or interactively prompted. No implicit defaults.

docs.title: CI/CD Quick Reference
docs.text:
Common invocation patterns for automated environments:

Scenario Command Create project, no interaction boilerplate new template dest --ci Create project, no interaction, env var instead of a flag (POSIX shells) BOILERPLATE_CI=1 boilerplate new template dest Create project, no interaction, env var instead of a flag (PowerShell) $env:BOILERPLATE_CI = "1"; boilerplate new template dest Create with answers file boilerplate new template dest --ci --data-file answers.yml Create from an untrusted source, tasks allowed boilerplate new template dest --ci --allow-tasks Update project boilerplate update --ci Add a template layer boilerplate add template --ci Validate template boilerplate validate ./my-template/ JSON output for scripting boilerplate list --format json Dry-run update boilerplate update --dry-run --format json

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This document specifies the lifecycle of a Boilerplate-managed project: creation, update, layer addition, adoption, and ejection — covering workflows, lock file management, staging, and migration records.

docs.title: Project State Files
docs.text:
A Boilerplate-managed project contains the following state files after creation:

File Owner Purpose boilerplate.lock Boilerplate Records exact versions, commit hashes, and checksums of all template layers used .copier-answers.<layer>.yml Copier One file per template layer; records answers collected during interactive prompting for that layer. Each first-party template declares its file via _answers_file: (see 04-composition-engine.md §Render Behavior). .boilerplate/migrations.yml Boilerplate Append-only audit log of all update operations (project domain)

Environment-domain state files (.boilerplate/environment.yml) are documented in §08 State Files.

Ownership invariants: - Boilerplate MUST NOT write to any .copier-answers.<layer>.yml file (one per template layer). Those files are owned by Copier. - External tools MUST NOT write to boilerplate.lock. That file is owned by Boilerplate. - boilerplate.lock MUST only be written after a fully successful operation (creation or update). It MUST never reflect a partial state.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
The universal advisory-lock rule and timeout default are defined in 07-operational-quality.md §Concurrency Control. It applies to every mutating Boilerplate operation: new, update, add, adopt, eject, env apply. Project-domain specifics:

  • Lock target (existing project): a boilerplate-operation.lock file in the project's git directory, at the path git rev-parse --git-path boilerplate-operation.lock prints, so each worktree of the project has its own lock. The target is not boilerplate.lock for two reasons: Boilerplate writes that file by replacing it with a renamed file, which Windows refuses on a file the operation holds open, and a lock file inside the working tree would dirty the tree and fail the clean-tree check. A project that is not a git repository uses the new target below.
  • Lock target (new): a .boilerplate-lock-{destination_name} file created in the destination's parent directory. The file is created if absent and removed after the new operation completes.

Network filesystem detection: boilerplate doctor MUST detect and warn when the project directory or staging root resides on a network filesystem (advisory file locking is unreliable there; see §07 Network Filesystems).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Project creation takes a template reference, resolves its full dependency graph, composes a merged configuration, renders each template layer atomically into a destination directory, and writes boilerplate.lock.

docs.title: Creation Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Resolve   →  Dependency graph from boilerplate.yml extends chains
2. Compose   →  Merge configurations from all layers
3. Render    →  Atomic: stage → copy → verify → commit
4. Lock      →  Write boilerplate.lock after successful commit
5. Init      →  Append initial MigrationRecord to .boilerplate/migrations.yml (status: created)

docs.title: Step 1: Template Resolution
docs.text:
Resolve the template reference via the catalog and traverse the extends chain to build the full dependency graph. See Composition engine for the resolution algorithm and graph validation.

Version constraint resolution: Template references resolve to either the latest version (unversioned "name") or an exact version ("name@version"). See the Resolver's template lookup behavior described in Composition engine.

docs.title: Step 2: Composition
docs.text:
• Extract copier.yml configuration from each template in topological order
  • Merge configurations using the CopierConfigMerger (see Composition engine)
  • Produce an immutable CompositionArtifact

docs.title: Step 3: Atomic Staged Write
docs.text:
This step follows the Atomic Staged Write Pattern. Project-creation specifics:

  • Intent journal name: .boilerplate-commit-intent.json, written in the staging directory.
  • Phase enum: staging, committing, locking (recovery rules in §02 IntentJournal).
  • Stale-staging window: 1 hour, owner-checked (POSIX UID match; Windows ACL full-control check).
  • Recovery rule: on failure or signal, delete staging and leave destination untouched.

Project-specific invariants beyond the shared pattern:

  • Git submodules MUST be initialized recursively before YAML parsing. Failure aborts with BP_RENDER_SUBMODULE_FAILED.
  • Layers are rendered in topological order (dependencies first). Later layers completely override earlier layers for files at the same path (no content merging).
  • Answers are collected once on the first layer; subsequent layers reuse them. Tasks run on the final layer only.
  • After tasks execute, path safety validation MUST re-run on staging contents (closes the TOCTOU window for malicious tasks). This applies to both standard rendering and --render-to.
  • The commit phase moves staging to destination. With --force, the existing destination is backed up first. On Windows, directory rename is not atomic — best-effort crash safety only.

docs.title: Staging cleanup on retry
docs.text:
On retry, the staging directory and its intent journal MUST be completely removed and recreated before the next attempt. Retrying into a staging directory with partial output could produce corrupted results.

File overlay semantics: File overlay follows the composition engine's full-file replacement rule. See 04-composition-engine.md §Managing Shared Files Across Layers. Layers are rendered in topological order; later layers completely replace earlier layers' files at the same path.

docs.title: Step 4: Lock File Generation
docs.text:
After a successful commit, write boilerplate.lock to the project root. See Data models for the full BoilerplateLock schema and invariants.

The lock file records the following per layer: name, version, source, commit (git SHA or null), and checksum (SHA-256 of template source directory content). It also records schema_version, boilerplate_version, copier_version, root_template, copier_answers_file_hashes (the per-layer answers-file hashes), and timestamps. See Data models for the full BoilerplateLock schema.

Key concepts:

  • checksum fields use "sha256:{hex}" prefix format (forward-compatible with future algorithms). The per-layer copier_answers_file_hashes values use bare hex (always SHA-256 by definition).
  • Checksums are computed over all files in the template source directory content (excluding .git/, __pycache__/, .mypy_cache/, .pytest_cache/, .ruff_cache/, node_modules/), sorted lexicographically by relative path, concatenating path and content. This list is fixed and MUST NOT depend on .gitignore. Template authors MAY declare additional exclusions via checksum_excludes in boilerplate.yml (see Data models). See Data models for the authoritative checksum computation specification.
  • Each layer MAY include optional bundle_uri and bundle_checksum fields. These are air-gap / enterprise restoration fields, populated by external catalog infrastructure (not Boilerplate itself) and not part of the core provenance contract. The wheel_bundle source type and its source_bundle / subdirectory lock fields are deferred with the seed cache they support (ADR-006); layers sourced from the published first-party repositories record null for both.

docs.title: Lock File Recovery
docs.text:
If boilerplate.lock is corrupted (unparseable YAML, truncated write, invalid schema version), Boilerplate MUST:

  1. Fail with BP_LOCK_READ_FAILED and remediation guidance: "Lock file is corrupted. To recreate: delete boilerplate.lock and run 'boilerplate new <template> . --force' to regenerate from the current project state."
  2. NOT attempt automatic repair — the lock file records provenance data (commit hashes, checksums) that cannot be reconstructed from the project alone.
  3. The status command MUST report lock file corruption as a top-level diagnostic.

Prevention: Lock files MUST be written atomically (temp file + rename) so interrupted writes cannot leave a partial file.

docs.title: Lock File Versioning
docs.text:
The schema_version field ("boilerplate/lock@1") enables forward-compatible evolution. Boilerplate MUST parse any lock file whose schema version shares the same major version (e.g., boilerplate/lock@1 through boilerplate/lock@1.x). Minor version bumps add optional fields; major bumps may change semantics.

A lock whose schema_version major exceeds the major the running tool supports MUST be refused (fail closed). The tool MUST NOT read from or mutate a lock from a newer schema generation; on encountering one it MUST fail closed with a clear error (BP_LOCK_SCHEMA_UNSUPPORTED): "This project was created with a newer version of Boilerplate. Please upgrade." It MUST NOT silently ignore the version mismatch or attempt to partially parse the newer schema. This guards every lock-reading operation (update, status, lock verify).

docs.title: Step 5: Project State Initialization
docs.text: After the lock file is written: 1. Append the initial MigrationRecord to .boilerplate/migrations.yml with status: created (the audit log's first entry; id: "1", from_version: null, to_version: <root template specifier>, classification: null). The file is created with this record as its only entry — no separate "empty initialization" step. The created record is the project-creation provenance entry required by §01 Safety-first operations. 2. Initialize a git repository if --git-init is specified (see CLI reference)

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text: Scenario Expected Outcome Valid single template Template rendered, boilerplate.lock written, exit 0 Valid composed template All layers rendered in order, lock includes all layers, exit 0 Template not found DependencyNotFoundError, no output written, exit 1 Circular dependency DependencyCycleError with full cycle path, exit 1 Non-empty destination without --force DestinationNotEmptyError, exit 3 Rendering fails mid-stream Staging deleted, destination untouched, exit 1 Same inputs repeated with --force Bit-identical output (idempotent), exit 0

docs.title: Performance Contracts
docs.text: See Operational quality for all performance targets.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Project update takes an existing Boilerplate project (with boilerplate.lock), resolves the new target template version, computes what changed, applies a three-way merge to preserve local modifications, writes a new lock file, and appends a migration record.

Safety model: Update computes a plan, displays it to the user, and prompts for confirmation (Proceed? [y/N]) before applying. --dry-run prints the plan and exits without prompting. --yes skips the prompt and applies immediately. See CLI reference for the full CLI contract.

docs.title: Pre-Flight Check
docs.text:
Before starting the update pipeline, Boilerplate MUST run these checks in order:

  1. The project is a git repository root with at least one commit.
  2. Take the operation lock (07 §Concurrency Control). Every check below runs inside the lock, so no second Boilerplate operation interleaves with a check.
  3. Run the restore-marker rules. A cut-off run's marker is finished (and the command then ends), discarded or reported before anything reads the working tree, which that run may have left dirty. When the ref refs/worktree/boilerplate/restore exists and the marker does not, a crash fell between the two steps of the copy back's bracketing; remove the ref (git update-ref -d) and continue.
  4. The project has no uncommitted changes, untracked files included. This is Copier's own rule: Copier refuses to update a project whose git status --porcelain is not empty.
  5. The project has no submodules (a .gitmodules file). Otherwise Boilerplate MUST stop with BP_UPDATE_SUBMODULES_UNSUPPORTED and exit code 3, naming the submodule paths, because git's worktree documentation says multiple checkouts of a superproject are not recommended (git-worktree).

When check 1 or check 4 fails, Boilerplate MUST fail immediately with BP_UPDATE_PROJECT_NOT_READY and exit code 3. Check 1 reports "Not a git repository root with at least one commit." and check 4 reports "Working tree has uncommitted changes. Commit them, or run 'git reset' and then 'git stash --include-untracked', before running boilerplate update." update has no override; the tree is clean, or the update does not start.

docs.title: Update Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Load     →  Read boilerplate.lock + each layer's .copier-answers.<layer>.yml
2. Resolve  →  Resolve each layer's target version
3. Plan     →  Compute UpdatePlan (diff old vs new)
4. Apply    →  Walk the layers in a staging worktree, then copy the result back (after user confirmation)
5. Lock     →  Write new boilerplate.lock
6. Record   →  Append migration record to .boilerplate/migrations.yml

docs.title: Step 1: Load Current State
docs.text:
• Read boilerplate.lock to determine the current template versions, dependency graph, and per-layer answers-file hashes.
  • Read each layer's .copier-answers.<layer>.yml to retrieve the answers used for the current project state. Each layer's answers file records the answers to its own and its ancestors' questions, the questions of its scoped view; the walk passes each layer's copier update invocation the data design 04 §Safe Update specifies.
  • For each layer, compute the SHA-256 hash of the raw .copier-answers.<layer>.yml file contents and compare against the corresponding entry in copier_answers_file_hashes in boilerplate.lock. If any layer's hash differs, emit a WARNING: "Answer state for layer '{layer}' may have been externally modified since the last Boilerplate operation. The update will use the current .copier-answers.{layer}.yml contents.". The update proceeds despite the mismatch — the warning is informational, not blocking.
  • If any required answers file is missing or corrupted, fail with a clear error before proceeding.
  • Before any layer runs, three more checks, each stopping the update with its own error listed in the outcomes table below, look for layer drift, an incomplete answers file and, on a resume, targets that differ from the pending conflict record's (design 04 §Safe Update).

docs.title: Step 2: Resolve Target
docs.text:
• Each layer the lock lists resolves its own target version, using the same deterministic rules as project creation. Default: the latest available version of that layer that the extends constraints of the lock's layers allow.
  • Support explicit target versions: --target-version <version> names the root template's target, and --target-version <layer>@<version>, repeatable, names the target of the layer called <layer> in the lock.
  • A target that names a layer the lock does not list MUST stop update before anything is staged with BP_UPDATE_LAYER_UNKNOWN, naming each unknown layer and listing the project's layers.
  • An explicit <layer>@<version> that the extends constraint of another layer in the lock excludes MUST stop update before anything is staged with BP_UPDATE_TARGET_EXCLUDED, naming the layer, the requested version and the constraining layer.
  • Downgrades MUST be rejected, with no flag to override. Before the walk starts, update MUST compare each layer's target version with the version that layer's answers file records in _commit, parsed the way Copier parses it, with Copier's own Template.version (a git describe string such as v2.0.0-3-gabc1234 reads as a post-release of 2.0.0, which sorts after 2.0.0). When any target is older, update MUST stop before any layer changes with BP_UPDATE_DOWNGRADE_REJECTED, naming the layer, its recorded version and the target. The same rule applies when a recorded _commit yields no version. The way back from an applied update is reverting the commit that recorded it.

docs.title: Step 3: Build UpdatePlan
docs.text:
The UpdatePlan summarizes what will change if the update is applied.

UpdatePlan fields:

Field Description current_root Current root template specifier target_root Target root template specifier layer_changes List of per-layer version changes classification Overall change classification: PATCH, MINOR, or MAJOR migrations_required List of required migration actions (if any)

Classification rules (highest wins): - Any layer MAJOR bump → overall MAJOR - Any layer MINOR bump (no MAJOR) → overall MINOR - All PATCH bumps → overall PATCH

Per-classification safety guarantees. Each classification carries a contract that template authors MUST honor and that update tooling relies on:

Classification Guarantees Migration required? PATCH No removed files (except transient cache artifacts); no question name changes (defaults MAY adjust); lock differences limited to version + checksum bumps No MINOR Existing file semantics preserved; new files additive (conflict only if user created a colliding file); new questions appended with defaults; existing answer values retained No (unless compatibility.breaking: true flagged on the target version, which forces classification escalation to MAJOR for planning purposes) MAJOR Potential breaking changes: removed files, renamed questions, relocated paths, replaced dependencies Yes

Migration trigger conditions. The migrations_required list MUST be non-empty when ANY of the following hold for the target version:

  • MAJOR version increment (across any layer).
  • Target template metadata declares compatibility.breaking: true.
  • A previously-required question is removed from the merged composition.
  • A structural file relocation alters expected import paths.
  • The extends chain replaces a dependency with one that is not API-compatible (e.g., python-base → python-core).

Optional (advisory) migrations MAY be offered when files are soft-deprecated or configuration keys are superseded; these do NOT block update execution.

Pre-release version handling. Pre-release identifiers (1.0a1, 1.0rc1, etc.) are lower precedence than final releases of the same release version, per §02 Version PEP 440 ordering. Update target resolution skips pre-release versions by default; the user MUST pass --allow-prerelease to opt in. A transition from pre-release to its corresponding final release (e.g., 1.0a1 → 1.0) is classified as PATCH for planning purposes if all release-version segments are unchanged; otherwise it is classified per the standard rules.

Example UpdatePlan output: 

Update plan for my-app:
  project    0.1.0 → 0.2.0  (MINOR)
  streamlit  0.1.0 → 0.1.1  (PATCH)
Overall classification: MINOR
Migrations required: none

When --dry-run is active, print the UpdatePlan and exit without prompting or modifying the project.

Structural changes to the extends chain: When a template update adds or removes parent templates (changes to the extends list), the UpdatePlan MUST detect and report this:

  • Added dependency: A layer the root's target version reaches through extends that was not in the previous composition. The UpdatePlan MUST list it as an ADDED layer, and its lock entry records joined_via: extends. It has no merge base, so Boilerplate MUST render it as a copy that writes only paths not already present, with a skip pattern matching every path (skip_if_exists=["*"]): Copier checks skip_if_exists before overwrite (Worker._solve_render_conflict tests match_skip before overwrite, read at Copier 9.18.1), and the Worker's patterns join the template's in Worker.all_skip_if_exists. A descendant's file therefore keeps its precedence as at compose, where a rendering with overwrite would replace it and the descendant's step would then see that as a user change. The update MUST report each colliding path it left.
  • Removed dependency: A layer that joined through extends (LockLayer.joined_via, 02 §BoilerplateLock) and that the root's target version no longer reaches. The UpdatePlan MUST list it as a REMOVED layer. Boilerplate drops the layer from the managed layer set and lock; it does NOT infer file provenance and does NOT auto-delete the removed layer's files. Cleanup of a removed layer's artifacts is the responsibility of a Copier _migrations script in the template that removed the dependency. When no such migration is provided, the removed layer's files are left in place (now unmanaged) and the user is WARNED: the warning names the removed layer and points to the migration as the cleanup mechanism. See ADR-007. The rule never applies to a layer that joined through add: the root's target does not govern it, so it stays in the lock and in the walk until it is removed on purpose. That holds when a later root target reaches the layer through extends: it keeps joined_via: add, is not reported as ADDED, and the extends constraint still bounds the version it walks to.
  • Classification: Any structural change to the extends chain (addition or removal of layers) MUST be classified as at least MINOR, regardless of version bumps within existing layers.

docs.title: Step 4: Three-Way Merge
docs.text:
Three-way merge semantics preserve local modifications while incorporating template changes. Boilerplate does NOT implement its own three-way merge. All merging is performed by Copier's per-template update mechanism; Boilerplate orchestrates the per-layer invocations and owns the staging worktree around them.

Why per-layer Copier update? Copier enforces a "1 template = 1 Git repository" rule, so the documented mechanism for multi-template projects is one copier update -a <answers-file> invocation per template. Boilerplate MUST NOT reimplement three-way merge — Copier already provides three-way semantics per layer via that template's own Git history; Boilerplate only orchestrates the per-layer invocations.

Merge inputs (per layer, owned by Copier): - Base: The layer's old copy, rendered under its scoped view at the versions it was last rendered against: the layer's own _commit for its own template and boilerplate.lock's versions for its ancestors (design 04 §Safe Update). - Theirs: The layer's template content at the target version (the new commit). - Ours: The current project files (potentially modified by the user since last render).

Safe update:

  • Single-layer projects (no extends): Run the one layer's update through the same Worker subclass; its scoped view is the layer's own schema. Boilerplate writes boilerplate.lock afterward.

  • Multi-layer compositions (templates with extends): Boilerplate orchestrates per-layer updates by running Copier's update per layer in lock order (copier update -a .copier-answers.<layer>.yml --vcs-ref=<target> is the operation), each through the layer's scoped view (design 04 §Safe Update). Each layer's three-way merge is performed by Copier against that layer's own Git source — the published first-party repository, or an org-local clone or mirror of it (ADR-006). Layer-level success/failure is each layer's own atomic-from-Copier operation; Boilerplate stages the walk in a git worktree and brings the result back as uncommitted changes (see Staging worktree and Step 5).

The per-layer answers files (.copier-answers.<layer>.yml) record the answers each layer's update starts from, written at creation time per the _answers_file: contract. Design 04 §Safe Update owns where each answer in a layer's step comes from, how the step prompts and checks recorded answers, how --data and --data-file replace a rejected one, and when the walk runs tasks.

Non-git template sources: If any locked template layer's source is a non-git source type (filesystem without a .git/ directory, or archive), it has no commit for Copier to diff against — Copier has no three-way or two-way fallback for it (ADR-015 §Verification). Boilerplate surfaces this:

  1. Warn the user prominently before proceeding: "Template source '{name}' is a non-git source; skipping it — 'copier recopy' is the manual refresh for this layer."
  2. Skip the layer; the walk continues with the remaining git-backed layers.
  3. Log the skip at WARN level with the source type and template specifier.

The refusal Boilerplate is working around here is Copier's existing behavior; the skip-and-continue walk above is Boilerplate's orchestration policy around it.

docs.title: Copier version management for update
docs.text: boilerplate.lock records the Copier version the project was last rendered or updated with (copier_version). boilerplate update runs with the installed Copier. When the installed Copier version differs from the recorded one, boilerplate update MUST emit a warning naming both versions, then proceed. The new lock records the Copier version this update ran with.

docs.title: Source repository unavailability
docs.text:
If the template source repository referenced in the lock file has been deleted, relocated, or had its history rewritten (force-push removing the locked commit), Copier cannot reach the locked commit needed for its per-layer three-way merge. Boilerplate's role is detection and surfacing the override path:

  1. Raise BP_LOCK_SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE (not BP_LOCK_READ_FAILED) with remediation guidance.
  2. The update command MUST support a --template-source <path-or-url> override that allows the user to point Copier at an alternative source (e.g., a fork, mirror, or local copy) so its per-layer three-way merge can resolve the locked commit.
  3. If no alternative source is available, that layer's update cannot proceed — Copier has no built-in two-way fallback (ADR-015 §Verification). Boilerplate skips the layer with a prominent warning and continues the walk with the remaining layers; copier recopy is the manual refresh once the source is restored.

Template source repositories SHOULD be treated as critical infrastructure. The lock file records the source URL and commit hash per layer, but does not embed the template content itself — source availability is required for updates.

docs.title: Staging worktree
docs.text:
update runs the walk in a detached git worktree of the project, so the user's checkout changes only when the update has finished or paused on a conflict. add uses the same staging (Part 2.4).

The copy back is the step that reproduces the walk's result in the user's checkout. It is git restore --source=<commit> --worktree -- :/ run in the checkout, where <commit> is the staging worktree's last per-layer commit. git(1) says git restore "is about restoring files in the working tree from either the index or another commit. This command does not update your branch", so the copy back moves neither HEAD nor the branch and leaves the uncommitted changes plain Copier leaves. git-restore adds: "If a path is tracked but does not exist in the restore source, it will be removed to match the source", so files the walk deleted are removed along with the ones it added or modified (git-restore).

The diagram follows one update from the pre-flight check to the removal of the worktree. The restore marker and its ref bracket the copy back, so a run cut off inside it leaves state in git. On a conflict, the run skips the tasks and the lock and appends a conflict record.

sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: One update from pre-flight check to worktree removal
    accDescr: Boilerplate runs the pre-flight, lock and marker rules on the user's checkout and adds a detached staging worktree with hooks off, which starts at the same commit. For each layer, ancestors first, Copier updates the layer in the worktree and Boilerplate commits it, then Boilerplate confirms the checkout is unchanged, pins the ref and writes the restore marker, copies back into the checkout, runs tasks, writes the lock, appends the record, and removes the marker, the ref and the worktree.
    participant B as Boilerplate
    participant U as Your checkout
    participant S as Staging worktree
    participant R as Repository and git dir
    participant C as Copier
    B->>U: Pre-flight, lock, marker rules
    B->>R: worktree add --detach, hooks off
    R-->>S: Detached at the starting commit
    loop Each layer, ancestors first
        B->>C: copier update in the worktree
        C->>S: Merge the layer
        B->>R: Plumbing commit of the layer
    end
    B->>U: Checkout unchanged, no obstruction
    B->>R: Pin the ref, write restore marker
    B->>U: Copy back
    B->>U: Run tasks
    B->>U: Write lock
    B->>U: Append record
    B->>R: Remove marker and ref
    B->>R: Remove the worktree
Hold "Alt" / "Option" to enable pan & zoom
  1. Create. After the pre-flight check and the user's confirmation, Boilerplate MUST create a detached worktree of the project at its current commit (git -c core.hooksPath=<null device> worktree add --detach) in the system temp directory, inside a uniquely named folder, created owner-only (10 §File Permissions), whose own name is the project folder's name. Copier exposes the destination folder's name as _folder_name, and templates use it as a default, so the staged render matches a render in the user's folder.
    • The worktree shares the repository's config, so line-ending, filter and LFS settings match the user's checkout.
    • A detached HEAD adds no branch to the repository.
    • git worktree add runs the repository's post-checkout hook (observed with git 2.55), so Boilerplate MUST create the worktree with hooks disabled, as Copier runs its own git commands where a hook would interfere (-c core.hooksPath=<null device>, as Worker._apply_update does, read at Copier 9.18.1). The null device is os.devnull.
    • Boilerplate MUST commit in the worktree with git's plumbing (git write-tree, git commit-tree, git update-ref), so the user's hooks do not run.
  2. Walk. Boilerplate MUST run the walk (design 04 §Safe Update) in the worktree, ancestors first, and commit after each layer. Copier refuses to update a project with uncommitted changes, so the commit is what lets Copier update the next layer.
  3. Fail. Any error, a cancelled prompt or a rejected answer MUST remove the worktree. The user's checkout never changed, and no lock is written.
  4. Succeed. Before copying back, Boilerplate MUST verify that the user's checkout is still at the starting commit with no changes; if not, it MUST discard the worktree and stop with BP_UPDATE_CHECKOUT_CHANGED and exit code 3. It MUST likewise stop with BP_UPDATE_PATH_OBSTRUCTED, before any file changes, when a path the walk added already exists in the checkout as a file or directory git ignores, naming each path, because the restore would overwrite that file or delete that directory without warning. Before the copy back changes a file, it MUST pin the copy back's source commit with the ref refs/worktree/boilerplate/restore and then write the restore marker (Interrupted copy back). If the copy back fails partway, Boilerplate MUST undo it (Undo), keep the staging worktree, remove the marker and the ref, and stop with BP_UPDATE_COPY_BACK_FAILED, naming the worktree's path, so the walk's result is not lost; it appends no record, because the undo returns the checkout to its pre-update state. Otherwise the copy back leaves the uncommitted changes plain Copier leaves, and Boilerplate runs the tasks, writes the lock, appends the record, removes the marker and the ref, and removes the worktree. Because the copy back restores from a commit, files the walk added and files it deleted both apply; a copy of the worktree's files cannot carry a deletion, such as one Copier's _remove_old_files makes (the _remove_old_files call in Worker._apply_update, read at Copier 9.18.1).
  5. Conflict. When a layer's update returns conflicts (Copier inserts standard <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> markers in affected text files), Boilerplate MUST stop the walk, copy back the layers finished so far together with the paused layer's changes and Copier's conflict markers, and write no lock. The paused layer is not committed in the worktree, so after the restore the copy back also applies the worktree's remaining working-tree changes (files the paused layer added or modified are written and files it deleted are removed, as git status --porcelain=v1 -z lists them) and replays its unmerged index entries: Copier records each conflicted file as index stages 1, 2 and 3 (the if conflicted: block of Worker._apply_update, read at Copier 9.18.1), which the copy back reads with git ls-files --stage in the worktree and writes with git update-index --index-info in the checkout, after a line that drops the path's stage 0 as Copier does. The worktree shares the checkout's object store, so the staged blobs resolve in both. The conflicted files then show as unmerged and git commit refuses them, as with plain Copier. The restore marker of this copy back has kind paused and holds the layers the walk finished and the paused layer; the run appends the conflict record and then removes the marker and the ref. See Step 5.

Stale worktrees left by an interrupted run are removed by the stale-staging cleanup of 07 §Atomic Staged Write Pattern.

docs.title: Undo
docs.text:
Undo restores every tracked file, in the working tree and the index, from the starting commit, and removes the untracked files that git does not ignore (git clean -d -f, without -x). It does not reverse files git ignores, anything inside .git (a commit a task made, a moved HEAD) or anything outside the project, so an effect a task has there stays. Task authors SHOULD keep tasks idempotent, so that running one again after an undo is safe (ADR-014). update and add refuse to start while untracked files are present (Pre-Flight Check, check 4), so every untracked file the undo removes came from the run. Boilerplate lists the untracked files before it asks the user to keep or undo, and passes only the listed paths to git clean, so a file the user makes while that prompt waits is not removed. A copy back that fails is undone the same way, without a prompt.

Before the tasks run, Boilerplate notes the entries git ignores in the checkout (git ls-files --others --ignored --exclude-standard --directory). After an undo that follows a task failure, it names the ignored entries that are new and never deletes them. The note lists an ignored folder that already existed, such as .venv, as one entry, so Boilerplate cannot see changes inside it, and the message says so. A rerun that finishes a run cut off during its tasks (Interrupted copy back, rule 5) takes the note when the rerun starts, so it does not name an ignored entry the cut-off run's tasks made.

docs.title: Merge behavior and ordering
docs.text:
Per-file merge behavior: Per-file merge semantics (clean updates for unchanged files, conflict-marker insertion for text-file conflicts, binary-conflict reporting for binary files, modify/delete handling, etc.) are owned by Copier's update mechanism. Boilerplate does not specify or implement these semantics; they are documented in Copier's own update reference.

Cross-layer ordering: Per-layer Copier update invocations are always issued in lock order, which is topological as at creation: dependencies before dependents, so a migration that renames a question rewrites the ancestor's answers file before a descendant's update reads it (design 04 §Safe Update). A failure or conflict in any layer halts the walk; subsequent layers are not invoked.

docs.title: Step 5: Failure and conflict
docs.text:
Failure. Any error, a cancelled prompt or a rejected answer before the copy back removes the staging worktree, writes no lock and appends no migration record, because the user's checkout never changed. The exit code is the error's own (1 for an unexpected failure, 3 for a rejected answer, 130 for a cancelled prompt). A copy back that fails partway is undone and appends no record. A task failure after the copy back follows design 04 §Safe Update, for update and add alike: a terminal offers to keep the files or undo the run (Undo), and keeping the files, which --non-interactive does, writes the lock, appends a failed record, names the failed task and how to rerun it, and exits 1.

Conflict. When a layer's update returns conflicts, Boilerplate:

  • stops the walk, so later layers are not invoked;
  • brings back the layers finished so far into the user's checkout as uncommitted changes, with Copier's conflict markers in the conflicted files;
  • reports each conflicted file path and the originating layer;
  • appends a conflict record, exits with code 4 (ACTION_REQUIRED) with BP_UPDATE_CONFLICT_PAUSED and writes no lock;
  • prints the remediation "Resolve conflicts and commit, then run 'boilerplate update' again. 'git reset' and then 'git stash --include-untracked' set the partial update aside."

The user resolves and commits as with plain Copier, then reruns boilerplate update. The rerun resumes from the conflict record (design 04 §Safe Update), which names each layer's target version and the layers the walk finished: it skips the finished layers, walks the remaining layers to the recorded targets, runs the accumulated task list once, writes the lock and records success. An explicit --target-version that differs from the record stops with BP_UPDATE_TARGET_MISMATCH until the user sets the partial update aside, after which the record no longer binds and update plans afresh. A rerun on an uncommitted tree stops at the pre-flight check, so the mismatch is reached only after the user commits, when Setting a partial update aside applies. A run cut off before it appends its record is finished or set aside as Interrupted copy back describes.

An update that fails before the copy back completes, or pauses on a conflict, leaves the previous lock in place; a task failure whose files are kept writes the lock.

docs.title: Interrupted copy back
docs.text:
A run cut off while it copies its result back, or while it finishes afterwards, is completed by running the same command again, or set aside as Setting a partial update aside describes. No flag is involved.

The restore marker keeps the state of such a run in git. It is a JSON file at git rev-parse --git-path boilerplate-restore.json, paired with the ref refs/worktree/boilerplate/restore, which pins the copy back's source commit (git update-ref). The fields are in 02 §RestoreMarker. Boilerplate MUST write both after the checkout-unchanged and obstruction checks and before the copy back changes a file, for update and for add; advance the marker's phase as the run proceeds; and remove both, file and ref (git update-ref -d), after the run appends its record. It MUST pin the ref first and then write the marker, and remove the marker first and then the ref, so a crash between the two steps leaves at worst a ref without a marker, which the next run's pre-flight removes. It MUST write the marker, and rewrite it for each phase, with the single-file recipe of 07 §Atomic Staged Write Pattern (a sibling temporary file, then an atomic rename), so a crash never leaves a truncated file. A marker that still does not parse as the RestoreMarker stops the command with BP_UPDATE_INTERRUPTED naming the file; the remediation sets the partial update aside as below, and deleting the file and running git update-ref -d refs/worktree/boilerplate/restore discards the marker.

  • kind is complete for a walk that finished every layer, and paused for one a conflict paused, which runs no tasks and writes no lock.
  • phase is copy_back from the moment the marker is written until the copy back ends, tasks while a complete run's tasks run, and recording until the record is appended. add runs its tasks before the lock and the record (Part 2.4), so its marker passes the same phases and rules 4, 5 and 6 below apply to add unchanged.
  • result_commit is the staging worktree's last per-layer commit, the starting commit when no layer finished.
  • finished lists the layers whose steps the walk finished, in walk order, and paused_layer names the layer whose merge left conflict markers, which follows them. A complete run has an empty finished and no paused_layer.

A copy back that fails is undone (Undo), the staging worktree is kept and named in the error, the marker and the ref are removed and no record is appended.

When update or add starts and the marker exists, Boilerplate MUST apply these rules in order, inside the operation lock and before any layer runs. The first rule that matches decides.

  1. The run finished. The log's last record has a timestamp after the marker's started_at and matches its targets: a conflict record has the same targets, and any other record has a to_version equal to <name>@<version> for the entry of targets that belongs to the root template (for add, the added layer's entry), because an update record's to_version is the root template specifier (02 — Data Models) and an added layer sits after the root in the walk's order. Remove the marker and the ref and continue as a fresh run.
  2. The marker no longer binds. The working tree is clean, so the partial update was set aside or committed. Remove the marker and the ref, warn naming the marker's targets, and plan afresh. A committed partial update then meets the drift rules of design 04 §Safe Update.
  3. The marker belongs to another run. The marker's operation differs from the command, or HEAD is not start_commit. Stop with BP_UPDATE_INTERRUPTED; for a different operation, the error names the command to rerun.
  4. The copy back was cut off (phase is copy_back). When kind is complete, every path that differs from start_commit matches result_commit, modified, added and deleted alike, and every path the run adds that already exists in the checkout, one that git ignores included, matches result_commit too, repeat the copy back from result_commit, which writes the same files on every run. Then run the tasks, write the lock, append success and remove the marker and the ref. Otherwise stop with BP_UPDATE_INTERRUPTED: a paused copy back also applies the paused layer's changes and its unmerged index entries, which no commit holds, and a path that differs from result_commit is an edit since the interruption, a file the cut-off run left half written, or a file made since at a path the run adds, which the repeated copy back would overwrite. A path the cut-off run itself wrote matches result_commit and is repeated. The comparison goes through git, so line-ending and filter settings apply as they do to the copy back; a byte comparison against the blobs fails on every text file under Windows core.autocrlf. git status --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=all lists the paths that differ from start_commit, git diff --quiet <result_commit> -- <path> decides each tracked path, and for an added path git hash-object -- <path> is compared with git rev-parse <result_commit>:<path>. The status listing omits ignored files, so the check on added paths does not rely on it: git diff --no-renames --name-only --diff-filter=A -z <start_commit> <result_commit> lists the paths the run adds, and each one that exists in the checkout, ignored or not, is compared the same way before the copy back repeats. A directory at an added path counts as differing.
  5. The tasks were cut off (phase is tasks). Run the tasks again, as Copier runs a template's tasks on every update (Worker.run_copy runs _execute_tasks inside Phase.use(Phase.TASKS) unless skip_tasks is set, and Worker._apply_update reaches it through the in-place render's run_copy, read at Copier 9.18.1), then write the lock, append success and remove the marker and the ref. A secret a task uses is asked again, because secrets are never recorded.
  6. The record was cut off (phase is recording). Write the lock if kind is complete and it is not already current, append the record (success, or conflict with exit code 4 for a paused run) and remove the marker and the ref. A conflict record takes its targets from the marker's targets and its finished from the marker's finished followed by its paused_layer; rule 6 does not read the answers files to build it.

Rules 1 and 2 hand the command back to the pre-flight, which continues with the clean-tree check and plans a fresh run. Rules 4, 5 and 6 finish the cut-off run and the command then ends with that run's exit code, 0, or 4 when rule 6 appends the conflict record of a paused run; they plan no fresh run, because the tree they leave holds the finished result and the clean-tree check would stop it. Rule 3 and every other stop exit with code 3.

Every stop names the interrupted run's targets and the remediation: set the partial update aside (Setting a partial update aside), then run the command again, which meets rule 2. The cut-off run's staging worktree is not reused; the stale-staging cleanup removes it.

Why the marker lives in git.

  • git keeps the state of its own multi-step operations under the git directory, never in the working tree: git cherry-pick --continue reads .git/sequencer (git-cherry-pick).
  • git rev-parse --git-path resolves under the current worktree's git directory, so each worktree of the project has its own marker.
  • A ref under refs/worktree/ is not shared between worktrees (git-worktree), keeps result_commit reachable after the stale-staging cleanup removes the staging folder, and is not pushed with the branches.
  • A marker in the tracked tree could be committed and pushed.

docs.title: Setting a partial update aside
docs.text: Before the partial update is committed, git reset and then git stash --include-untracked set it aside, modified and added files alike, and keep it recoverable. The reset comes first: a paused run leaves its conflicted files as unmerged index entries, which git stash refuses (error: could not write index), and git reset returns the index to HEAD and keeps the working tree. git clean is not the remedy, because it would also delete any file the user has created since. Once the partial update is committed, git revert of the commit that holds it sets it aside.

docs.title: Step 6: Post-Update State
docs.text:
On successful update:

  1. Write new boilerplate.lock (same format as creation, updated updated_at)
  2. Append a migration record to .boilerplate/migrations.yml
  3. Remove the restore marker and its ref (Interrupted copy back)

docs.title: Migration Records
docs.text:
.boilerplate/migrations.yml is an append-only YAML file. Each entry records one finished operation.

Each MigrationRecord tracks: id (sequential), from_version, to_version, timestamp (ISO 8601 UTC), status (full enumeration in 02 — Data Models: success, failed, conflict, adopted, created), error, and classification (PATCH/MINOR/MAJOR). See Data models for the full schema.

Invariants (the status values are specified in §02 MigrationRecord; the project-specific timing below is owned here):

  • Entries MUST be append-only. An existing entry MUST NOT be modified.
  • A finished operation appends exactly one record: success, conflict, failed, created or adopted. There is no in_progress status. A run that leaves the checkout unchanged appends none: a failure before the copy back, or a copy back that fails and is undone. The state of a run cut off while it copies back is kept in the restore marker, not in the log (Interrupted copy back).
  • A conflict record MUST be appended when a conflict pauses an update, and a failed record when a task fails after the copy back and the files are kept.
