MUST be unique across all entries. type enum Yes — One of: filesystem, git, archive. wheel_bundle is a deferred seed-cache type (ADR-006), not yet available for configuration. The http, github, and oci types are reserved for future versions. location string Yes — URI or filesystem path to the source. Interpretation depends on type. credentials string or null No null Reserved for Phase 4 (remote / third-party sources). Reference to a credential — an environment variable name or vault path. MUST NOT contain a literal secret value. See Validation Rules below. priority integer No 100 Lower number = higher priority. Ties broken by registration order (position in the sources list). trust_level enum No untrusted trusted or untrusted. Governs sources configured in this file; the implicit first-party source — the published per-template repositories (ADR-006) — is trusted by default and does not appear here. Trusted sources may execute tasks with user consent; untrusted sources execute tasks only with explicit user authorization via --allow-tasks (or --allow-untrusted) — see §03 Task Execution Safety. A lock file MAY record an independent free-form string field (trust_tier) for forward compatibility, but resolution logic treats only this binary enum. Absence of a recorded trust value MUST NOT fail resolution. expected_commit string or null No null For TOFU (trust-on-first-use) pinning: the expected commit hash on first clone of a git source. When set, Boilerplate records the commit on first use and rejects subsequent fetches whose tip does not descend from it. Ignored for filesystem and archive types.

Source types that define additional fields (checksum for archive) are specified in the corresponding source model section: ArchiveSource. Those fields are included inline in the YAML entry alongside the common fields above.

Example:

sources:
  - name: official
    type: git
    location: https://github.com/org/templates.git
    trust_level: trusted
    priority: 10
  - name: team-local
    type: git
    location: /home/dev/templates
    trust_level: untrusted
  - name: offline-archive
    type: archive
    location: /opt/boilerplate/archives/starter-kit.tar.gz
    checksum: "sha256:a1b2c3..."

Validation rules:

  1. Credential safety (Phase 4): The credentials field is reserved for Phase 4 (remote / third-party sources). Until then, when the field is present, Boilerplate MUST reject values that appear to be literal credentials. Literal secrets MUST never appear in this file.
  2. Trust enforcement: A source entry with trust_level: trusted enables task execution subject to the user consent prompt; trust_level: untrusted (the default) blocks task execution unless the user explicitly authorizes it with --allow-tasks (or --allow-untrusted); see §03 Task Execution Safety. There is no intermediate tier.
  3. File permissions (POSIX): On POSIX systems, the file MUST be readable only by the owner. Boilerplate SHOULD warn or refuse to load the file if permissions are more permissive.
  4. Duplicate rejection: Duplicate name values across entries MUST be rejected at parse time. Duplicate YAML keys within a single mapping MUST also be rejected.
  5. Unknown fields: Unknown fields within a source entry SHOULD produce a warning but MUST NOT cause a hard failure, to allow forward compatibility with newer schema versions.

See 10-security.md §Catalog Source Configuration for the full security constraints on catalog source configuration (YAML tag rejection, path traversal validation).

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
Target model

This describes the target security model. For what is enforced today, see ADR-003 and the Status page.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document specifies the cross-cutting security rules for Boilerplate. Security rules that are inseparable from local context live in their owning documents; this document does not restate them. Related specs:

  • Trust model (binary trusted/untrusted classification, task-execution consent gating): Template system and discovery
  • Lock file integrity (checksums, atomic writes): Data models, Project lifecycle
  • Operational invariants that gate security checks (atomic-write pattern, concurrency control, retry policy): Operational quality
  • YAML parsing, input validation, privacy, threat model: this document

See Data models for exit codes. See CLI reference for CLI output conventions. See Settings and configuration files for the operator-authored configuration files referenced below.

docs.title: Threat Model
docs.text:
Boilerplate operates in a trust boundary between template authors (who provide executable content via Jinja2 extensions and _tasks) and project consumers (who run boilerplate new). The threat scenarios that the design mitigates:

Scenario Vector Impact Tampered template source Git repo compromise; commit replaced after publication Malicious code in rendered project Malicious Jinja2 extension Unsafe extension loaded at render Code execution at render time Malicious _tasks execution Template tasks run shell commands at user privilege Code execution post-render Dependency-chain poisoning Transitive template replaced with malicious version Integrity loss; unexpected behavior Answers-file manipulation User-supplied answer values hijack rendering Misconfiguration; secret leakage Lock-file forgery Stale or fabricated lock claims success Reproducibility failure; bypass of verification Catalog metadata spoofing False version, author, or trust claim Trust erosion; misattribution Credential leakage Secrets in logs, URLs, or error messages Authentication compromise Supply-chain compromise Boilerplate's own dependencies tampered Tool-level code execution

Each threat is mitigated by a specific design control:

Threat Mitigation Reference Tampered template source Commit-pinned lock + per-layer checksum §06 Lock Files; §02 boilerplate.lock Malicious Jinja2 extension Module-import blocklist + SandboxedEnvironment + user consent (--allow-extensions) §03 Jinja2 Extension Safety Malicious _tasks execution Default-deny task gating: tasks run only after the consent prompt or --allow-tasks; --no-tasks skips them entirely §03 Task Execution Safety Dependency-chain poisoning Lock integrity verified before render; per-node provenance recorded §06; boilerplate lock verify Answers-file manipulation Immutable answers on update (Copier contract); answer values bypass Jinja2 pipeline §03 Copier Integration Contract; §Answer Preset Safety below Lock-file forgery Lock integrity check before render/update boilerplate lock verify Catalog metadata spoofing Trusted/untrusted source classification; metadata hash + provenance per source §03 Trust and Verification Levels Credential leakage Git credential helper exclusivity; redaction processor; URL credential stripping §Credential Handling below; §07 Redaction Supply-chain compromise Pinned dependencies + lock; out of scope for the spec but addressed in repo CI (engineering practice)

docs.title: Verification Pipeline
docs.text:
Security checks run at defined phases — never lazily. A check that detects a violation MUST fail the operation with a BP_* error before any irreversible work proceeds:

Phase Security check Failure mode Fetch Verify resolved commit matches lock (if lock present); record content checksum BP_FETCH_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH Resolve Every node in the dependency graph has provenance (source URL + commit-or-checksum; trust value optional) BP_RESOLVE_PROVENANCE_MISSING Render (pre) Lock integrity verified; extension allowlist evaluated; user consent gates fired BP_LOCK_INTEGRITY_FAILED, BP_RENDER_UNSAFE_EXTENSION, BP_RENDER_TASKS_NOT_AUTHORIZED Update New resolution diffed against existing lock; unexpected source changes flagged BP_UPDATE_SOURCE_DIVERGED

docs.title: Security Invariants
docs.text:
Across all operations, the following invariants MUST hold; violation is a contract bug:

  • Every resolved template node in boilerplate.lock MUST record its source URL, its commit, and its checksum; a node missing any of these MUST fail resolution. The commit and checksum MUST be verified before render or update proceeds. A trust value (the optional trust_tier field) MUST be recorded when the source declares one, but its absence MUST NOT fail resolution (local sources declare no trust value).
  • The full template source MUST be available before YAML parse or Copier invocation; the canonical statement of this submodule-initialization-before-render rule lives in §03.
  • A Jinja2 extension MUST NOT be loaded unless its package is on the system-wide allowlist AND user consent has been granted.
  • Answer-preset values MUST never pass through jinja2.Environment.from_string() (architectural, not validation-based).

docs.title: Credential Handling
docs.text:
Boilerplate MUST use the Git credential helper (git credential fill / git credential approve) as the exclusive mechanism for authenticating to remote Git repositories. Embedding credentials directly in Git URLs (e.g., https://token@host/repo) is prohibited. Credentials in URLs are exposed in process argument lists (visible via ps or Task Manager), shell history, CI logs, and Git's own diagnostic output.

If the Git credential helper is not configured or fails to provide credentials, Boilerplate MUST fail with BP_GIT_AUTH_FAILED and provide remediation guidance directing the user to configure git credential-manager or the appropriate platform credential helper.

docs.title: File Permissions
docs.text: Boilerplate MUST create files and directories with sensible default permissions unless the template explicitly overrides them. Staging directories MUST be restricted to owner-only access to prevent other users from reading or modifying in-progress renders. On Windows, Boilerplate relies on the default ACL inheritance of the parent directory.

docs.title: Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
All external inputs MUST be validated at trust boundaries before processing. A trust boundary exists wherever data enters Boilerplate from an external source: user CLI arguments, YAML files on disk, answer presets, and template content.

  • Remote template source responses: Content fetched via git clone from remote repositories transitions from untrusted network data to local filesystem content. The initial fetch is trust-on-first-use (TOFU); subsequent fetches are validated against the lock file's commit hash and content checksum.
  • Proto plugin execution: WASM plugins executed by proto during environment provisioning represent a trust boundary. Plugins are fetched from the proto plugin registry and execute tool installation logic. Reserved for Phase 4 (remote / third-party sources): a proto WASM plugin allowlist that constrains which plugins are permitted. Currently, toolchains are provisioned from local, operator-authored profiles only.

docs.title: Checksum Scope
docs.text:
Checksum scope clarification: Two distinct checksums appear in Boilerplate's data model:

  1. Template source checksum: computed from the template directory contents at the locked commit (pre-render). The exclusion list for this checksum is: .git/, __pycache__/, .mypy_cache/, .pytest_cache/, .ruff_cache/, node_modules/. See §06 Project Lifecycle for the authoritative list.
  2. Rendered output checksum: computed from the project directory contents after rendering. The exclusion list for this checksum SHOULD be extensible: template authors MAY declare checksum_excludes in their boilerplate.yml to add project-specific exclusions (e.g., .venv/, .tox/, node_modules/, .pytest_cache/). Boilerplate ships with default exclusions: .git/, __pycache__/, .boilerplate/. Exclusions are matched as prefix paths relative to the project root.

docs.title: Catalog Source Configuration
docs.text: Catalog sources beyond the default filesystem directories are configured in a boilerplate-sources.yml file. This file defines catalog sources with their type, location, priority, and trust classification. The full schema, validation rules, and read protocol are specified in 09-settings-and-configuration.md §Catalog Source Configuration File, including credential references, file permissions, and trusted/untrusted classification.

docs.title: YAML Parsing Security
docs.text: YAML parsing MUST follow the security rules defined in 03-template-system.md §YAML Parsing Rules.

docs.title: Jinja2 Sandbox
docs.text: See §03 Template System §Jinja2 Sandbox for the normative spec.

docs.title: Answer Preset Safety
docs.text:
Answer preset values MUST be treated as literal strings and passed to Copier without Jinja2 rendering. Implementations MUST NOT attempt to detect or reject Jinja2 syntax in answer values (a value like {{ example }} may be a legitimate literal string, e.g., documenting a Jinja2 template). Instead, the safety guarantee is architectural: answer values bypass the Jinja2 rendering pipeline entirely. They are injected as pre-resolved answers into Copier's data context, never passed through jinja2.Environment.from_string().

Double-rendering risk: An answer value containing Jinja2-like syntax (e.g., {{ secret }}) is passed to Copier as a literal and never re-rendered, so its curly braces appear in output as text, not as a Jinja2 expression. This single-pass guarantee is a property of Copier's pipeline, not Boilerplate's. Implementations MUST verify this behavior against the supported Copier version range in integration tests.

Note: each layer's .copier-answers.<layer>.yml is a separate artifact owned by Copier (per the per-layer pattern). Boilerplate MUST NOT write to or validate any of them.

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text: All user-provided inputs -- CLI arguments, interactive prompts, and file-based inputs -- MUST be validated against expected formats before use. The BP_INPUT_INVALID_FORMAT error code MUST be raised for any input that fails validation.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
• Logs, error messages, and diagnostic output MUST NOT contain secrets, passwords, API tokens, or PII.
  • Personal data MUST be redacted before emission to any output channel (terminal, log file, structured log event).

Answers to questions marked secret: true (Copier's secret question flag) MUST NOT reach any file Boilerplate writes. Copier leaves them out of each .copier-answers.<layer>.yml, which is why that file is safe to pass to --data-file as an answer preset; a secret answer is supplied again on the next run through --data from an environment variable, or through a --data-file kept outside version control; a literal on the command line lands in shell history.

See also §07 Redaction for the systematic log redaction mechanism and §07 Structured Logging for required log fields and privacy invariants.

docs.title: Error Message Hygiene
docs.text:
Error messages presented to users MUST NOT leak internal file paths, stack traces, or implementation details. Diagnostic details SHOULD be available only via --verbose or DEBUG-level logging.

In --verbose mode, Boilerplate MAY include additional diagnostic context such as resolved template paths, Copier invocation arguments (excluding credentials), and timing details. Verbose output MUST NOT include: credential values, answer values marked as secret (secret: true), full file contents, or environment variable values. Template source URLs are acceptable in verbose output but MUST have any embedded credentials stripped.

docs.title: CI/CD Lock Verification
docs.text:
RECOMMENDED CI gate: Include boilerplate lock verify as a step in your CI pipeline. This step SHOULD run before any boilerplate update invocation in CI.

boilerplate lock verify checks:

  • All template layer sources are reachable and contain the locked commits
  • Template layer content checksums match recorded values
  • Each .copier-answers.<layer>.yml hash matches its entry in copier_answers_file_hashes (if present)

It does NOT verify:

  • Lock file integrity (no cryptographic signature; the file is trusted as-is)
  • That re-rendering would produce identical output (Copier behavioral differences across versions may affect output)
  • Answer correctness (only that answers haven't changed since last operation)

lock verify is a supply chain drift detector, not a full integrity guarantee. For stronger assurance, combine with content signing (planned for a future release). Example GitHub Actions step:

- name: Verify template lock integrity
  run: boilerplate lock verify

docs.title: ADR-001: Build vs. Adopt Analysis
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Scope note. This ADR records the build-vs-adopt decisions and the supply-chain assessment. The Copier integration mechanism is recorded separately in ADR-002.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Each responsibility was evaluated against the modern tool landscape to decide build vs. delegate. This ADR records the architectural decisions and supply chain assessments.

docs.title: Guiding Principles
docs.text:
1. Prefer modern, proven third-party solutions. Build only what doesn't exist.
  2. Enterprise-grade: evaluate supply chain risk of every dependency.
  3. No shim-based tools in the stack. Every dependency must provide native Windows execution.
  4. "Orchestrate, don't replace" — applied consistently across all pillars.

docs.title: Decision: Two-Pillar Orchestration Architecture
docs.text:
Boilerplate is an orchestration layer with two pillars:

Pillar Orchestrated Tool Boilerplate Adds Templates Copier (rendering, answers, three-way merge) Composition (extends DAG), lock files, catalog, trust model Environment Provisioning proto (tool installation, 800+ tools, cross-platform) Profile composition (extends), .boilerplate/environment.yml (profile provenance), enterprise trust. Tool-level locking delegated to proto's .protolock.

docs.title: Template Composition is the Core Differentiator
docs.text: Composition gives "the experience of a singular template, built from many variants." This is Boilerplate's reason to exist. No other tool provides declarative template composition on top of Copier. Copier's own template inheritance (Issue #934) has been open since Jan 2023 with no implementation.

docs.title: Environment Provisioning Orchestrates proto
docs.text: proto (moonrepo) handles the hard part of environment management: installing 800+ tools across platforms via WASM plugins. Boilerplate uses proto's native .prototools schema and adds what proto lacks: profile composition, .boilerplate/environment.yml (profile provenance), and enterprise trust/validation, with tool-level version locking delegated to proto's .protolock, and proto invoked via subprocess behind a ProtoWorker interface.

docs.title: Implementation Language: Python
docs.text:
Python is the right choice because Boilerplate builds directly on Copier (a Python library) — Rust would force subprocess invocation, losing type safety, shared error handling, and direct use of Copier's Template/Worker objects. Performance is not a concern: operations are I/O-bound (YAML, files, git), not CPU-bound.

Copier integration mechanism. Boilerplate depends on Copier's internal Template/Worker classes (not its public API): it subclasses Template to present a merged question schema and hands each layer's scoped view, the merged schema of the layer and its ancestors, to Copier, at compose and at update, through a Worker subclass that holds that view in its fields. This coupling is deliberate and contained behind a single audited import shim — see ADR-002 for the mechanism, rationale, and version pin. (A file-based merged-template approach, which avoids the internal dependency, was evaluated and not adopted.)

docs.title: Supply Chain Decisions
docs.text:
Last assessed: 2026-03-20. These ratings should be re-assessed periodically (at least quarterly or when a dependency releases a major version).

Dependency Risk Decision Last Assessed Copier MEDIUM Accept — internal Template/Worker used via the audited shim in ADR-002. Mature project, active development, BSD-3 license. See copier-org/copier; check scorecard.dev for current OpenSSF score. 2026-03-20 proto MEDIUM Accept — abstracted via a ProtoWorker interface. Younger project from moonrepo, active development, MIT license. Note: the unstable-lockfile feature flag signals .protolock is not yet stabilized — monitor for breaking changes. 2026-03-20 uv LOW Python toolchain foundation (no shims). Check scorecard.dev for current OpenSSF score. 2026-03-20 Typer MEDIUM-LOW Accept — wraps Click (Pallets); fallback straightforward. 2026-03-20 packaging LOW Accept — PyPA, no alternative for PEP 440. Declared as a direct dependency. 2026-06-09 logging (stdlib) NONE Chosen — logging via the stdlib logging module (Rich console on TTY, plain formatter otherwise). structlog was evaluated but not adopted; there is no third-party logging dependency. 2026-06-09 graphlib NONE Python stdlib 2026-03-20 deepmerge HIGH Rejected — inactive maintenance; merge strategies built inline (composition/merging/). 2026-03-20 mise HIGH Rejected — shim-based on Windows (violates the no-shims principle). 2026-03-20 oras-py HIGH Deferred (remote distribution) — immature Python SDK. 2026-03-20

Zero shim-based dependencies in the final stack.

docs.title: proto Plugin Trust
docs.text:
proto's value is its 800+ tool plugins, but each plugin is third-party WASM code. Boilerplate SHOULD mitigate this by:

  1. Maintaining an allowlist of vetted plugins in the environment profile schema.
  2. Evaluating plugin signature verification when proto supports it.
  3. Documenting the trust boundary: Boilerplate trusts proto; proto trusts its plugin authors; the user trusts the profile author's plugin selections.

This is an accepted residual risk for the environment subsystem, documented so it is not forgotten.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Environment management orchestrates proto rather than building first-party tool resolvers.
  • Merge strategies are built inline rather than depending on deepmerge.
  • Remote (OCI) template distribution is deferred.
  • A first-party trust model is required by Phase 4 entry, per ADR-003; OCI signatures are deferred until remote distribution lands.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Copier Template Inheritance — Issue #934
  • proto (moonrepo)
  • uv (Astral)
  • Copier Comparisons
  • deepmerge health (Snyk)
  • ORAS — OCI Registry As Storage (CNCF)
  • OpenSSF Scorecard

docs.title: ADR-002: Depend on Copier's internal Template/Worker via a single audited shim
docs.text: Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Copier does not expose Template or Worker in its public API (copier.__all__ is load_settings, run_copy, run_recopy, run_update, Phase, Settings, VcsRef). Boilerplate's composition engine is built on these internal classes: MergedTemplate subclasses Template to present a consolidated question schema, and every layer's render, at compose and at update, runs through a Worker subclass that exposes the layer's scoped view, the consolidated schema of the layer and its ancestors (design 04 §Scoped view), rather than through Copier's public run_copy/run_update. These are private symbols Copier may relocate without a deprecation cycle.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Funnel all coupling to Copier internals through one module, src/boilerplate/integrations/copier_types.py, importing from the modules where Copier actually defines them (copier._main.Worker, copier._template.Template), and pin Copier to a tested range (copier>=9.15,<10 in pyproject.toml). A relocation of these symbols then breaks one file, loudly, via the guard test (tests/boilerplate/integrations/test_copier_types.py) during CI rather than at render time for a user.

Compose and update share one way in. Both hand Copier each layer's scoped view through the same Worker subclass, built on the Worker that copier_types.py imports. Compose renders every layer through it, boilerplate update runs Copier's update once per layer through it, and every use of Copier internals on either path MUST go through the shim.

The scoped views live in fields of a Worker subclass, two per update step, and the subclass's template property builds template from the view in those fields that matches the render Copier is making, together with the src_path: the scoped view joined from the recorded versions of the layer and its ancestors for the old copy, which renders the layer's recorded source at its recorded _commit, and the scoped view joined from their target versions for the in-place render and the new copy. The property tells the old copy from the other two renders by the render's destination, not by vcs_ref, because the three renders can carry one ref when only an ancestor moves; the name prefixes it reads are listed under Audited internals, and the in-place render's destination is the project. Copier's update builds its three renders (the old copy, the in-place render and the new copy) with dataclasses.replace, which constructs each new worker from dataclass fields. A template set on one worker instance reaches none of the three renders; replace copies a view held in fields into all of them.

Audited internals (read at Copier 9.18.1). The shim and its guard test MUST cover each Copier internal Boilerplate depends on: copier._main.Worker and copier._template.Template; Worker._apply_update's construction of its three renders with dataclasses.replace; the copier._main.old_copy. and copier._main.new_copy. temporary-directory name prefixes (the prefix arguments of those two TemporaryDirectory calls), which the template property reads to tell the old copy from the other renders; the vcs_ref the old copy (the subproject template's commit) and the new copy (resolved_vcs_ref) carry, which is why the property cannot select a view by ref; and the private copier._main._operation ContextVar, which the post-walk task run sets to "update" because only run_copy, run_recopy and run_update set it (the as_operation decorator) and Copier's task runner reads it (in Worker._execute_tasks). The post-walk task run also enters Copier's tasks phase (copier._types.Phase.TASKS, the phase Worker.run_copy sets with Phase.use around Copier's own task run), so a task's when: sees _copier_phase == "tasks" as it does under Copier. The Worker subclass also overrides and calls Worker._ask, which compose's questionnaire pass calls to ask the full merged schema once without rendering, since Copier has no public call that only asks. It calls Worker._execute_tasks for the post-walk task run, and Worker._render_context and Worker._external_data for the rejected-answer check, which validates a recorded answer through copier._user_data.AnswersMap and Question as _ask does. A template Copier never builds itself registers its cleanup through Worker._cleanup_hooks and Template._cleanup, because rendering a VCS template clones it into a temporary directory that only _cleanup removes.

A relocation of Worker or Template inside Copier breaks compose and update in copier_types.py alone, where the guard test reports it, and the copier>=9.15,<10 pin bounds the Copier versions both paths run on. A test MUST drive one per-layer update through the subclass, since a symbol check does not see the dataclasses.replace contract the update walk depends on.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Scattered from copier import … across the codebase — every upgrade break surfaces in many files, and the top-level import path emits a deprecation warning.
  • Reimplement Copier's render/merge — large, duplicates Copier, contradicts ADR-001.
  • Vendor/fork Copier — maintenance burden out of proportion to the need.
  • Single audited import shim + version pin (chosen) — one change point on upgrade; the deep _main/_template paths avoid the deprecation warning.
  • Selecting the view by vcs_ref — rejected: when only an ancestor moves, the old copy, the new copy and the in-place render carry one ref and need different views.
  • A merged template set on one worker instance — rejected: dataclasses.replace rebuilds the update renders without it (Verification (2026-09-30)).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One file changes when Copier relocates these symbols; the import stays warning-free; ruff + pyright-strict clean.
  • Coupled to a private API: every Copier upgrade must be re-validated against the shim's guard test and the per-layer update test.
  • The >=9.15 floor is pragmatic, not a verification gap: 9.15 is the version in use and tested, and we deliberately do not support or look further back (possibly ever). The <10 cap forces re-validation at Copier's next major.
  • Re-architecture: this decision stands until the Copier integration is re-architected (e.g., adopting the evaluated file-based merged-template approach); this ADR is then rewritten in place.

docs.title: Verification (2026-06-09)
docs.text: copier_types.py is the only site importing Copier internals (grep); MergedTemplate subclasses the shim's Template (composition/rendering/models/merged_template.py:14); the guard test is present.

docs.title: Verification (2026-09-30)
docs.text:
Empirical run against the bundled project and streamlit templates (Copier 9.18.1, Windows, local git clones, --defaults, skip_tasks): both layers cloned into tagged git repositories, a project composed by boilerplate new and rehomed to the clones. Each new tag edited the README line that renders project_name and appended a file rendering seven inherited answers; a user line appended to the README before the first update had to survive.

Mechanism Orders Result A Worker subclass holding the merged questions and the extension union in fields, template built from them; Worker.run_update() called on the subclass instance per layer with the union of the per-layer answers files as data (the merge order of the union was not recorded) project then streamlit, and streamlit then project; v2 then v3 All 8 updates exit 0, with no conflict markers, no .rej files and no unmerged paths; the five inherited answers that Copier records persist in streamlit's answers file after every update; the two derived values render (widget_co, widget-co); the package directory and the user line survive worker.template set to the merged template on one instance Both orders The first streamlit update exits 0 but its answers file loses the five inherited answers and the derived values render empty; the second update pauses with conflict markers in README.md and the probe file

docs.title: Verification (2026-10-06)
docs.text: Empirical run against the bundled project and streamlit templates (Copier 9.18.1, Windows, git 2.55, one tagged git repository per layer, project and streamlit composed at v4 under their scoped views): project v5 removed a question its v4 files rendered, and project was updated v4 to v5 through a Worker subclass holding one scoped view per ref. The old copy rendered under the v4 view with the value recorded in project's answers file, also in a control run that passed no data at all, and the update finished with no conflict markers, no .rej files and no unmerged paths; the answers file then dropped the removed question. The per-layer views, their answers files and their extensions are recorded in ADR-015 §Verification (2026-10-06).

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs
docs.text:
• ADR-001 records the decision to adopt Copier. This ADR records the mechanism of that integration: Boilerplate depends on Copier's internal Worker and Template through the shim. A file-based merged-template approach that would avoid the internal dependency was evaluated and not adopted.
  • ADR-015 — the update walk this shim serves: every render of every layer's update sees the layer's scoped view at the versions it renders.

docs.title: ADR-003: Render with Copier unsafe — no task/extension consent gate
docs.text: Status: Accepted (current posture; deliberately diverges from the target security model)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The security design (Security model, Template system and discovery) specifies a default-deny posture: template tasks and Jinja2 extensions run only behind user consent (--allow-tasks/--allow-extensions), a package allowlist, an import blocklist, a SandboxedEnvironment, and a binary trust model. None of that is implemented — see Implementation status (trust / sandbox / consent: "no code exists").

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Every operation that runs a layer through Copier's Worker grants unsafe per layer, exactly where that layer needs it: when the _jinja_extensions union of the layer's scoped view is non-empty (04 §Copier Worker Interface) or when the operation will run the layer's tasks or migrations. Compose, update and add follow this one rule. A layer's update step reads two views, the recorded release's and the target's, and needs the grant when either does. A layer that needs nothing keeps Copier's own consent gate. There is no prompt, sandbox, trust level, or blocklist anywhere — whatever a template declares, executes.

Public exposure is sanctioned under this posture while template sources are local and deliberately chosen: strangers installing the CLI and rendering templates is in scope and does not wait for the trust model.

The posture keys on the template's source, not the destination, so new and add are equal under it.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
• The trust / consent / sandbox infrastructure is not built; gating on a non-existent system would block all rendering.
  • Template sources are local-only — the bundled first-party templates, plus local directories the user supplies deliberately (--templates-dir), which are user-chosen rather than first-party: build_template_catalog (cli/utils.py) constructs a DirectoryTemplateRepository directly, and a Git-backed repository remains unimplemented. The code an unsafe render executes is code the user already has on disk and chose to render — the same trust act as running any downloaded script.
  • Publication changes who runs boilerplate, not where template code comes from, so going public leaves that boundary intact.
  • Recording the gap explicitly so it is a conscious posture, not silent drift.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rendering a template that declares tasks or extensions executes them as arbitrary local code with no gate. Acceptable only while sources are local and deliberately chosen — bundled first-party templates or user-supplied directories.
  • This MUST be tightened before remote/Git sources, a catalog with third-party entries, or community templates ship. That work is the trust model in Security model and will get its own ADR when built.
  • The design docs describe the target (default-deny); this ADR is the honest record of the current posture and the divergence.

docs.title: Expiry
docs.text: This ADR records a temporary posture, not the target. It expires when the trust / consent / sandbox model (Security model) is implemented — which MUST happen before any remote, catalog, or community template source ships. A new ADR will then record default-deny as the current posture and supersede this one.

docs.title: Verification (2026-08-15)
docs.text: composition/rendering/engine.py computes layer_needs_unsafe from the merged extension union and the layer's runnable tasks, and passes "unsafe": layer_needs_unsafe per Worker invocation. Grep across src/ for trust|sandbox|consent|blocklist → no implementation.

docs.title: ADR-004: Coarse exit-code taxonomy, with fine diagnosis in BP* codes
docs.text: Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A CLI can expose either a rich set of numeric exit codes or a coarse set plus a separate diagnostic channel. The design (Data models) argues against exit-code proliferation.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The CLI defines exactly six exit codes — SUCCESS=0, FAILURE=1, CONFIG_ERROR=2, VALIDATION_ERROR=3, ACTION_REQUIRED=4, USER_CANCELLED=130 (constants.py; the canonical table is Data models §Exit Codes) — and maps the BoilerplateError exception hierarchy onto them in one place, the cli_error_handler decorator (cli/utils.py); the ActionRequiredError base exception routes to ACTION_REQUIRED=4. USER_CANCELLED=130 uses 128+SIGINT, the Click/Typer convention for Ctrl-C, and cli_error_handler maps UserCancelledError, raised when the user cancels an interactive prompt, to it (Data models §Exit Codes). Fine-grained diagnosis is carried by per-exception BP* codes and remediation hints (surfaced as Fix: lines), not by additional exit codes.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Rich numeric exit codes per error class — couples scripts to internal taxonomy; proliferates.
  • Six coarse codes + structured BP* codes/remediation (chosen) — stable script contract, with rich human/machine diagnosis carried out-of-band.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Scripts branch on a small, stable set; detail comes from the BP* code + message.
  • A new error maps to one of the coarse codes; contributors add a BP* code + remediation rather than a new exit code.
  • ACTION_REQUIRED=4 is reserved for recoverable workflow pauses (Data models §Exit Codes) — the operation needs user intervention before it can complete, as distinct from a hard failure (exit 1). MergeConflictError (the composition config-merge error) is a hard failure and stays on exit 1; the update file-conflict pause is the condition that exits 4.

docs.title: Verification (2026-06-09, re-verified 2026-07-16)
docs.text: constants.py defines the six-value ExitCode IntEnum; cli/utils.py cli_error_handler maps exception classes to them; common/exceptions.py carries error_code + remediation; covered by tests/boilerplate/cli/test_utils.py.

docs.title: ADR-005: Integrity model — filesystem-permission-based; cryptographic signing deferred
docs.text: Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
In Boilerplate's current operational model, one file carries security-relevant content that could be tampered with to alter behavior:

  1. The lock file (boilerplate.lock) — records the committed state of every template layer in a composition, the per-layer Copier-answers hashes, and the resolved layer ordering. lock verify uses it as the source of truth for supply-chain drift detection.

An attacker who can write to this file can neutralise a key control: corrupting or substituting the lock file silences drift detection. Its integrity therefore matters.

It is a local file on the operator's machine. The immediate threat the current control addresses is an unprivileged local process with write access to it — not remote substitution. The current release addresses this with filesystem permissions and defers cryptographic signing, which the spec names as "planned for a future release."

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The current release relies on filesystem-permission-based integrity for the lock file (boilerplate.lock) — the sole filesystem-permission-protected artifact — and performs no cryptographic signature verification.

For the lock file, the spec states (10-security §lock verify):

Lock file integrity (no cryptographic signature; the file is trusted as-is)

and:

lock verify is a supply chain drift detector, not a full integrity guarantee. For stronger assurance, combine with content signing (planned for a future release).

docs.title: (a) Cryptographic content signing — DEFERRED to a future release
docs.text: Sign the lock file (e.g., with a project-scoped key, Sigstore, or a similar content-signing scheme) so that tampering is detectable regardless of filesystem ACLs. The spec explicitly names this as "planned for a future release." It is the stronger long-term control. It is deferred for now: the signing infrastructure is not yet built, and at the current scope filesystem permissions are the proportionate control for a file that lives on the operator's own machine.

docs.title: (b) Filesystem-permission-based integrity — CHOSEN (current)
docs.text: Rely on OS-level access controls (POSIX permissions / Windows ACLs) to prevent unauthorised writes. Warn at runtime on overly permissive configurations. No implementation cost beyond the warning check; consistent with the current posture of treating the lock file as a local file guarded by filesystem permissions.

docs.title: (c) No integrity control at all — REJECTED
docs.text: Treating the lock file as fully trusted without any check or guidance would silently degrade the security posture below what the spec intends and provide no operational signal when ACLs are mis-set. The warning-on-permissive-ACL requirement distinguishes option (b) from this rejected baseline.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• lock verify is a drift detector, not an integrity guarantee. A local adversary with write access to the lock file can substitute values undetected.
  • This limitation is acknowledged in-spec and is acceptable today, where the lock file lives on the operator's machine and cryptographic content signing is not yet available.
  • This decision SHOULD be revisited when cryptographic content signing — the spec's "planned for a future release" — is implemented, which strengthens integrity beyond filesystem ACLs; a new ADR will record that change.

docs.title: Authoritative spec references
docs.text: • 10-security §lock verify — lock-file integrity scope and the deferred content-signing note

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs
docs.text: ADR-003 records a related gap: permissive unsafe rendering with no consent gate, ahead of the trust model. Like this ADR, it is a conscious, bounded current posture that expires when the target control is implemented — there, the trust model; here, cryptographic content signing.

docs.title: ADR-006: Git-backed template distribution — monorepo authoring, published per-template repos
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Scope note. This ADR commits the PROD-001 item first_party_template_distribution — the update spine depends on it. For what exists in code today, see Implementation status.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
boilerplate update orchestrates copier update, which performs the three-way merge. Copier's update is git-only: it computes the merge base by diffing the template's old git ref against the new ref. Templates authored as subdirectories of the package have no per-template git history and no version tags, and a pip install-ed wheel carries no .git at all, so a layer rendered from the wheel cannot be updated by copier update.

ADR-015 sharpens what a distribution channel has to satisfy: the per-layer answers file is the distribution contract. Whatever Copier records there as _src_path and _commit must stay resolvable by vanilla Copier, on any machine, indefinitely — that is what keeps every git-backed layer updatable, by boilerplate update and by the escape hatch, a hand-run vanilla copier update -a .copier-answers.<layer>.yml per layer with its ancestors' answers passed as data (ADR-015). A channel that cannot be named in an answers file and re-resolved later is not a channel.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Templates are authored in a monorepo (templates as subdirectories — good authoring DX, atomic cross-template changes). At release time each template is deterministically extracted (git subtree split) into its own git repository carrying full history and vX.Y.Z tags. Those repositories are published, and they are the canonical first-party distribution channel.

  • What gets recorded. new and compose render first-party layers from the published repository, so the answers file records the published URL as _src_path and a real tag as _commit, and the lock records the same. Nothing a user's project points at is machine-local.
  • Versioning. Per-template tags (vX.Y.Z). The Template Specifier name@version maps to "the name repo at tag vX.Y.Z", and Copier's --vcs-ref is an honest passthrough. One repository per template gives each template its own version stream natively, with no mapping layer.
  • A repository is a release train. Templates share a version stream only when they genuinely release together — one repository carries exactly one PEP 440 tag series, and Copier resolves "latest" from it.
  • The wheel bundle is deferred. Shipping bundles inside the wheel and cloning them to a per-user cache remains available as an offline seed cache, built only on demonstrated demand. A cache path MUST NEVER be recorded as _src_path: Copier records the source it actually used, and masking a local path behind a canonical URL would mean rewriting Copier's answers file, which ADR-015 forbids. Until such a cache exists, the offline and air-gapped story is org-local clones or mirrors of the published repositories — pure Copier mechanics, portable inside the org, with rehoming a one-line _src_path edit.
  • Third-party parity. A single-template repository is Copier's mainstream idiom, so third-party authors get first-party treatment by doing the ordinary thing. Monorepo authoring plus extraction is tooling we may share later, never a convention anyone must adopt to be a first-class template.
  • Reproducibility invariant. The extraction is deterministic over un-rewritten history: same source commit → same extracted SHA across builds, so a lock's and an answers file's recorded commit keeps resolving against the published repositories. Published repository history is therefore append-only — never force-pushed, never re-created — because users' answers files and locks record commit SHAs from it, and a re-extraction that produced different SHAs would orphan every recorded commit.

URL durability is a cutover coupling. Published repository names are recorded permanently in user projects, so their naming rides the public-cutover naming decision and must be settled before the first release that records them.

Sequencing. The build-pipeline responsibility is deterministic extraction plus publishing; the per-user cache leaves the critical path entirely. One consequence is open, not settled: because a project is only updatable if its answers files name a resolvable git source, un-stubbing the git source became a prerequisite of the updatable-project outcome rather than a catalog-federation nicety. The roadmap owns that sequencing question.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Shared bundle or monorepo served directly to Copier (one repository, templates as subdirectories via _subdirectory:, simplest build) — rejected on two independent grounds. Copier reads _subdirectory from the repository's root config, so serving several templates from one repository requires a root copier.yml with a dynamic _subdirectory and every template's questions when:-gated in that one file; per-template question schemas stop being self-contained artifacts. And one repository carries exactly one PEP 440 tag series, so independently versioned templates either release in lockstep — exporting spurious version bumps to downstream extends constraints — or become invisible to Copier's version resolution.
  • Published per-template repositories (chosen) — clean Copier semantics (one template, one repository, plain tags, no _subdirectory:), forkable artifacts, per-template version streams, at the cost of build-time extraction and a determinism discipline: don't rewrite history, pin the split tool.
  • Authoring in separate repositories from the start, federated by submodules — dominates on artifact realness but makes a coupled cross-template change three commits, adds contributor friction at debut, and turns a pinned set back into lockstep by another name. Deferred as an organization convention, not the first-party mechanism.
  • Extraction into bundles shipped inside the wheel — rejected: the per-layer answers file is the distribution contract, and a per-user cache path recorded as _src_path does not resolve on any other machine. The bundle survives only as the deferred seed cache above, which is never the recorded source.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A new build-pipeline responsibility: deterministic per-template extraction plus publishing, with tags kept in sync with each template's boilerplate.yml version — the release-pipeline half of that is INT-010 (see the intentions register). Publishing the extracted repositories falls outside INT-010 as currently scoped: its not_included excludes template publishing and registry hosting, so no intention owns the canonical channel today. Either INT-010 widens or a new intention takes it; that ownership question is open, and this ADR does not settle it.
  • First-party templates become ordinary remote git sources, which meets ADR-003's own stated trigger for tightening: its permissive render posture is acceptable only while sources are local and deliberately chosen, and its rationale — that an unsafe render executes code the user already has on disk — does not hold for a template fetched over the network. Whether that trip-wire re-scopes (to third-party or otherwise untrusted provenance) or fires as written (consent gating lands with the git source) is an open question ADR-003 owns and must resolve before the git source ships. This ADR does not decide it.
  • A default install needs network access on first use: first-party layers render from the published repositories, so scaffolding no longer works from the wheel alone. That interacts with the designed --offline semantics (design 05) — an offline run depends on an org-local clone or mirror already being present — and it is what the deferred seed cache would address.
  • The create path carries the git dependency as well as update: a project is updatable only if what new and compose recorded is a resolvable git source.
  • update dogfoods against the published repositories, or against local clones during development — Copier treats the two identically.
  • Air-gapped environment provisioning is a separate, harder problem (proto/tools) owned by Environment Provisioning (design 08), not here.

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs
docs.text:
• ADR-001 — "orchestrate Copier"; this is how first-party templates become git-orchestratable.
  • ADR-003 — making first-party templates remote git sources meets ADR-003's own trigger for tightening the permissive render posture; whether that trip-wire re-scopes to untrusted provenance or fires as written is ADR-003's open question, to be resolved before the git source ships.
  • ADR-007 — consumes the per-template git history this ADR ships.
  • ADR-015 — supplies the answers-file-as-contract invariant this decision is derived from.

docs.title: ADR-007: Safe-update model — conflict is a pause, structural change is migration-driven
docs.text: Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: boilerplate update performs a per-layer copier update; Copier performs the only merge (INT-003, 04 §Safe Update). Three questions bear on the update model: (1) what happens on a merge conflict, (2) what happens when the template's extends chain changed since lock time (the ADR-001 HIGH-severity gap), and (3) whether update must walk one version at a time within a layer when a template version can carry a migration. On (1), 06 §Step 5 specifies that a conflict brings back the finished layers with Copier's markers and exits 4 (ACTION_REQUIRED), after which the user resolves, commits and reruns boilerplate update, and Data models records the pause as the conflict MigrationRecord state. The MergeConflictError → exit 1 row in the Data models Error-Hierarchy table is a different condition — the composition-time config-merge error (two layers declaring incompatible values for one key, per Composition engine) — unrelated to the update file-conflict. This ADR states the model on (1) and decides (2) and (3).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A conflict is a designed pause, not a failure. On a layer reporting conflicts, update stops the walk, copies the layers finished so far into the working tree as uncommitted changes with Copier's conflict markers, records a conflict MigrationRecord, writes no lock, and exits 4 (ACTION_REQUIRED). The user resolves the markers, commits as with plain Copier, and reruns boilerplate update; the rerun resumes from the conflict record, which names each layer's target and the layers the walk finished, and writes the new lock and a success record. The user sets the partial update aside as 06 §Setting a partial update aside describes. Every other error before the copy back removes the staging worktree (06 §Staging worktree), which leaves the working tree unchanged with no lock and no migration record, and exits by the error's class (1 for an unexpected failure). INT-003's "atomic, no partial state" guarantee applies to failures; a pause is intentional.

A changed extends chain is handled by author migrations, not provenance inference.

  • Added layer → a fresh copier copy that writes only paths not already present, so a descendant's file keeps its precedence as at compose, + new answers file, folded into the lock; the update reports the colliding paths it left.
  • Removed layer (one that joined through extends and that the root's target no longer reaches; a layer add introduced stays, 06 §Step 3) → Boilerplate drops it from the managed set; file cleanup is the job of a Copier _migrations script in the template that removed the dependency (the removed layer's own migrations never run, because it is no longer in the chain). Copier runs migrations across the version range in a single pass — Boilerplate does not loop (see §Version jumps).
  • No migration provided → safe-orphan + WARN: leave the files in place (now unmanaged), name them, and give guidance. Boilerplate never infers file provenance and never auto-deletes.
  • Dry-run preview cannot predict migration file effects (they are arbitrary scripts — Copier's --pretend has the same limit); the plan shows version/layer deltas and which migrations will run.

Update behavior is per-layer, keyed on git-backing (see ADR-006): published-repo and local-git layers update three-way. A plain local-directory layer (commit: null, marking a non-git source) does not update: Copier has no two-way fallback, so a layer with no recoverable old ref refuses to update, and boilerplate update skips it with a warning (ADR-015 point 5; §06).

commit: null costs a ref to check out, not recoverable information — but it does not heal itself. The lock records the layer's version even when commit is null, and Copier reconstructs the three-way merge base by re-rendering the old version rather than storing one, so nothing needed for a later merge is lost. What a null commit does withhold is the ref Copier checks out to do that re-render, and Copier resolves that ref from _commit/_src_path in its own answers file — which ADR-015 forbids Boilerplate from rewriting. A first-party layer created before ADR-006's published repositories exist therefore stays copy-only until its _src_path is rehomed to the published repository by hand: the documented one-line edit of ADR-015 point 5. After that edit the recorded version resolves to a tag, Copier reconstructs the base by re-render, and the three-way merge proceeds normally. Copy-only is permanent only for genuinely non-git sources (a user's plain local directory, which never gains a tag). Recording the real commit at creation stays strictly stronger (an immutable pin vs. a mutable tag) and remains the target.

Git-backed distribution (ADR-006) is not a prerequisite of lock creation. Because a commit: null lock withholds only a ref and no recoverable information (above), new / lock / verify / adopt do not wait on the published distribution; what they cannot promise for a layer created before it is a clean three-way update, which needs the one-line _src_path rehome first. The rehome is a user-run edit, so the distribution work gates the clean-three-way quality of update-apply and does not block lock creation. Where it lands in the sequence is the roadmap's call.

docs.title: Version jumps stay single-pass; migrations are jump-safe by authoring contract
docs.text:
update crosses a layer's version range in a single pass and does not walk one version at a time, even when the crossed versions carry migrations. The evidence is in §Verification, which established:

  • Copier's migration model is fix-up, not replay. A migration's version: key is a gate (target ≥ version > source), not a checkpoint. In a v1→v3 jump every crossed migration runs exactly once, in list order, all against the same tree — the pre-update tree for before-stage entries, the fully rendered target tree for after-stage ones (the default stage). No intermediate tree is ever materialized. A migration that assumes it sees the tree as of the version it names is therefore wrong under any jump.
  • The migration list comes only from the target version's copier.yml. Nothing is read from intermediate tags. Two consequences bind template authors: every historical migration entry MUST be carried forward in every later release, or jumpers silently skip it; and a stepped walk executes each intermediate tag's own copy of a migration, so stepping and jumping can run different code for the same nominal migration — stepping is not a safer subset of jumping, it is a different execution.

Why stepping is not adopted anyway (reasoning from the above, not separately measured): each step is another three-way merge against the same layer, so each is another chance to pause on the same overridden files, and — because migrations are arbitrary commands with no layer awareness (below) — another chance for a base-layer migration to touch overlay-owned files. Stepping also requires Boilerplate to enumerate and walk intermediate tags: a loop Copier does not provide (verified absent from its update path in 9.15.0), which ADR-001 says we do not build for ourselves.

The authoring contract that makes single-pass safe (first-party templates MUST; documented for third parties):

  1. Jump-safe: a migration inspects actual state before acting and is idempotent — never "the tree is at version N-1, so move X to Y" but "if X exists, move it to Y." It must be correct when run against the target tree with any supported older version as the source.
  2. Carried forward: historical migration entries stay in _migrations in every later release, in ascending version order — Copier executes the list in declaration order rather than sorting by version (read from Copier's source; ordering was not exercised empirically).
  3. Layer-scoped by discipline: a migration touches only files its own template owns. Copier has no ownership model — a base-layer migration can overwrite an overlay-owned file silently, and a later update of the owning layer will not detect, conflict on, or repair it.
  4. Conflict-aware: an after-stage migration MUST tolerate conflict markers in files it reads. Migrations run even when the merge left unresolved conflicts — Copier reports exit 0 and writes the new _commit regardless — and a migration that exits non-zero fails the whole update. Destructive or parsing work belongs behind a state check, not in a bare after migration.

Orchestration consequences. boilerplate update MUST detect the conflict pause itself — via git unmerged paths or a marker scan, never Copier's exit code — and MUST halt the layer walk at the first paused layer rather than running later layers over an unresolved tree. --skip-tasks does not skip migrations (documented Copier behavior), so there is no built-in defer; the pause envelope is Boilerplate's. An update that actually crosses a declared migration requires Copier's --trust (a template whose migrations all fall outside the crossed range does not), which boilerplate update supplies for first-party templates under ADR-003 and must gate for untrusted sources — note that the first release introducing a migration is where an otherwise-working non-interactive pipeline starts failing (Copier exits 4 and applies nothing at all) unless trust is passed.

A paused update resumes from its conflict record, not from version comparison. The conflict MigrationRecord names each layer's target version and the layers the paused walk finished (02 §MigrationRecord). When it is the last record, update skips the finished layers, walks the remaining layers to the recorded targets and refuses an explicit --target-version that differs from them (04 §Safe Update). A layer whose own version did not move still ran under its ancestors' new versions in the paused walk, so only the record tells a finished layer from an unfinished one.

Deferred, not rejected: an opt-in --via <version> stepped walk, if a first-party migration is ever found that cannot be made jump-safe. That is a template-authoring failure with a tooling escape hatch, not the default model; building it before such a case exists would add a version-walking loop with no demonstrated need.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Rollback-on-conflict — simpler (drops the conflict-pause path), but it throws away the merge attempt and hands the user nothing to resolve; it fights Copier's native model. Rejected.
  • A Boilerplate-owned backup directory with update --continue and update --abort — rejected: the staging worktree leaves the checkout untouched until the walk ends, a paused update can be set aside (06 §Setting a partial update aside) and a rerun of update finishes it, so a second state machine adds nothing Copier and git lack (ADR-001).
  • Pause-with-markers (chosen) — Copier-native, preserves work, costs the continuation slice.
  • Removed layers: auto-delete uniquely-owned files (needs a per-layer file manifest in the lock; carries deletion risk) vs migrations + safe-orphan (chosen) — author-declared, no data-loss risk.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The update CLI is update, rerun after a conflict (git/Copier idiom), with --skip-answered (Copier's name); --dry-run (preferred over Copier's --pretend where git and Copier idioms clash); --prereleases (Copier's name). Operationally-scoped flags may be set per-layer via an allowlisted params object; answers stay merged (the singular-template experience).
  • Migrations are arbitrary code — fine for first-party templates (ADR-003), gated behind the trust model before untrusted templates run them.
  • Authoring guidance (removed-layer cleanup migration, breaking-change migration) is owned by INT-009; init-template may scaffold a commented _migrations stub.

docs.title: Verification (2026-07-28)
docs.text:
Copier 9.15.0 on Windows, git 2.55. Fixtures: a single-template repo tagged v1/v2/v3, each tag changing a probe file whose content names its version, with version-gated _migrations entries whose commands append a JSON record of the migration id, stage, VERSION_FROM/VERSION_TO/VERSION_CURRENT, and the probe file's content as read at execution time — so the log proves which tree each migration saw. Two-layer variants added an overlay template overwriting a base-rendered file. An independent adversarial run repeated the two load-bearing claims with differently shaped fixtures and a marker distinguishing each tag's copy of a migration.

Claim Result Jump v1→v3 runs every crossed migration exactly once Confirmed — both fired, ascending, one update Intermediate migrations see the target tree, not an intermediate one Confirmed — after-stage probes read the v3 tree; before-stage probes read the pre-update tree; no v2 tree ever existed The migration list is read only from the target version's config Confirmed — a migration present only in v3's config still fired for a v1→v3 jump, and a stepped walk ran each tag's own copy A step-wise walk runs each migration once against a true intermediate tree Confirmed — and re-running an already-current update is a no-op Migrations run despite unresolved merge conflicts Confirmed — the after-stage migration read a file containing conflict markers; exit 0; the answers file advanced to the new tag A migration can silently overwrite another layer's file Confirmed — a base-layer migration replaced overlay-owned content, and the overlay's own later update neither detected nor repaired it

Read from Copier's source rather than exercised: _migrations executes in declaration order rather than sorted by version; --skip-tasks does not gate migrations (also stated in Copier's own configuration docs); trust is demanded only when a version-gated migration falls inside the crossed range. Measured incidentally: an update crossing a migration without --trust exits 4 and applies nothing at all.

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs
docs.text:
• ADR-006 — supplies the per-template git history that update diffs against.
  • ADR-015 — the per-layer walk this ADR's update model executes; its verification records the companion per-layer run, while the migration evidence is recorded in §Verification above.
  • ADR-003 — migrations share the task/extension trust surface.
  • Data models and Project lifecycle — own the conflict model this ADR states: the update conflict state exits 4.

docs.title: ADR-008: Distribution name — publish as boilerplate-cli, keep boilerplate as the command and brand
docs.text:
Status: Pending — the default decision below stands unless the current PyPI boilerplate owner agrees to surrender the name. A voluntary-transfer request to the incumbent is outstanding; PEP 541 is the fallback escalation. This ADR must resolve to Accepted before the first PyPI publish, because a PyPI distribution name is effectively immutable once published. It does not gate the git-URL-first launch (uv tool install git+https://github.com/TheRealBillSiegler/boilerplate.git) or the first public tag, which publish no wheel.

Scope note. This is a packaging / go-public decision, not an architecture one. It gates INT-007 (PyPI installability) and INT-010 (publish pipeline), both in the intentions register — the PyPI path only; it does not gate the git-URL-first launch, which consumes no PyPI distribution name. It does not touch the import package, the CLI surface, or any persisted schema.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The PyPI distribution name boilerplate is already taken by an unrelated package — Kuba Janoszek's "Easy to use tool for painless project layout templating" (latest 1.2.4, 6 releases). That is not a bare name collision: it is the same niche (project templating) and it is already at 1.x while this project is at 0.2.0. A pip install-ed wheel needs a unique PyPI name, so the project cannot publish under boilerplate.

Everything else in the project — the import package (src/boilerplate/), the CLI command (boilerplate new), the repository, the docs, and the brand — uses boilerplate, and the maintainer values the name: it is self-referential (a tool that emits boilerplate, named Boilerplate), a wink that fires on contact with no jargon. An exploration of replacement names (four rounds, ~220 candidate-evaluations) found no free standalone name that reproduces that wink: the wink-firing words (plate, boil, boiler, chase, forme, stamp) are all taken precisely because they are common, and the free survivors are either footnote-jokes (potboiler, stetlock) or flat descriptions (roughcut). Verified free as of 2026-06-20: boilerplate-cli on both PyPI and GitHub.

Mis-install hazard (the load-bearing risk). pip install boilerplate does not fail — it silently installs the other, same-niche package. A user who guesses the obvious command gets someone else's project. This is worse than a dead name; it is an active mis-install trap, and it is the primary reason to pursue acquiring the bare name.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Conditional on the outstanding name-acquisition request:

  • Default (name not acquired): the PyPI distribution name is boilerplate-cli. The import package, the [project.scripts] console command, the repository, and the brand stay boilerplate. In pyproject.toml: name = "boilerplate-cli", with [project.scripts] boilerplate = "..." unchanged. This rename lands at/before the first PyPI publish, not for launch: pyproject.toml name currently remains boilerplate (with get_version("boilerplate") in __init__.py), and the git-URL install consumes no distribution name, so no rename is required to go public.
  • Contingency (name acquired): if the current owner transfers boilerplate (voluntary surrender, or failing that a granted PEP 541 request), the distribution publishes as boilerplate and the -cli suffix is dropped. The distribution name lives in pyproject / wheel metadata and install docs, not in any persisted user file (the lock and the EnvironmentProvisionRecord store no distribution name), so a switch is a packaging change, not a user-data migration — but it must land before the first PyPI publish.

The primary install path is the bootstrap installer (scripts/install.ps1 on Windows; see Install), which provides uv and installs boilerplate from git (uv tool install git+https://github.com/TheRealBillSiegler/boilerplate.git) — consuming no PyPI distribution name. If/when published to PyPI, the PyPI-specific install instructions MUST lead with the exact pip install line for the chosen distribution name and carry a one-line disambiguation note ("not the unrelated boilerplate package"). The OIDC trusted publisher binds to the chosen PyPI project name plus the release repo and workflow; if the name changes after acquisition, that binding changes with it.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• boilerplate-cli distribution, boilerplate everything-else (chosen default) — keeps the brand the maintainer values; cost is a permanent install-name ≠ command-name asymmetry and the mis-install trap, both mitigated only by documentation.
  • Acquire boilerplate (pursued in parallel) — the best outcome: no papercut, no trap, brand intact. Rejected as the plan of record because it depends on a third party (and, as fallback, PyPI's discretion under PEP 541, where the incumbent's same-niche 1.x package makes a forced claim weak). The launch cannot be gated on it; it is upside, not the baseline.
  • Real rename (e.g. boilerkit) — a clean single-token brand with no papercut and no trap. Rejected because it discards the literal boilerplate brand and its printing-plate heritage, which the maintainer explicitly wanted to keep.
  • Fully-clean alternate token (e.g. plateworks) — PyPI and GitHub both free, but the self-referential wink is weak (most developers do not bridge "plate" → boilerplate). Rejected.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The default path ships an install-name/command-name asymmetry that surfaces only on PyPI. The primary install surfaces (README, quickstart, install docs) lead with the bootstrap installer / git-URL install and are unaffected by the distribution name; if/when published, the PyPI-specific instructions use pip install boilerplate-cli (or uvx --from boilerplate-cli boilerplate).
  • This decision must be resolved (Accepted, under one branch or the other) before the first PyPI publish — not merely before the first public tag, since a git-URL-first public tag publishes no wheel. After the first PyPI publish the distribution name is fixed. See the release gate in Build-out roadmap.
  • The OIDC trusted-publisher configuration is downstream of the final name and of the decision to publish to PyPI at all; it is not required for the git-URL-first launch. Do not configure it until this ADR is Accepted and a PyPI publish is imminent.

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs and intentions
docs.text:
See the intentions register for the full definitions of both:

  • INT-007 — org-independence / PyPI-installability gate; this decision is a prerequisite of "installable from PyPI."
  • INT-010 — publish pipeline / OIDC trusted publisher; binds to the name chosen here.

docs.title: ADR-009: Environment provider protocol — proto is one provider, not the floor
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Scope note. The shape recorded here — proto as one provider behind an abstraction — is load-bearing for how the pillar grows, and it reconciles a coherence gap (see Context).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Environment Provisioning is specified around proto as the toolchain installer (08-environment-provisioning.md, ADR-001) — ProtoWorker is the only provisioning interface. Two pressures push against that single-tool shape:

  1. Proto-optional provisioning. The bootstrap script (install.ps1) provisions tools via winget, not proto. A user who wants a winget-based toolchain with no proto at all has no first-class way to express it; with ProtoWorker as the only interface, proto is a floor, not a choice.
  2. A "custom command" escape hatch with a promotion path. The desire to run an ad-hoc provisioning step and later "roll it up into something managed."

Both collide with the project's non-negotiable Reproducibility is mandatory (01-overview.md §Core Principles) and the fail-closed trust model: an arbitrary command is non-deterministic, non-pinnable arbitrary code.

A design exploration (prior art: mise backends, asdf plugins, devcontainer Features vs lifecycle hooks, Copier _tasks, proto/Nix; plus adversarial verification against this repo's own principles) converged on the model below. install.ps1 invoking winget is user-run bootstrap — the user invokes the package manager, not Boilerplate. The orchestrated provider protocol (Boilerplate invoking a gated installer) is the only path by which Boilerplate installs a package, and the Trust paragraph below gates it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Generalize ProtoWorker into a Provider Protocol; proto becomes one kind, not the interface. A profile MAY contain zero proto. The abstraction is a closed set of declarative provider kinds dispatched by a registry — explicitly not an open arbitrary-command runner (an open runner is the exact thing that voids reproducibility and the fail-closed trust model).

Every provider kind implements three methods:

  • provision(spec) — idempotent; converges to the pinned target. Idempotency is a precondition because "re-run env apply" is the only recovery contract (02 §EnvironmentProvisionRecord). Absent → install; present and satisfies the pin → adopt (record provenance + observed version, no reinstall); present but violates the pin → fail closed (BP_ENV_ADOPT_PIN_CONFLICT).
  • verify(spec) — integrity + an exact-version post-condition probe (presence-only command -v checks are insufficient). Shared typed return carrying an integrity-strength tier so env status renders all kinds uniformly.
  • resolved_state(spec) — a deterministic pinned-state record.

Initial kinds (closed enum):

  • proto — declarative versioned tools; keeps its WASM-sandbox trust posture and .protolock. Its resolved_state delegates to (hashes) .protolock — no competing env.lock, so "orchestrate, don't replace" holds (02 §Environment Lock Strategy).
  • pinned-artifact — the disciplined form of "custom command": a content-pinned fetch-verify-run (exact version + per-platform https URL + mandatory per-platform sha256 + a version-assertion probe). Byte-reproducible. This is genuinely first-party (nothing external to orchestrate), which ADR-001's two-pillar-orchestration framing must admit alongside orchestrated providers. Free-form shell, unpinned fetch, curl | sh, and host-mutating sudo are prohibited in this kind.
  • system-package — winget / apt / brew. This is "make the existing advisory packages / PackageRequirement field (already carrying source + optional version) actually provision, gated," not a new concept. Optional version: absent → latest today; exact/range later (plural-shape, additive). Records the resolved version into the lock. Best-effort tier (see Reproducibility).
  • package-index — folds the duplicated uv.toml fetch/verify/seed out of install.ps1 / setup-wsl-env.sh. (Note overlap with the plain-file profile.toml loader of ADR-010 — see Consequences.)

Raw arbitrary shell is CUT from this decision. Its effect cannot be locked (you can hash the command string, not its side effects). If ever added, it needs its own ADR and an explicit amendment to the "Reproducibility is mandatory" principle — not a smuggled reproducible:false carve-out.

"Roll up into managed" = promote a definition, not a snapshot. Scaffold-not-snapshot (operator supplies version + URL + per-platform sha256 + verify-probe; a past side-effect's content hash and upstream URL cannot be auto-recovered on a fresh host), operator-performed, out-of-band (never self-declared in the file that ships the step — self-promotion through composition is privilege escalation). Identity / lock-key stays stable across rungs (inline → catalog-named → registered); only the locator changes, so promotion is a registration, not a rewrite.

Lock & reproducibility. No separate env.lock; per-provider resolved state lands in the provider_states map of the EnvironmentProvisionRecord (.boilerplate/environment.yml). Integrity tiers, surfaced honestly (never hidden behind a uniform interface):

Tier Providers Guarantee Checksum-locked proto (.protolock), pinned-artifact (sha256) same bytes across time Version-pinned (best-effort) system-package same declared version; bytes are the package manager's word

Recorded version is a floor honored on re-apply: declaration > recorded floor > latest. env status reports drift floor-vs-latest without silently re-pinning; a deliberate relock advances it. This promotes provider_states from a "state, not audit" projection to a resolution input — 02 §EnvironmentProvisionRecord must be amended to say so. Unpinned-latest is allowed (the declaration says "latest"; env apply records the resolved version) — state plainly that this extends the principle's scope-note logic to the provider domain. An explicit pin that cannot be satisfied fails closed (BP_ENV_*, record not written) — silently installing something else would reduce determinism.

Trust. Control is allowlist-as-ceiling + mandatory pins (parallel to the existing allowed_proto_plugins ceiling, 08 §allowed_proto_plugins Enforcement): allowlisted + pinned providers need no per-apply consent; ad-hoc / un-allowlisted inline entries prompt interactively and refuse in CI until promoted. The new gate extends the WASM-sandbox trust exemption at 08 §allowed_proto_plugins Enforcement to non-WASM providers — pinned-artifact fetches an https URL and system-package shells out, so the sandbox rationale that justified the exemption evaporates the moment a profile uses a non-proto kind.

Signing. Local executable-bearing profiles → note + filesystem-permission expectation (the same ADR-005 posture as boilerplate.lock); signing stays deferred (a writable-FS attacker who can edit the profile can edit PATH/binaries directly, and local verification is only as strong as a trust root the attacker can't touch). Remote/third-party provenance → signing belongs in the catalog trust model (03 §Trust, 10-security.md), not here.

Naming. The OS-host axis is platform (windows/wsl2/linux/macos, the existing packages key) — not substrate, which is locked to the enforcement-mode meaning (enforced/preconfigured, PROD-001, glossary).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Open arbitrary-command runner — maximally flexible; rejected: voids reproducibility-mandatory and fail-closed trust. Convergent prior art (Copier _tasks default-deny, devcontainer Features-vs-hooks) draws the same managed-vs-escape-hatch line.
  • Closed declarative kind-set (chosen) — every kind must implement verify with a real post-condition; a candidate that can't is, by construction, not a provider (the type-level test for escape-hatch abuse).
  • Separate Boilerplate env.lock — rejected; duplicates .protolock, violates orchestrate-don't-replace. provider_states in the existing record instead.
  • Reuse the template trust gate as-is — rejected; 08 §allowed_proto_plugins Enforcement exempts profiles because proto runs in WASM. Non-proto providers have no sandbox, so the gate must be extended, not reused unchanged.
