  • Capture as target (chosen) vs. keep the pillar thin in vision too — a design review flagged Environment Provisioning as "a second product for users who don't exist yet." Capturing the protocol as target honors both that concern and "can't YAGNI a vision"; building it now was rejected as scope creep against the scripts-first decision.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Installation is gated. Boilerplate installs a package only through an allowlisted, pinned provider, or through one the user consents to at the prompt, per the Trust paragraph above. The user-run install.ps1 bootstrap invokes the package manager itself, so it sits outside this rule.
  • Design-doc changes this decision forces: generalize ProtoWorker → Provider Protocol in 01 and 08; admit first-party providers (pinned-artifact) in ADR-001's pure-orchestrator framing; amend 02 §EnvironmentProvisionRecord (provider_states is a resolution input, recorded-version-as-floor) and resolve the tools-map vs provider_states duplication (derive tools).
  • Naming hazards: the plain-file profile.toml loader (ADR-010, settings/profile.py) vs the EnvironmentProfile (boilerplate-env.yml) overload; "provider" also names catalog/template git-sources. The package-index kind overlaps the profile.toml loader — prefer extending that loader over reinventing it.
  • Build decomposition (target): Unit 1 = Provider Protocol + provider_states + pinned-artifact (the proto-less tracer-bullet that proves the abstraction) → Unit 2a = proto refactored in + system-package + package-index → Unit 2b = active/named configs. Strictly sequential; 2a/2b depend on Unit 1's registry + schema. Substrate/platform becoming required on boilerplate-env.yml is a breaking change → major bump, spec the migration.

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs
docs.text:
• ADR-001 — "orchestrate, don't replace"; this widens Environment Provisioning to admit first-party providers (pinned-artifact) beside orchestrated ones (proto).
  • ADR-003 — the executable-bearing-provider trust gate shares the task/extension consent surface; full gating lands with the trust model.
  • ADR-005 — signing stays deferred; local profiles inherit the filesystem-permission integrity posture.

docs.title: ADR-010: Profiles are plain default-answer files
docs.text: Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
An organization generating projects from shared templates needs to point those projects at its own private package index and container registry. Both are template answers: a value the template asks for, which the organization wants pre-filled on every run.

Default answers are the right shape for this need, for three reasons:

  1. Public by default. The public product resolves packages from PyPI and GHCR. A default answer overrides that resolution for one user without any template or installer assuming an authenticated organization feed.
  2. Two values, not an apparatus. The need is two values (package_index.simple_url, container.registry). A typed model, a layered resolution chain, and a CLI command group are a deep apparatus around a shallow need.
  3. Answers, not an interface. Exposing a typed model as an interface invites more maintenance than the values earn, and "pluggable org profile" suggests an extension point the product does not offer.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A profile is a plain file of default answers to template questions. A per-user profile.toml at the config root supplies default answers to template questions, merged into Copier as overridable pre-fills (load_profile(template) → ExecutionContext.profile → Copier's user_defaults= channel, not the forced data= channel). Templates declare ordinary Copier questions (project.package_index_url, streamlit.container_registry) and read them as ordinary answers.

Grammar: two reserved tables, [defaults] (any template) and [templates.<name>] (one template, overrides [defaults]). Keys are open: they are template question names, validated by nothing. A missing file yields {}; a malformed file raises ProfileError. Templates validate values, not the loader: a profile value's validation belongs in the declaring template's own Copier question (copier.yml), never in load_profile.

The interface contract (how it stays coherent as the catalog grows):

  • [defaults] X is best-effort: it fills question X only in templates that declare it, and silently no-ops elsewhere. This is by design, not a gap.
  • Consistency comes from a canonical shared-question vocabulary owned by base templates and propagated by extends. Declare a cross-cutting question once in a base (e.g. package_index_url on project); every descendant inherits the exact name/type; [defaults] then reaches the whole subtree. Verified: a [defaults] value reaches streamlit because it inherits the question from project (inherited questions reach every render of a descendant through its scoped view — ADR-015).
  • No per-template mandatory variable set. Forcing every template to declare a fixed set is overexposure and couples unrelated templates. Authors declare only the few first-class variation points they intend.
  • No [templates.<base>] cascade. The loader keys on the invoked template name; use [defaults] for family-wide values, [templates.<name>] for one-template overrides. Cascading would couple the settings loader to composition resolution.
  • Scope boundary. A profile covers declared questions only — the customizations a template chose to make first-class. Structure the template didn't ship is a layer (extends); anything unanticipated is your own script after generation. A profile is one of three taps, deliberately the least powerful; it is not "the customization interface." (See ADR-011 for the structured-content gap this leaves.)

Two answer channels, kept distinct (ExecutionContext):

  • profile → Copier user_defaults= — pre-fills the prompt, overridable interactively, taken as-is under --non-interactive. This is what a default means.
  • context_data → Copier data= — a forced answer (prompt skipped); also holds answers threaded between composition layers. Merging profile values into this channel would make them non-overridable.

Org configuration lives outside the product. An organization layers its private config after the canonical public installer via an org-owned script that writes two plain files: uv.toml (machine package resolution + keyring/artifacts-keyring) and %APPDATA%\boilerplate\profile.toml (generation defaults). An organization keeps its real setup in its own repository; the public repo documents the generic pattern (fictional acme) in Customization.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Typed Profile model with a resolver chain and a config command group — rejected: adds typed-model weight, a CLI surface, and a resolution chain for two values that are just answers.
  • Profile via the forced data= channel — rejected: makes defaults non-overridable (skips the interactive prompt); contradicts "pre-fill, overridable."
  • Mandatory per-template variables — rejected: overexposure; impossible to anticipate every downstream need anyway.
  • Env-var / CLI override layers on the loader — rejected: per-invocation overrides already exist (the interactive prompt over the pre-fills, and Copier's forced data= channel for scripted runs), so new layers would duplicate channels. The loader stays a plain function, never a source-pluggable resolver; an environment layer returns only if a concrete second configuration source appears.
  • Profile as default answers (chosen) — a thin merge over Copier's native user_defaults; orchestrate-don't-reimplement (ADR-001).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• boilerplate.settings exports Settings, ProfileError, and load_profile; the loader lives in settings/profile.py.
  • ADR-009's package-index provider kind extends the plain-file profile.
  • A missing profile.toml legitimately yields {}, so the loader has no declared profile that fails to load state to guard against silently falling back to the public index. The publish-safety concern belongs where publishing happens: a generated project's publish step should fail closed when no explicit target is configured. Boilerplate core stamps values and holds no publish opinion.
  • Deferred (each with its own trigger):
    • Named default sets: one file per set plus an active pointer, switched by a config command; every render announces the active set — the loud toggle is part of the design, not polish (a silently stale org/personal switch is the failure mode). Build when a user actually juggles contexts.
    • Warn-on-unknown-key lint + per-template key discoverability — the best-effort model's safety net. Build when the catalog is large enough for key collisions and typos to bite.
    • Profile-declared user tasks: a tasks = [...] list appended to the composition engine's existing _tasks accumulation, run last after all template tasks. Interim answer: your own script after boilerplate new. Build when someone demonstrably re-runs the same script after every generation.
    • Shareable-set trust: profiles are trusted only because they are user-local files. If sets ever become distributable, fetching needs SHA-pinned verification — the trust boundary changes the moment the file crosses a machine boundary. Until then, distribution is the org script's business.

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs
docs.text:
• ADR-001 — orchestrate, don't reimplement: the profile is a merge over Copier's own channel, adding only the profile.toml grammar.
  • ADR-009 — its package-index provider kind extends the plain-file profile.
  • ADR-011 — the structured-content customization gap that the profile (values only) does not close.

docs.title: ADR-011: Structured overlay-merge for downstream customization
docs.text:
Status: Proposed (deferred; not in the open-source release). Captured because the customization design work surfaced it as the real developer-experience capability for arbitrary structured-file customization; deferred — the 0.x releases ship without it — the three taps of ADR-010 plus the post-generation script escape hatch stand as the release story.

Scope note. This records a target decision and changes nothing in the release. It is written now so the gap and the chosen direction are on the record before someone reaches for the wrong tool (post-generation tomlkit surgery) as if it were the pattern.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-010 gives three customization taps: values (the profile), structure (layers via extends), and behavior (your own post-gen script). A real gap sits between them: a downstream that wants an arbitrary structured edit to a generated file — e.g. change requires-python mid-pyproject.toml and append a [tool.acme.audit] section — has only poor options today:

  • Profile — only reaches declared questions; an arbitrary mid-file edit is not a declared slot.
  • Own the file — the layer ships its own pyproject.toml.jinja, duplicating the base's whole file and drifting when the base changes. Brittle for "add one block."
  • Post-generation script — edit the rendered file with tomlkit (Python stdlib can read TOML but cannot write it), guarded for idempotency. Clunky, hand-rolled per edit. Unacceptable as the standing answer for a developer-experience tool.

Copier renders each layer independently with no merge primitive, so "reach into the base's output and change it" always bottoms out in one of the above.

Key insight: for a structured file, "edit in the middle" and "append a section" are the same operation — the file is a tree, not lines. Both are "set these nodes," expressible declaratively.

docs.title: Decision (proposed)
docs.text:
Extend the composition engine to deep-merge structured-content overlays. A layer ships <file>.overlay.{toml,yaml,json}; after all layers render, the engine deep-merges each overlay into its target file on disk (then removes the overlay marker). Position-independent by construction — one fragment expresses both a mid-file edit and a new section:

# pyproject.overlay.toml — shipped by an org layer
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.12"     # overwrites that leaf, wherever it sits
[tool.acme.audit]             # adds a new table
endpoint = "https://audit.example/..."

Scoped to structured formats only (TOML/YAML/JSON). Free-text patching of unstructured files is explicitly out — that stays "own the file or script it." Fits the composition engine's mandate (it already merges questions and tasks across layers; this is the same idea applied to file bodies) and fills a gap Copier leaves, so it is build-not-reinvent per ADR-001.

docs.title: Open questions to resolve before building
docs.text:
• List / array-of-tables merge semantics — append vs replace vs merge-by-key. This is where every merge system lives or dies (kustomize strategic-merge, Helm values). Proposed default: deep-merge, overlay wins on scalar conflict; offer JSON-Patch-style ops (RFC 6902: replace /project/requires-python, add /tool/acme) for surgical array targeting when deep-merge is ambiguous.
  • Comment/formatting preservation — a re-serialize is best-effort; acceptable for a generated file (semantic correctness over textual layout).
  • Residual not covered — transforming an existing value as a function of its current content (append to a string, conditional rewrite) cannot be a static overlay; that stays a post-generation script. Rare tail; does not merit machinery.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Turns "edit the middle + append a section" from a hand-rolled tomlkit script into a three-line declarative fragment — the developer-experience bar this tool is held to.
  • Adds a post-render merge pass and per-format mergers to the composition engine; the list-semantics decision above is the central design cost.
  • No release impact: deferred. If a specific structured edit proves common across the catalog first, the cheaper interim move is to give the base template a typed list question for that slot (ADR-010 Tier-1), not to rush this.

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs
docs.text:
• ADR-010 — the profile handles values; this handles structured content the template did not parameterize. Complementary taps.
  • ADR-001 — build-not-reinvent: Copier has no structured merge; this is first-party composition of file content.

docs.title: ADR-012: Positioning relative to Copier
docs.text:
Status: Accepted; amended 2026-10-20 (one pitch on every surface)

Scope note. This is a documentation-framing decision, not an architecture one. It governs how public-facing docs (README first screen, docs home, the Why Boilerplate? page) frame Boilerplate's relationship to Copier, and records the evidence that framing rests on. It does not change any behavioral contract.

Epistemic status. Boilerplate has no public users yet. Nothing below is first-party data; it is public-signal research on adjacent ecosystems (issue trackers, adoption counts of proxy tools), and every conclusion drawn from it is an inference from proxies. Replace these inferences with first-party signals (issues, installs, feedback) as soon as any exist.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Boilerplate was extracted from an internal platform team's tooling and generalized for public release. Its public-facing story can be told two ways, and before this decision the repository told neither deliberately:

  1. The narrow pitch — a composition engine for Copier templates (extends, merged questions, deterministic precedence). Concrete and verifiable, but it invites the immediate objection "Copier already documents applying multiple templates."
  2. The broad pitch — an opinionated Python development system (curated toolchain, layered templates, planned lock/update lifecycle). Differentiated, but its value only fully demonstrates as the catalog and lifecycle features land.

Primary-source research (2026-07) resolved how to weigh these:

Interest is documented, and upstream leaves it to the community. Template composition/inheritance is Copier's longest-running unresolved feature request — 15+ distinct threads from 13+ authors, 2018–2025. The canonical thread, copier-org/copier#934 ("Updatable templates for template hierarchies and reuse", open since January 2023), sits in Copier's Community contribution milestone, whose own description is design-approved but not something the core team will build. Individual maintainer quotes need their context kept: yajo's "a different thing than copier" (2023) addressed a proposed fork/squash-merge update mode, and "with Copier, 1 template = 1 repo" a meta-template repo layout — neither is a blanket rejection of hierarchies, and yajo's first #934 response was a constructive meta-template prototype. The durable signal is the milestone itself. Copier's documented alternative, applying multiple templates to one subproject with one answers file each, officially works only when templates touch disjoint file sets; merging shared files such as pyproject.toml across templates is the acknowledged unsolved gap (discussion #1485, issue #1738).

In the closest proxies, composition alone attracted few users; updatability attracted many. The nearest prior art: cookie-composer (declared multi-template layering for cookiecutter) drew ~21 stars and ~150 downloads/month over four years (as of 2026-07), while cruft — update-tracking only, same base ecosystem — has ~1,600 stars, and the highest-engagement thread in the space is cookiecutter's update request (cookiecutter#784, 43 reactions). This gap is suggestive, not conclusive — the tools differ in timing, marketing, and audience. Consistent with it: #934's own title asks for updatable hierarchies, and the users who articulate composition pain are platform teams whose stated motive is maintenance scaling, not initial scaffolding.

Positioning norms among comparable tools are consistent. Across uv, ruff, pnpm, pixi, biome, polars, and hatch: every tool that answers "why not X?" does so on the first screen or behind a first-screen link; none buries it; none uses an in-README feature table. The form splits by relationship — replacement tools (uv, ruff) lead with benchmarks and parity claims; tools built on an incumbent's ecosystem (pixi on conda; hatch on packaging standards) frame the incumbent as foundation, never attack, link outward to its docs, and defer extended comparison to a prose docs page.

Honest caveats. Per-thread engagement on composition asks is modest (single-digit reactions); Stack Overflow traffic on the topic is near zero; the one purpose-built predecessor flopped. The addressable market is thin and concentrated in platform teams. Separately, two competitive risks exist: upstream movement on #934 (a maintainer has sketched a "fork-like approach"), and uv absorbing scaffolding scope from below.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Position Boilerplate as a Python development environment paired with templates that build on one another, with Copier as their foundation — foundation framing, not replacement framing (the pixi/hatch pattern):

  • Name Copier in the first paragraph as the foundation. State the gap in one sentence: Copier applies multiple independent templates by hand; Boilerplate lets template authors declare composition, giving consumers one command, one merged question set, and deterministic precedence when layers overlap.
  • Cite the documented gap, respectfully. The README and the Why Boilerplate? page may link Copier's own multi-template documentation and #934 — engaging prior art head-on, in the incumbent-as-foundation tone. No benchmarks, no feature-table combat.
  • Scope the compatibility claim to what ships. Current-state docs say: templates remain standard Copier templates; composition metadata lives in a separate boilerplate.yml; copier.yml is never modified; a template becomes a layer by adding that one file. The stronger claim — vanilla Copier templates consumable with no added metadata — is not current behavior (the catalog requires boilerplate.yml) and MUST NOT appear in current-state docs unless that changes.
  • One pitch on every surface. The README, the docs home, the package description and the CLI's help line lead with the same role line: a Python development environment, one tool for each job, paired with templates that build on one another. Copier stays the named foundation in the README's first paragraph. Extended "why not plain Copier?" prose lives on the Why Boilerplate? docs page, not in the README.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Foundation framing, first-screen gap statement (chosen) — matches the norm for built-on-incumbent tools, preempts the predictable "just use -a" objection with the upstream's own words, and costs one paragraph.
  • Replacement framing (uv/ruff pattern) — rejected: Boilerplate has no speed or drop-in-parity story against Copier, and it depends on Copier; attack framing would be both false and self-undermining.
  • Not naming Copier at all — rejected: six of seven comparable tools name the incumbent, and Boilerplate's entire early audience consists of Copier users who will raise the comparison themselves if the docs don't.
  • Splitting the pitches by surface (the narrow composition pitch in the README, the broad system pitch on the docs home) — chosen at first, then replaced on 2026-10-20: the model of what Boilerplate is gives the development environment the same weight as the templates, and one role line on every surface keeps the front door and the docs from describing two different products. The verifiability argument no longer decides the lead: the environment half is as checkable as the composition half (the installer and the configured picks ship), and Copier stays named as the foundation in the README's first paragraph.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The proxy evidence (cruft vs. cookie-composer; #934's title) suggests the lock/update workstream (roadmap Phase 3, adr-007) may matter more for adoption than composition alone. Weigh this when prioritizing; treat it as a hypothesis to test against first-party signals, not a settled fact.
  • At public debut, the most directly reachable audience that has already expressed interest is the copier-org/copier#934 thread; a respectful pointer there is low-cost outreach. Caveat: the Community contribution milestone invites contributions into Copier, not external tools — the comment may present Boilerplate as one experiment toward the ask, never as "the" invited answer.
  • Watch items: activity on #934 (upstream building or blessing an approach would change the gap statement), and uv's scaffolding scope. If either materializes, revisit this ADR.
  • The mis-install hazard from adr-008 (bare pip install boilerplate installs an unrelated same-niche package) remains a positioning liability at every surface that names the package; install docs continue to lead with the git-URL path.

docs.title: ADR-013: The Interactivity Contract
docs.text: Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
boilerplate new renders in one of two modes: interactive (Copier prompts for unanswered questions) or non-interactive (--non-interactive / --ci, where every answer must come from a default, profile.toml, or a forced answer). Prompting has a failure mode with no natural backstop: when stdin cannot host a real terminal session, Copier's prompt layer (questionary / prompt_toolkit) does not always raise cleanly on EOF — it can retry-loop, growing memory without bound instead of exiting. This is not hypothetical: an equivalent failure was confirmed live on this project (Windows, stdin redirected from NUL, which isatty() misreports as a terminal) reaching the prompt layer and hanging before the guard was hardened. It is also a category-wide problem — see Evidence.

This ADR records the decision rationale for the interactivity contract of boilerplate new (src/boilerplate/cli/commands/new.py, src/boilerplate/composition/rendering/engine.py) and its error codes (design Operational quality §Error Code Registry; design Data models §Error Hierarchy), surveyed against primary sources across CLI standards and peer tools, July 2026.

docs.title: 1. Prompt gating is a proactive stdin-TTY check
docs.text:
Immediately after flag composition (--ci / --non-interactive resolved to their effective values), and before the template catalog, resolver, composer, or render engine are touched, new checks whether stdin can host prompts. If interactive mode is in effect, stdin is not a real TTY, and --dry-run was not passed, the command fails closed with BP_INPUT_TTY_REQUIRED (exit 3) and a remediation naming the substitute flags (--non-interactive, the global --ci).

Rationale: Copier's prompt layer can retry-loop on EOF instead of raising. A proactive check refuses the render before that failure mode can occur, rather than relying on the reactive layer (Clause 2) to catch it after the fact.

docs.title: 2. A reactive second layer stays
docs.text:
isatty() alone can lie. On Windows, NUL is a character device and isatty() reports True for it — confirmed live to pass a naive TTY check and hang in the prompt layer. The proactive guard closes that specific gap with a GetConsoleMode probe on the stdin handle: GetConsoleMode succeeds only on a genuine console input handle, the same discriminator the prompt layer itself depends on.

Hardening the proactive check does not retire the reactive one. A terminal can pass both the TTY and console-handle checks and still be unable to host prompt_toolkit's rendering (Git Bash pseudo-TTYs, editor-embedded shells, some CI-provided pseudo-consoles). Prompt-layer failures that occur during rendering are still caught and translated to BP_RENDER_PROMPT_FAILED (exit 1). The translator additionally recognizes Copier's own copier.errors.InteractiveSessionError: Copier wraps EOF-during-prompt in this type with a builtins exception as its cause, which would otherwise evade a plain module-prefix match against prompt_toolkit / questionary. Neither layer subsumes the other — the proactive gate is cheap and catches the common case before any work starts; the reactive layer is the backstop for prompt-layer failures the proactive gate cannot anticipate.

docs.title: 3. No input-mode switching on CI environment variables
docs.text:
CI=true and vendor equivalents (GITHUB_ACTIONS, TF_BUILD, and similar) never flip new into a defaults-accepting mode. The only mode switches are explicit flags (--non-interactive, --ci) and their env-var equivalents, BOILERPLATE_NON_INTERACTIVE and BOILERPLATE_CI, which are tool-scoped opt-ins following the PIP_NO_INPUT pattern (an environment variable defined and documented by the tool it controls) — not a heuristic read of ambient CI-identity variables.

Rationale: a CI environment variable answers "am I running in CI?", not "should this tool skip prompting?" Those questions happen to have the same answer on the major CI providers today, but that is not a contract any of them make. A scaffold silently built with wrong defaults propagates through every rendered layer and is discovered late, if at all; a failed pipeline step is discovered immediately, at the point of cause, with a named fix.

docs.title: 4. Every prompt has a non-interactive substitute
docs.text:
No template question is reachable only through a prompt:

  • Defaults (--non-interactive) — accept the template's declared default: for every question.
  • Persistent pre-fills (profile.toml) — per-user [defaults] and [templates.<name>] tables that ride Copier's user_defaults channel; an interactive answer, or a forced answer, overrides them.
  • A per-invocation answers channel (--data / --data-file) — forced answers for a single invocation, on Copier's data channel.

--non-interactive (and BOILERPLATE_NON_INTERACTIVE) is the only defaults-accepting mode for questions; --yes governs confirmation prompts only (CLI reference).

docs.title: 5. Read-only operations are exempt
docs.text: --dry-run never prompts. It is checked ahead of the TTY guard (Clause 1) and short-circuits it, so a piped --dry-run invocation stays legal — there is nothing to answer and no render to protect.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Reactive-only enforcement (no proactive TTY gate) — rejected: relies entirely on Copier's own EOF handling, which is insufficient on its own (see Evidence — copier-org/copier#2436) and leaves the unbounded-retry-loop risk live for every non-TTY interactive invocation, not just the Windows NUL edge case.
  • Sniff CI=true (or vendor equivalents) to auto-switch to non-interactive — rejected: binds correctness to an environment-identity contract no CI provider makes; the counterexamples (pnpm, uv) show that even narrowly-scoped CI heuristics are treated by their own maintainers as provisional or safety-only, never as a general "assume defaults" switch.
  • Silently substitute defaults on non-TTY stdin (the create-vite model) — rejected for this category: workable when output is a single-shot starter reviewed immediately after generation; wrong for a composition engine whose answers propagate through every layer a template extends.
  • Collapse to a single enforcement point — rejected: the proactive gate cannot see prompt-layer failures that only manifest mid-render (Git Bash pseudo-TTY, editor-embedded shells); the reactive translator cannot prevent Copier's retry-loop from starting in the first place. Each covers a failure mode the other cannot.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Verified against primary sources, July 2026.

The pattern this decision follows:

  • clig.dev §Interactivity: "Only use prompts or interactive elements if stdin is an interactive terminal (a TTY)... you should throw an error telling the user what flag to pass." §Arguments and flags: "Never require a prompt."
  • gh (cli/cli): CanPrompt() requires both stdin and stdout to be a TTY (pkg/iostreams); commands fail closed with named-flag errors when not interactive, e.g. pkg/cmd/pr/merge: "--merge, --rebase, or --squash required when not running interactively." No CI (or vendor-equivalent) detection anywhere in its environment-variable surface.
  • az (microsoft/knack): a stdin-only TTY check gates prompting; failure message: "Unable to prompt for confirmation as no tty available. Use --yes."
  • rustup-init.sh (rust-lang/rustup): [ ! -t 0 ] gates the install prompt; failure message: "Unable to run interactively. Run with -y to accept defaults."

Category peers get this wrong — the proactive guard (Clause 1) is ahead of the category, not behind it:

  • Copier itself reacts to EOFError only and still waits indefinitely on stdin that is open but never fed (copier-org/copier#2436).
  • cookiecutter has no EOF handling; a non-TTY prompt surfaces as a raw traceback.
  • Yeoman acknowledged the same gap in 2018 and closed the issue stale without a fix (yeoman/generator#694).

CI-detection counterexamples cut toward fail-closed, not toward auto-switching (Clause 3):

  • pnpm auto-enables --frozen-lockfile in CI specifically to prevent silent lockfile drift, not to relax behavior (pnpm/pnpm#1994).
  • uv venv silently deleting an existing venv when non-interactive is acknowledged by its own maintainers as provisional backwards-compatibility behavior, likely to change (astral-sh/uv#14309).

The alternative model exists, and is rejected for this category (Clause 3 / Clause 4):

  • create-vite silently substitutes defaults for non-destructive choices in non-TTY mode (argInteractive ?? process.stdin.isTTY), failing closed only on the overwrite prompt (vitejs/vite, packages/create-vite). Workable for a lightweight, single-shot starter whose output is reviewed immediately; wrong for a composition engine whose answers propagate through every rendered layer.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• new refuses to start an interactive render against non-TTY stdin instead of hanging or silently defaulting; the failure is immediate, attributed, and names the fix.
  • CI pipelines and other non-interactive callers must pass an explicit flag (--non-interactive or --ci). Ambient CI=true has no effect on boilerplate's behavior, by design; the tool-scoped env-var equivalents (BOILERPLATE_NON_INTERACTIVE, BOILERPLATE_CI) do not change this — they are explicit opt-ins, not a CI-identity heuristic.
  • The TTY check and the prompt-layer translator are two independent code paths (new.py and engine.py) with different failure signatures and different exit codes (BP_INPUT_TTY_REQUIRED is 3; BP_RENDER_PROMPT_FAILED is 1). A future refactor MUST NOT collapse them into a single check without re-verifying both failure modes — isatty() lying, and prompt-layer failures the proactive gate cannot anticipate — stay covered.
  • Clause 4's substitute set is complete: defaults via --non-interactive, persistent pre-fills via profile.toml, and per-invocation forced answers via --data / --data-file, plus the env-var equivalents (BOILERPLATE_NON_INTERACTIVE, BOILERPLATE_CI) for the flags themselves.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• clig.dev — Command Line Interface Guidelines, §Interactivity
  • cli/cli — GitHub CLI
  • microsoft/knack
  • rust-lang/rustup
  • copier-org/copier#2436
  • yeoman/generator#694
  • pnpm/pnpm#1994
  • astral-sh/uv#14309
  • vitejs/vite — create-vite

docs.title: ADR-014: Deferred task execution — accumulate per layer, run once on the final layer
docs.text: Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Copier's contract runs _tasks after generating a project, in the destination directory. Under composition, "the project" is the composed whole: layers render sequentially into one destination, and a layer's tasks (dependency installation, git init) generally assume the finished project, not that layer's partial contribution. Copier's own multi-template guidance — sequential independent applications — runs each template's tasks at its own apply time, against a project the later templates have not written yet. The closest prior art fails in the other direction: cookie-composer executes each layer's cookiecutter hooks inside a throwaway temp render, so environment side effects never reach the real project, and its documented mitigation is disabling hooks per layer.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Merge: _tasks accumulates across layers by ordered concatenation — topological order across layers (dependencies first, target last), declaration order within a layer, no deduplication. Tasks are effects; repetition and order are meaningful, so the append-only strategy is deliberate even though files use last-layer-wins.
  • Execution: every non-final layer renders with skip_tasks=True (a public Copier flag); the final layer executes the full accumulated list exactly once, after all layers' files exist. Conditions are evaluated by the final layer's worker against the merged answers.
  • Update: the update walk renders with skip_tasks=True in every render Copier makes during a layer's update (the old copy, the in-place render and the new copy), and the accumulated list runs exactly once against the finished project after the last layer's update, through the same Worker subclass under Copier's update operation, so a task's when: sees _copier_operation == "update" (design 04 §Safe Update). Copier would otherwise run each updated layer's own _tasks three times per update, twice in temporary directories, and never the merged list.
  • Shapes: task entries keep Copier's native forms end-to-end — plain string (shell execution), argv list (no shell), mapping with command and optional when/working_directory — so Copier, not Boilerplate, interprets execution semantics. Entries that match none of these shapes are dropped with a warning.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Per-layer execution (Copier-native timing) — rejected: runs a base layer's tasks against an incomplete project (e.g. dependency installation against a pyproject.toml a later layer still overrides); the sequential-application precedent inherits exactly this flaw.
  • Deferred single execution (chosen) — matches the pattern Yeoman institutionalized in its composeWith run loop (all composed generators' writing phases complete before any install/end phase runs) and preserves the object of Copier's contract: the completed project.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A child layer cannot remove or reorder an inherited task; the idiomatic gate is a when: condition on the task, which shape pass-through preserves.
  • Task provenance (which layer contributed an entry) is not yet carried through the merge. The trust-tier consent and audit design (03 §Task Execution Safety, Security model) requires per-layer attribution and selective execution; that needs a provenance-carrying merge and is deferred work this ADR explicitly does not cover.
  • Mid-list failure leaves rendered files with partially applied post-processing — Copier's own no-rollback property, inherited unchanged. Task authors SHOULD keep tasks idempotent.
  • {{ _copier_conf.src_path }} and _copier_operation inside task templates resolve against the final layer's worker, not the declaring layer's.

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs
docs.text:
• ADR-003 governs the permissive unsafe trust posture the deferred execution runs under.
  • ADR-002 localizes the Template/Worker coupling this mechanism drives; skip_tasks itself is public Copier API.
  • ADR-015 — the update walk whose renders skip tasks; its Verification (2026-10-06) records where Copier runs a layer's tasks during an update.

docs.title: ADR-015: Idiomatic artifacts, orchestrated engine — a composed project is plain Copier on disk
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Scope note. This ADR names the paradigm the composition and update designs assume, so later decisions can cite an invariant instead of re-deriving it. For what exists in code today, see status.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The composition goal (ADR-001) is the experience of a singular template built from many variants. Copier's own idiom for multiple templates in one project is N independent applications, each with its own answers file, each independently updatable — and Copier's update algorithm defines "user changes" as any difference between its own pristine re-render of one template and the actual working tree, which means it has no concept of, and no need for, cross-template awareness. Two pressures meet here: being true to Copier's interfaces and idioms (so users keep every guarantee Copier gives them), and the unified experience that is the product's reason to exist (one question flow, one compose, one update). A single canonical .copier-answers.yml written by Boilerplate itself resolves that tension the wrong way: it forfeits per-layer updates and Copier's ownership of its own file.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A composed project MUST carry the same file set and the same file ownership as a project built by running Copier N times by hand, and every git-backed layer MUST stay updatable through the escape hatch of point 1, within the limits that point states — one measured exception, stated in point 4: each per-layer answers file records its own layer's and its ancestors' answers, which the update walk reads. Idiom governs what persists; product governs what it feels like.

Composition is Boilerplate's process, not a template property. A template's copier.yml declares its own questions and the parent questions it overrides or extends, and MUST NOT declare a parent question unchanged; a template does not join its own extends chain. Boilerplate joins every layer's questions into the full merged schema, which the questionnaire asks once, and joins each layer with its ancestors, every layer its extends chain reaches, into that layer's scoped view (design 04 §Scoped view); it hands the scoped view to every render of the layer, at compose and at update, each render receiving the join of the versions it renders. Copier does all rendering, answers-file writing and three-way merging, and Boilerplate implements none of them.

Composition therefore answers to two reference points at once, and each owns a different half of the result: rendering matches, for each layer, the single flattened template that layer and its ancestors would make if merged by hand (one question schema and one extension set per layer, tasks running once against the finished project), under one questionnaire that covers the whole composition, while artifact structure matches N independent Copier applications (one answers file per layer, each independently updatable where its source is git-backed). Where a mechanism looks un-idiomatic against one reference point, check it against the other before calling it a deviation. Concretely:

  1. Artifacts are Copier's. Each first-party template declares _answers_file: .copier-answers.<layer>.yml and ships the answers-file stub ({{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}.jinja) that causes Copier to write it — the directive alone is inert (the design 04 contract); Copier writes every answers file, and Boilerplate MUST NOT write or rewrite them. The escape hatch is a hand-run vanilla copier update -a .copier-answers.<layer>.yml for one git-backed layer, with its ancestors' answers passed as data, for example --data-file .copier-answers.project.yml; a base layer needs nothing passed, and a layer sourced from a plain directory is copy-only, per point 5. A child layer's answers file records its ancestors' answers, but a vanilla update sees only the layer's own copier.yml, and Copier keeps in the answers file only answers to questions the layer's template declares (Copier: the answers file), so the first hand-run update trims the file to the layer's own keys and the passed data is what supplies the ancestors' answers from then on; an undeclared answer left in an answers file survived one update and rendered empty on the next (Verification (2026-09-30)). The hatch updates one layer and does not compose, which bounds it twice, and it checks no recorded answer: where a target version retypes a question or tightens its validator, Copier drops an answer it reads from the layer's own answers file and records the new default with no warning. Copier renders the old copy from the layer's own answers file and never from passed data, so once the file is trimmed, a template edit on or beside a line that renders an ancestor's answer conflicts on every run. The next boilerplate update refills the file: the walk fills a trimmed file's keys for the old copy from the declaring layer's record, and the in-place render records the full scoped view's answers again. The stop applies only when no layer records a key, before any layer runs, naming the layer and the keys (design 04 §Safe Update). A child layer's derived answers are recomputed only by its scoped view, so the hand-run path pauses on the files that render them, visibly and with conflict markers, and never loses content silently. A layer whose _jinja_extensions import from the boilerplate package needs that package importable in Copier's environment; the first-party templates do.
  2. Update is orchestration of Copier's update through each layer's scoped view. boilerplate update runs Copier's update once per layer, always in composition order (lower layers first, so overrides are re-asserted against an already-updated base and a migration that renames a question rewrites the ancestor's answers file before a descendant's update reads it), and each render of that update sees the layer's scoped view at the versions it renders: the old copy of a layer renders the layer's own template at its own _commit and its ancestors at the versions boilerplate.lock records, under its scoped view joined at those versions, and the in-place render and the new copy render under its scoped view joined at the target versions, which matches Copier's own rule that the old copy renders exactly as it did. Copier performs the three-way merge, writes the conflict markers, reads each layer's own answers from that layer's answers file and prompts as it does for a vanilla update; Boilerplate passes each declaring ancestor's answers as data for the in-place render and the new copy, fills for the old copy the keys the layer's own file lacks from the declaring layer's record at the start of the walk, stops on a recorded answer the target view rejects, and runs the composition's accumulated task list once against the finished project after the walk, as at compose (design 04 §Safe Update owns these rules; ADR-014). The scoped view reaches those renders through the same Worker subclass compose renders every layer through (ADR-002). The order is recorded in a project artifact, so replaying the walk by hand does not require guessing it: boilerplate.lock lists layers in execution order (design 02), and it is plain YAML, so a user replaying the walk reads the order without running Boilerplate. The per-layer answers files do not carry the order; they record _src_path and _commit per layer and nothing about sequence. A project with no lock — never managed by Boilerplate, or ejected since — therefore has no on-disk order, and reconstructing it by hand means reading the templates' own extends chains.
  3. Layer stacking rides Copier's own merge model. During any one layer's update, every other layer's contribution is user-space by construction — Copier diffs its old pristine render against the working tree, so other layers' files and overwrites are preserved when disjoint from the update and surface as ordinary three-way conflicts when they collide. Composition never needs an all-layers-at-once operation.
  4. The unified prompt experience at compose is deliberate and stays. Prompting is ephemeral — no artifact records how questions were asked, and the rendered tree a unified compose produces is the tree N sequential Copier runs would produce from the same answers. The ADR-002 shim serves compose and update alike, and one artifact-level deviation follows from it and is deliberate: because every layer's Worker exposes the layer's scoped view, each per-layer answers file records the layer's own and its ancestors' answers rather than only that layer's own questions, and nothing of a sibling or a descendant. Copier's Worker._answers_to_remember keeps an answer only if the worker's template declares it as a question, and never keeps a hidden or secret one, so a worker that exposes the scoped view records the answers to that view's questions, and the update walk reads each declaring ancestor's recorded answers from that ancestor's file and passes them as data. Compose keeps its single unified pass over the full merged schema, because nothing is recorded and no migration runs at compose. Answers of when: false questions such as project_slug and package_name are derived: each render recomputes them and no answers file records them. A layer's files MAY use only questions its own layer or an ancestor declares; the single-owner pattern design 04 recommends for shared files applies this to a file assembled from several layers' answers. The view stops at the ancestors because a descendant's context hook or same-named filter would otherwise change an ancestor's files, and an update step takes each question's definition and default from the full merged schema because, without it, a descendant's override of a question its ancestor adds is lost (Verification (2026-10-06)). The bounded fallback for compose, should the internals coupling ever become untenable, is sequential per-layer run_copy with accumulated answers threaded through data= — shared questions still ask once, at the cost of grouped-by-layer ordering; for update, it is Copier's public run_update per layer with its ancestors' answers passed as data, with the limits of point 1.
  5. The source model is inherited from Copier wholesale, and updateability is a per-layer property. Remote git sources yield portable artifacts; a local git repository is a full source (tags, update) scoped to machines where the path exists, with rehoming a documented one-line _src_path edit; a plain directory is copy-only because Copier records no _commit for it — commit: null in the lock is the honest no-version-stream marker, not a placeholder. A mixed composition degrades per layer, not per project: update walks the git-backed layers and skips non-git layers with a prominent warning.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Boilerplate-owned composite answers file — rejected: wrong author and wrong shape; it forfeits per-layer update, Copier's file ownership, and the escape hatch.
  • Boilerplate-implemented cross-layer merge or update metadata — rejected: reimplements what Copier already provides per layer, contradicting ADR-001.
  • Fully idiomatic compose (sequential per-layer prompting) — rejected as the default experience: it forfeits the singular-template question flow, which is the product thesis at the moment of first contact; retained as the named fallback in point 4.
  • Idiomatic artifacts, orchestrated engine (chosen) — the invariant above.
  • The scoped view held in the fields of a Worker subclass (chosen) — the layer keeps its own copier.yml free of the join, Copier runs every render, and the view reaches all three of Copier's update renders.
  • Every render under the full merged schema — rejected: a descendant's context hook rewrote an ancestor's rendered files, and every answers file recorded siblings' answers (Verification (2026-10-06)).
  • The scoped view alone as the source of question definitions and defaults at update — rejected: an ancestor's update recorded the ancestor's own default for a new question its descendant overrides, in both walk orders (Verification (2026-10-06)); the step takes definitions and defaults from the full merged schema instead.
  • A later layer's recorded value over an earlier one's — rejected: passed data outranks the answers file in Copier's answer precedence (AnswersMap.combined), so a descendant's stale copy of an ancestor's answer, passed over the ancestor's, would shadow the value the ancestor's migration wrote.
  • One questionnaire pass before the walk — rejected: it asks for questions a migration answers, and a renamed question's default overrode the migrated answer in both layers and both orders (Verification (2026-10-08)).
  • A file-path extension registered once, from one source at the target versions — rejected: the old copy renders with the new code, so the update silently keeps the old output (Verification (2026-10-06)).
  • A merged template set on one worker instance — rejected: dataclasses.replace rebuilds the update renders without it (Verification (2026-09-30)).
  • Declaring inherited questions in each child layer so a vanilla per-layer update sees them — rejected: it duplicates the parent's schema by hand, and the copy drifts when the parent renames or retypes the question.
  • A Boilerplate-shipped context hook in each layer's _jinja_extensions that persists inherited answers into the answers file — rejected as the primary mechanism and kept as the runner-up: it updated cleanly in 8 updates across both orders and it also heals the hand-run hatch, but the template then ships the join mechanism, and the hook writes secret answers in clear text unless it filters them.
  • Carrying inherited answers through the child's answers-file stub with combine — rejected: it shares the hook's objection, and a stub cannot carry derived answers for projects that never recorded them.
  • Passing data to a vanilla update with --data-file — retained as the hand-run hatch with the limits in point 1, because the old render never sees passed data.
  • Asking project_slug and package_name as regular questions so the answers files record them — open: it would heal the hand-run hatch for child layers at the cost of two more compose-time prompts, and the project team has not decided it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A project carrying a single canonical .copier-answers.yml is a migration item; adoption accepts the legacy singular shape beside per-layer files (design 06).
  • The per-layer answers file is the distribution contract: whatever _src_path and _commit record must stay resolvable by vanilla Copier, on any machine, indefinitely. The distribution consequences are owned by ADR-006.
  • Non-git layers do not update (point 5): they are skipped with a warning, and copier recopy is the Copier-idiomatic refresh for such a layer when the user wants one. ADR-007's per-layer update model follows this.
  • Passages of the target corpus this decision binds: the non-git-layer glossary entry (01); the --no-base / two-way-comparison passages (05, 06); the trust tables (02, 03, 09), which name wheel_bundle as the trusted first-party mechanism — what replaces it depends on the open question ADR-003 owns, since first-party templates arriving over the network meet ADR-003's own stated trigger for tightening; this ADR does not settle it; the LockLayer.source_bundle / subdirectory fields (02); and INT-001's _subdirectory expectation.

docs.title: Verification (2026-07-28)
docs.text:
Empirical run against Copier 9.15.0 (Windows, git 2.55, core.autocrlf=true): stacked two-template fixtures (base plus an overlay overwriting a base-rendered file), per-layer answers files, vanilla copier CLI only — six scenarios plus an independent adversarial re-run with differently shaped fixtures.

  • Survival confirmed. Updating the base while its diff is disjoint from the overlay's overwrite leaves the overlay's content intact and the other layer's answers file hash-identical; the updated layer's answers file advances to the new tag.
  • Collision pause confirmed. When the base update changes a file the overlay overwrote, Copier writes inline conflict markers (<<<<<<< before updating / >>>>>>> after updating) with the overlay's content preserved on the "before" side and git reporting unmerged paths — never a silent revert, in both a line-edit and a whole-file-rewrite variant.
  • Overlay independence confirmed. Updating the overlay layer alone lands its changes and leaves base-rendered files and the base answers file hash-identical.
  • Plain-directory degradation confirmed. Copy from a non-git directory succeeds and records no _commit; copier update against that layer fails specifically ("Cannot update because cannot obtain old template references", exit 1) — there is no built-in two-way fallback — while the git-backed layer beside it stays fully updatable.
  • Dirty-HEAD author loop confirmed. --vcs-ref=HEAD includes uncommitted template changes (with DirtyLocalWarning) and records a git describe-shaped _commit (v1.0.0-1-g<hash>); without the flag, the latest tag renders clean. That hash names the automated draft commit Copier makes inside its own throwaway clone, so it exists in no repository afterwards: a dirty-HEAD render is an authoring convenience, never a provenance record, and new MUST NOT use it.

Caveats the run surfaced, now part of the record:

  • The _answers_file: directive is inert without a stub. Copier writes an answers file only by rendering a template-shipped {{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}.jinja; a template lacking one composes with exit 0 and silently produces no answers file. Design 04 names both halves of the contract, and a template offered for composition without a stub is copy-only by construction.
  • copier update exits 0 with unresolved conflicts in the tree, and the updated layer's answers file already records the new tag while markers sit unresolved. Orchestration and CI must detect the pause via git unmerged state or a marker scan, never exit codes — this lands on ADR-007's conflict-pause envelope.
  • Byte-identity must be stated in git's content sense. With core.autocrlf=true, Copier's git-based update rewrites line endings of files it otherwise leaves untouched — content-identical but raw-hash-different, and reported as modified by git status in most runs (one run's git diff suppressed it, others did not); an autocrlf=false control preserved exact bytes. Checksum-based drift detection must normalize line endings, and "unchanged" must never be asserted from git status alone.
  • Small files conflict more than edit-distance intuition suggests. On a three-line file, a template edit and a user append at opposite ends still conflict, because the diff hunk's context spans the whole file. The pause is honest; "non-overlapping edits merge cleanly" holds only for files larger than the diff context window.
  • Compose-time ref pinning is mandatory. Bare copier copy resolves the latest tag, so layer application must pin --vcs-ref per the resolved specifier (Boilerplate's version resolution already provides the pin).

docs.title: Verification (2026-09-04)
docs.text:
Empirical run against the bundled project and streamlit templates (Copier 9.18.1, Windows, git 2.55): each template copied into a local git repository and tagged; a project composed by boilerplate new from the wheel's plain directories, then rehomed by editing each answers file's _src_path to the clone and adding _commit; vanilla copier update -a .copier-answers.<layer>.yml per layer after tagging a new version of each template, in both orders.

  • Real-template defects found. project declared _exclude: [_extensions], which replaces Copier's default exclusions rather than extending them, so the update copied the clone's .git over the project's own (the engine reinstates the defaults at compose; vanilla Copier does not). streamlit's files and paths used package_name, project_name, and package_index_url without declaring them, so its vanilla per-layer re-render, which sees only the layer's own copier.yml, produced a different Dockerfile and the update paused on a conflict no edit had caused. For the rest of the run, project restated the default exclusions and streamlit declared those questions.
  • With those fixes, both layers updated cleanly in either order. The changed layer's answers file advanced to the new tag, the other layer's file stayed hash-identical, and new files and edits landed without conflict.
  • A vanilla per-layer update drops foreign keys on its first rewrite. The project layer's answers file lost container_registry on its first update.
  • The vanilla update needed Boilerplate importable. project's _jinja_extensions imports a filter from the boilerplate package. boilerplate new could not compose from git-backed template directories at the time of the run, which is why the run rehomed the answers files by hand.

docs.title: Verification (2026-09-30)
docs.text:
Empirical run against the bundled project and streamlit templates (Copier 9.18.1, Windows, local git clones, --defaults, skip_tasks): streamlit/copier.yml reduced to its own questions and overrides (dependencies, sample_module, container_registry), both layers cloned into tagged git repositories, a project composed by boilerplate new and rehomed to the clones with _commit: v1 (the 2026-09-04 recipe). Each new tag edited the README line that renders project_name and appended a file that renders seven inherited answers, five recorded and two derived; a user line appended to the README before the first update had to survive.

  • A Worker subclass holding the merged view updated cleanly. Copier's update, run per layer through a subclass that holds the merged questions and the extension union in fields and builds template from them, with data= the union of the per-layer answers files (the merge order of the union was not recorded), exited 0 on all 8 updates in both orders (project then streamlit, streamlit then project; v2 then v3). Copier left no conflict markers, no .rej files and no unmerged paths, and it persisted all five inherited answers in streamlit's answers file after every update. The derived values rendered (widget_co, widget-co), the package directory stayed intact and the user line survived.
  • A template set on the worker instance lost the inherited answers. Copier's update, with worker.template set to the merged template on one instance, exited 0 on the first streamlit update in both orders and dropped all five inherited answers from the answers file. The derived values rendered empty, and the second update paused with conflict markers in README.md and the probe file.
  • The hand-run hatch kept the user's work and paused on derived answers. After two engine updates, copier update -a .copier-answers.streamlit.yml --defaults --trust --data-file .copier-answers.project.yml --data package_name=widget_co --data project_slug=widget-co, with a template edit on a far line only, exited 0 in one run, left no .rej file, kept the user line and the package directory, and rendered the new line. The file that renders derived answers paused with a conflict marker, because the old render cannot compute derived answers when no answers file records them, and Copier trimmed the answers file to the layer's own keys.
  • Scratch-fixture probes of vanilla updates (2026-09-29 and 2026-09-30) found three limits. --data and --data-file rendered the new copy correctly and never reached the old copy, so a template edit on or beside a line that renders a passed-in answer conflicted every time. _external_data pointing at another layer's answers file worked at copy and rendered empty on update, because Copier's temporary renders lack the file. An undeclared answer left in an answers file survived one update and rendered empty on the next.

docs.title: Verification (2026-10-06)
docs.text:
Empirical run against the bundled project and streamlit templates and synthetic layers (Copier 9.18.1, Windows, git 2.55): one tagged git repository per layer, every view built by Boilerplate's own Resolver and Composer, and every compose and update run through a Worker subclass holding one view per ref, in lock order and in reverse. Every view joined the layer and its ancestors at one shared ref name per step; a view joining independently versioned ancestors was not exercised, and neither was a step whose ancestor moved while the layer's own version did not, the case in which the old copy, the new copy and the in-place render carry one ref and the recorded-versions and target-versions views differ.

  • The full merged schema let a descendant change an ancestor's files. A streamlit context hook that overwrote description rewrote project's pyproject.toml and package __init__.py to the hook's value when every layer rendered under the full merged schema, and project's answers file recorded streamlit's container_registry. Under the scoped view, project rendered the answered description and recorded only its own questions.
  • Each answers file recorded exactly its scoped view. In a diamond (docs extends project; app extends streamlit and docs), each answers file recorded its own and its ancestors' questions and no other, and the updates of docs and app left no conflict markers, no .rej files and no unmerged paths. A three-layer chain (project, streamlit, and a layer extending streamlit) updated cleanly in both orders.
  • The questionnaire pass carried a descendant's override of a new ancestor question. When project added license (default MIT) and streamlit overrode its default to Apache-2.0, the scoped view with no pass rendered and recorded MIT in project in both orders, with no error. With one non-interactive pass over the full merged schema at the target versions before the walk, the file and both answers files held Apache-2.0 in both orders.
  • A file-path extension declared by an ancestor needed registration per layer and ref. A streamlit file using a filter that project declares as a file path failed to render with no registration (No filter named 'probe_shout'). Registered per layer and ref from project's source at each ref, the update moved the file from the old ref's output to the new ref's with no conflict markers; registered once from one source at the target ref, the old copy rendered with the new code, the old and new copies matched, and the file silently kept the old ref's output with no error. A streamlit context hook never reached project's files, at compose or at any update.
  • Copier's update replaced a rejected recorded answer silently. project v2 retyped port from str to int, dropped GPL-3.0 from a license choice list, or added a validator the recorded author_email failed. With the recorded answers passed as data, the in-place render's questionnaire raised a ValueError before it wrote any file and left the tree and the answers files untouched, while a castable value ("8080") carried over as 8080. With no data passed, Copier dropped the recorded answer and recorded the new default (8080, MIT, a valid default address), exited cleanly and printed no warning; a new default that also failed the validator failed the update.
  • Copier ran a layer's tasks three times per update. With a marker task in project and in streamlit, compose ran each task once in the destination. A Copier update with tasks enabled ran the updated layer's own task three times, in the old-copy temporary directory, in place and in the new-copy temporary directory, and never ran the other layer's task.
  • Only ancestors-first order carried a renamed question. project v2 renamed author_name to maintainer_name and shipped a before-stage migration that rewrote the key in its own answers file. In lock order the value carried over in both layers. In reverse order, with the migration in project alone, streamlit's update found neither name, recorded the template default Your Name with no error or conflict, and kept it after project's later update; with the same migration in streamlit too, both orders carried the value.

docs.title: Verification (2026-10-08)
docs.text:
Probe scenarios against Copier 9.18.1, on the bundled project and streamlit templates.

  • A questionnaire pass run before the walk forced a renamed question's default over the migrated answer. project v2 renamed author_name to maintainer_name behind a before-migration. The pass ran before that migration, found maintainer_name unanswered, and its forced default Your Name replaced the migrated value in both layers and both orders.

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs
docs.text:
• ADR-001 — "orchestrate, don't reimplement"; Boilerplate drives Copier's own copy and update per layer and adds one thing, the join: the full merged schema the questionnaire asks, and each layer's scoped view, which reaches every render of that layer through the ADR-002 shim. Boilerplate implements no merge, update or answers-file algorithm of its own.
  • ADR-002 — the shim's charter covers compose and update: both run each layer through its scoped view, which is a property of the worker class, and the guard test reports a relocation of Worker or Template while the version pin bounds the Copier versions both paths run on.
  • ADR-006 — distribution must satisfy the answers-file-as-contract constraints.
  • ADR-007 — the conflict-pause contract is how point 3's collisions surface, and its per-layer update skips non-git layers per point 5.
  • ADR-013 — the unified prompt flow of point 4 exists only in interactive mode; --ci/data-file flows bypass prompting entirely.

docs.title: ADR-016: The project vocabulary as one ontology in CONTEXT.md
docs.text:
Status: Proposed

Scope note. This ADR fixes how Boilerplate keeps its vocabulary: the names of its concepts, what each one means, how the concepts relate, and where each one lives in files and code. For what exists today, see status.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
CONTEXT.md at the repository root is the domain glossary. The design overview's glossary renders it, and docs/agents/domain.md tells the engineering skills to read it before they work in the code. Tenet 14 in .claude/rules/docs.md asks for one name per concept, and the glossary's Avoid lists name retired synonyms. The vocabulary still drifts in four ways.

  • Copies disagree. The sweep found the glossary's dev loop entry, the Environment guide and the Quickstart each writing out a different sequence for the same everyday loop.
  • One word names unrelated concepts.
    • "Profile" names profile.toml, a user's default answers, and EnvironmentProfile (boilerplate-env.yml), the tool versions a project pins. The glossary calls the two "unrelated despite the shared word".
    • "Layer" names a composition layer and, in the key enforcement_layers of PROD-001, an enforcement area.
    • "Stack" names the development tools in the brand line, templates building on one another on the home page, and an application's dependencies in the Streamlit template's dashboard.
    • "Workflow" names the general kind of a golden path in the glossary and the reference model, and a GitHub Actions workflow file in the CI guide (docs/governance/ci.md).
  • A concept and its file are split in two entries, merged in one, or missing a side. The glossary separates EnvironmentProvisionRecord from .boilerplate/environment.yml and the Answers File from .copier-answers.<layer>.yml; it merges the lock with boilerplate.lock in one entry; it gives boilerplate.yml an entry with no template-metadata concept beside it; and it defines Profile by its file.
  • Relations are prose only. A relation such as "the Toolchain is part of the Development Environment" exists as a sentence, so nothing shows the whole, and a relation to a renamed term goes unnoticed.

Boilerplate's data shapes already have a source of truth: hand-written Pydantic models, such as BoilerplateLock and TemplateMeta in src/boilerplate/models/, and AGENTS.md requires Pydantic at boundaries.

This repository's own history shows what written rules do and do not do (Verification). A written rule is the specification every check here encodes: each automated check names the prose rule it enforces. A written rule with no check behind it did not reduce drift: the glossary's Avoid lists were followed by more uses of the names they retire. A checked rule held: the docstring-mood check has kept zero violations while the code grew. Whether written vocabulary also improves a coding agent's work is unmeasured; the published study of repository context files found no general gain in task success and a cost increase above 20%.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
CONTEXT.md MUST be the project's one vocabulary document, organized as an ontology: concepts grouped in modules, each concept with one name, a namespaced identifier and a fixed set of labeled relation lines. The document records each vocabulary decision once and is the specification later checks encode. Pydantic MUST stay the source of truth for data shapes.

  1. Modules. The rendered part of CONTEXT.md has one section per module, in this order: core (concepts every module uses), model (the reference model), composition, customization, provisioning and trust. A concept moves to core only when a second module uses it.

  2. Entries. Each entry opens with its <a id="term-…"> anchor, its term in bold and its identifier, module:Name, then one or two sentences of definition, then these lines in this order, each left out when it does not apply:

    Label Holds Example Kind of The concept this one is a kind of model:Workflow, for the golden path Part of The concept this one is a part of model:DevelopmentEnvironment, for the toolchain Related Other concepts it works with core:Template, composition:ScopedView Not to be confused with A concept with a similar name and a different meaning, and the difference provisioning:EnvironmentProfile, for Profile Stored in The files that store the concept profile.toml Defined in The source files that define or enforce it src/boilerplate/settings/profile.py See The design section that owns its mechanics design 04 §Scoped view Avoid Retired names, as phrases org profile, config profile Carve-out An allowed use of an avoided phrase "template skeleton" names init-template's output Matches An equivalent term in another vocabulary, its source, and exact or close paved road (Netflix, exact)

  3. One concept, one name, one entry. A term MUST be unique across all modules, compared without case, and MUST NOT appear in another entry's Avoid line. Two concepts that share a word each get their own term and entry, and each one's Not to be confused with line MUST name the other.

  4. A file is not a concept. A file appears on the Stored in line of the concept it stores. A file gets its own entry only when its format is a concept in its own right.
  5. Data shapes stay in code. An entry's Defined in line points at the Pydantic model or module that defines it; the entry does not restate the model's fields.
  6. Relations across modules. The section "Rules across modules" holds only statements that span modules and that no labeled line states, such as the customization ladder Profile < Layer < Task.
  7. Drift is found by a sweep. A read-only sweep compares the docs, the README and user-facing strings against CONTEXT.md and lists every synonym, conflicting copy and undefined term; the fixes land as ordinary pull requests. The sweep of 2026-10-18 found 161 findings, the baseline each later sweep's count is compared with.
  8. Automation follows evidence. When a sweep finds drift of a kind an earlier sweep already fixed, the vocabulary moves to the form in When the vocabulary is automated.

docs.title: Maintaining the vocabulary
docs.text:
• Add a concept: add an entry in its module with every label that applies, and link the pages that introduce the term to its anchor.
  • Rename a concept: change the term and its anchor, keep the old anchor beside the new one so inbound links still resolve, move the old name into Avoid, and fix the prose the next sweep reports.
  • Split a word that means two things: give each meaning its own term in its own module and point each one's Not to be confused with at the other.
  • Change behavior: update the entry's definition and its Defined in line in the same pull request as the code.
  • Record a mistake: when a contributor or an agent confuses two concepts, add or sharpen the Not to be confused with line on both.

docs.title: When the vocabulary is automated
docs.text:
The labeled lines of decision 2 are built to convert mechanically into this form, which is designed and not adopted:

  • One concept file per concept, Markdown with YAML frontmatter, whose fields are the labels of decision 2.
  • CONTEXT.md generated from the concept files, with a test that fails when the two differ.
  • A pytest module that validates the frontmatter with a Pydantic model and fails on a duplicate id or term, a relation to a missing id, a cycle in Kind of or Part of, and a Defined in path, or a Stored in path under src/ or docs/, that does not exist. A Stored in line may also name a file that lives in a generated project or the user's data directory, such as profile.toml, and the check skips those.
  • Each domain model declaring its concept's identifier in model_config["json_schema_extra"]["x-concept"], with a test that every declared identifier has an entry.
  • A Vale vocabulary generated from the Avoid lines for the prose check, so the retired names have one source and an established tool applies them, with severities: error for a name that collides with another concept's term, warning for a softer preference.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• One ontology in CONTEXT.md, found by sweeps (chosen). One document is the only copy of each definition, the engineering skills keep reading the file they already read, the site keeps rendering it, and the labels give structure without new tooling.
  • One concept file per concept now — deferred to automation. Without a generator, the concept files and CONTEXT.md hold two copies of every term and summary with nothing to keep them equal.
  • A SKOS concept scheme in Turtle as the source — rejected as the source and kept as a possible export. SKOS fits the content: it models concepts as individuals rather than classes, and its hidden label matches Avoid. As the source it puts definitions in string literals that people and skills edit by hand and needs rdflib, pySHACL and a generator to produce the Markdown everyone reads, and SHACL Core cannot check Kind of for cycles without SHACL-SPARQL.
  • TBX (ISO 30042) as the source — rejected as the source and kept as a possible export. TBX is the published standard closest to this entry model, a concept entry holding terms with preferred, admitted and deprecated status, and it is XML built for translation and exchange between termbases.
  • LinkML as the source — rejected. LinkML describes data shapes, and many of Boilerplate's concepts (golden path, toolchain, curation) are not data shapes. Generating the domain models from LinkML makes two sources of the same shapes during the migration, and the models' hand-written validators would move into generator templates. Revisit if a data schema has to serve other languages as an equal, if RDF interoperability becomes a product feature, or if people who do not write Python need to own the model.
  • OWL — rejected. OWL is open-world and makes no unique-name assumption, so a missing required value is not an error, and nothing in Boilerplate needs inference.
  • CONTEXT.md as it was — rejected. Its Avoid lists retired names that prose then used more often, and relations it states only in sentences show no whole.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The old Relationships list becomes "Rules across modules"; its other statements move onto labeled lines.
  • Entries that name only a file fold into the concept they store, and their anchors stay beside the absorbing entry.
  • docs/agents/domain.md tells the engineering skills that entries follow these labels. The skills themselves are the maintainer's plugins, outside this repository, and change there.
  • Drift between sweeps is expected: nothing fails a build when prose uses a retired name.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. Placements. Some concepts fit two modules, such as Guardrails in model or trust, and slot in model or as a term of the tool landscape. The maintainer confirms each placement the restructuring proposes.
  2. An admitted tier. Terminology standards allow a tolerated synonym between the preferred term and a deprecated one. Whether Avoid needs that middle tier, for an abbreviation for example, is open.
  3. The enforcement area. The substrate entry says "area" where PROD-001 says "layer". Whether "area" needs its own term, and what to do about the enforcement_layers key in PROD-001, which still carries the word, is open.

docs.title: Verification (2026-10-18)
docs.text:
I checked each external claim against its primary source on 2026-10-18. The repository facts in Context come from the files they name.

  • SKOS models concepts as individuals. "the 'concepts' of a thesaurus or classification scheme are modeled as individuals in the SKOS data model … never as class or property axioms" (SKOS Reference §1.1). skos:hiddenLabel is "A lexical label for a resource that should be hidden when generating visual displays of the resource, but should still be accessible to free text search operations" (SKOS core RDF).
  • SHACL Core has no cycle check. sh:hasValue compares value nodes with a fixed RDF term and not with the focus node, and SHACL-SPARQL adds SELECT-based constraints (SHACL §4.8.2, §5). I infer the absence of a cycle constraint from the specification; no sentence in it states one.
  • OWL makes no unique-name assumption. "OWL does not make the assumption that different names are names for different individuals" (OWL 2 Primer).
  • LinkML is closed-world and writes pattern validators only by itself. "OWL is open-world, whereas LinkML is closed-world" (LinkML OWL generator); "Currently the only kind of slot-level validators that are created are for those slots that have a pattern property" (LinkML Pydantic generator).
