  • Terminology standards separate preferred, admitted and deprecated terms. ANSI/NISO Z39.19 links a non-preferred synonym to its preferred term (USE/UF) and separates whole-part from genus-species hierarchy (BT/NT); ISO 12620 lists preferred, admitted and deprecated term status. I read both through published summaries, not the standards' texts.
  • Vale reads vocabularies independently of its styles. Vale feeds a vocabulary's rejected terms into Vale.Avoid (Vale vocabularies), and GitLab fails its docs CI on error-level Vale rules (GitLab docs testing).
  • Context files have no measured general benefit. Gloaguen et al. report that context files "do not generally improve task success rates" and raise inference cost by more than 20% (arXiv 2602.11988). The study tested overviews and tooling instructions, not glossaries.
  • This repository's history. I measured rules at dated snapshots of the archive repository (2026-05-11 to 2026-09-04) and of develop (from 2026-09-04), and reran at least one number per rule.
    • Of 556 commits authored while the commit-message rules existed only in prose, 22 had a subject over 72 characters; of 667 authored once scripts/commit_lint.py existed, none did. A model new to the repository wrote most of the later commits, so the check is not the only cause.
    • The docstring-mood rule changed twice in prose, and neither change moved existing code; the count fell to zero when a sweep rewrote the code and the D401 check turned on, and it stayed at zero as public functions grew from 102 to 270.
    • After the Avoid lists were written, "template variable" rose from 14 to 16 uses in the docs and "overlay" for a layer from 0 to 8.
    • The limits: one project, no control group, gates record only what landed, and maintainer corrections made in conversation leave no trace in git.

docs.title: ADR-017: Build backend — uv_build by default, hatchling by choice
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Scope note. This ADR fixes which build backends the project template offers, which one it renders by default, how the uv_build version bound stays current, and how an existing project keeps its backend through copier update. For what exists today, see status.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The project template renders a pure-Python package with a static version and one src/<package_name> directory, and its toolchain is built on uv (dev-environment landscape). The streamlit template extends project, so it renders the same [build-system] table. The build backend is the one slot of that toolchain that the mapping table leaves unfilled, and Boilerplate's rule for slots is one opinionated pick each, with a named override.

Projects rendered before this decision declare hatchling with no version bound. Three facts bear on the pick:

  • uv ships its own backend. uv_build is the backend that plain uv init declares since uv 0.12.0, and uv's documentation calls it "a great choice for most Python projects" (uv build backend). It builds pure Python only.
  • uv's own docs name the escape hatch. The documentation advises that "when build scripts or a more flexible project layout are required, consider using the hatchling build backend instead" (uv build backend). hatchling runs build hooks and plugins, reads the version from git tags through hatch-vcs, and selects files with its own configuration.
  • A backend cap needs upkeep. uv bumps its minor version for breaking changes and its patch version for everything else (uv versioning policy), and its documentation tells uv_build users to cap the requirement at the next minor. uv released 0.12.0 on 2026-07-28 and 0.13.0 on 2026-10-09, so a cap of that kind needs a bump every few months.

A render that picks a backend also decides what happens when copier update meets a project rendered earlier. A new question with a default is applied silently by copier update --defaults, so adding the question without a migration moves every existing hatchling project to uv_build. That move drops any [tool.hatch] configuration and any dynamic = ["version"] entry the project relies on, and narrows the sdist from every file git does not ignore to the package and its metadata. Versioning § What qualifies as breaking classes "changing the default value of an option incompatibly" as breaking.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The project template MUST ask a build_backend question with two choices, uv_build (the default) and hatchling, and MUST render the [build-system] table, plus the [tool.hatch] table for hatchling, from that answer. The streamlit template inherits the question from project and does not redeclare it.

  1. The question. build_backend is a str question with choices, placed before package_index_url in the project template's copier.yml. Its choices are the two backend names, with no description on either; the project template guide says when to pick each.
  2. The uv_build render. The template renders requires = ["uv_build>=0.13,<0.14"] and build-backend = "uv_build", with no [tool.hatch] table. uv_build finds src/<package_name> without configuration.
  3. The hatchling render. The template renders requires = ["hatchling>=1.27"], build-backend = "hatchling.build" and the [tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel] table with packages = ["src/<package_name>"]. Hatchling 1.27.0 is the first release that writes the PEP 639 license fields (License-Expression, License-File) by default; 1.26.x writes the old License: field. The requirement has no cap, the same as hatch new writes it.
  4. The bound is a minor range. The uv_build requirement takes the current uv minor as its floor (>=0.13, not >=0.13.3), so every uv 0.13.x runs its bundled copy of the backend and fetches nothing from a package index. A private package_index_url therefore mirrors no build backend for a project inside the range.
  5. The bound moves with the Docker tag. The streamlit template's Dockerfile installs uv from the image tag ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:<minor>. For every uv minor, the uv_build range and that tag move together in one change, and a test renders streamlit and asserts that the range's minor equals the tag's minor. An image older than the range's floor fetches uv-build from the package index and fails offline with a cold cache, which is the reason for the pairing. The test catches drift between the two values and does not catch staleness, so the release checklist in RELEASING.md names the uv minor, and uv's own warning (point 6) tells a user that a generated project's cap is stale.
  6. uv's behavior outside the range. uv uses its bundled backend only when requires is a single uv_build entry whose range contains uv's version. A uv newer than the cap (0.13.3 against <0.13) builds with its bundled copy and warns on every uv sync and uv build. A uv older than the floor fetches uv-build from the index, as the documentation describes. The documentation's statement that an out-of-range uv "uses a compatible version of the uv_build package" describes only the second case.
  7. A before migration keeps existing projects on hatchling. The project template's copier.yml declares its first _migrations entry with when: "{{ _stage == 'before' }}" and no version gate: bundled layers share the repository's tag stream, so a gate at the version that introduces the question would skip a project rendered at the tag just before it, and the key check below makes the entry a no-op once the answer exists. The migration runs the update's Python ({{ _copier_python }}) to append build_backend: hatchling to the layer's answers file (.copier-answers.project.yml, passed to the script as {{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}) when that file exists and holds no build_backend key. copier update --defaults then keeps a project rendered before the question existed on hatchling, and an explicit --data build_backend=hatchling keeps it as well. A project that has a build_backend answer is untouched.
  8. Switching is a re-answer. A project that changes backend after generation re-answers the question with copier update --data build_backend=<choice>, which re-renders the [build-system] table and the [tool.hatch] table together.

docs.title: When to choose which backend
docs.text:
The table covers the nine backends a Python project most often meets; the two the template offers come first. It leaves out whey, which had four sdists in the Quansight Labs sample, py-build-cmake, which has about 31 thousand downloads a month, and enscons, which has about 10 thousand downloads a month and little activity. A backend outside the first two is a hand edit of [build-system] in the generated project, and the template scaffolds no Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt for the compiled rows.

Backend Choose it when Avoid it when Notes: PEP 639, editable installs, version bounds uv_build (default) Pure Python; static version; one src/<package>; uv toolchain Version from git tags; build hooks; generated files that git ignores inside the package; several top-level packages PEP 639 output. PEP 660 editable hook. Bound >=0.13,<0.14; uv's documentation caps at the next minor hatchling Build hooks; version from git (hatch-vcs); custom file selection; plugins A build that must fetch no build requirement (uv_build runs from uv's bundled copy); native extensions without a custom hook PEP 639 output by default from 1.27.0 (1.26.x writes the old License: field). Editable installs through a .pth file. Floor >=1.27, no cap setuptools Existing setup.py or cmdclass; small C extension through ext_modules; setuptools-rust New pure-Python project; non-.py data without package-data (the wheel silently omits it) PEP 639 from 77.0.1, the first release on PyPI (77.0.0 was never published); the PyPA tutorial uses >=77.0.3. Editable installs from 64.0.0; a binary extension is a snapshot flit-core Tiny module; __version__ as the version; nothing else Hooks; git versioning; generated files PEP 639 from 3.11. Flit's documentation: >=3.11,<5; the PyPA tutorial tab: >=3.12.0,<5 pdm-backend The team runs PDM; built-in SCM version A uv-run project, where PDM's workflow owns the lock PEP 639 from 2.4.0. Editable installs through path or editables. PyPA tutorial: >=2.4.0 poetry-core The team runs Poetry; no extension modules A uv-run project; extension modules (Poetry calls its build scripts "still considered unstable") [project] table from 2.0.0; PEP 639 from 2.2.0. Poetry's documentation: >=2.0.0,<3.0.0 maturin Rust through PyO3, cffi or uniffi Code with no Rust PEP 639 in full from 1.9.0 and the License-Expression fix in 1.9.2. A Rust edit needs a rebuild. uv init scaffolds it and writes cache-keys scikit-build-core C, C++, Fortran or Cython with CMake, pybind11 or nanobind A codebase with no CMake PEP 639 from 0.11.0. Editable redirect; rebuild-on-import is experimental. uv init --build-backend scikit scaffolds it meson-python A Meson codebase; the numerics stack (numpy and scipy build with it) A project that wants uv init scaffolding or automatic cache-keys PEP 639 from 0.18.0. Editable rebuild-on-import needs --no-build-isolation. uv init rejects it

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• uv_build default, hatchling by choice (chosen). The default covers the template's shape (pure Python, static version, one src/<package_name>) and is the backend uv itself scaffolds. hatchling is the one other backend that does a job uv_build does not for this template: hooks, plugins, and a version from git. Each of the two has a stated trigger in the question's help strings.
  • hatchling as the default (the runner-up). The PyPA packaging tutorial states "this tutorial uses Hatchling by default" (packaging projects), and the Scientific Python Development Guide says "If you don't have an existing preference, hatchling is an excellent choice" (packaging simple). hatchling needs no cap upkeep. PyPI recorded about 320 million hatchling downloads and about 15 million uv-build downloads in the month before 2026-10-19 (pypistats); pip build isolation and CI inflate both counts, so they are not adoption shares. Rejected: the template's toolchain is uv, uv recommends uv_build for this project shape, and the cap has cost only bumps so far, because each uv release note states "no breaking changes to the configuration of the uv build backend" (uv changelogs). What would change the call: uv dropping or loosening its cap advice, or a usage census that shows uv_build adoption stalling.
  • A wider menu (setuptools, flit-core, pdm-backend, poetry-core and the compiled backends). Rejected, because a menu is not a pick and each extra choice has to do a job neither default nor override does for this template.
    • setuptools adds extension and legacy-setup.py use, which the template does not scaffold, and its wheel omits non-.py data files without a package-data entry.
    • flit-core does less than uv_build for this shape.
    • pdm-backend and poetry-core belong to the PDM and Poetry workflows, whose tools own the lock; that contradicts the uv pick in the landscape mapping table.
    • The compiled backends need source scaffolding (Cargo.toml, CMakeLists.txt), cache-keys, and a compiler stage in the streamlit Dockerfile.
  • Derive the uv_build bound from the running uv at render time. Rejected. It matches what uv init does, and the project template has precedent: _extensions/context.py derives the Python version from the running interpreter. The render would then depend on the machine that runs it, and the bound would split from the static Docker image tag that point 5 pairs it with.
  • Choose the default by operation, so that copier update defaults to hatchling and copy defaults to uv_build. Rejected, because Copier exposes _copier_operation only in exclude and _tasks, not in a question's default (Copier: creating a template). The before-stage migration of point 7 is the mechanism Copier documents for changing answers across versions.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The cap needs upkeep. The uv_build range and the streamlit Dockerfile tag move for every uv minor (point 5). Dependabot's uv and github-actions ecosystems update only this repository's own files, so no updater reaches a .jinja file, and the release checklist is the reminder.
  • uv_build ships git-ignored files. It does not read .gitignore: a git-ignored file inside the package directory reaches both the wheel and the sdist. hatchling honors .gitignore. Nothing the template renders today sits in that position. A project that generates files into its package tree sets source-exclude and wheel-exclude under [tool.uv.build-backend], or chooses hatchling.
  • uv_build builds from static metadata. A non-empty dynamic list fails the build with "Dynamic metadata is not supported". A project that wants a version from git tags chooses hatchling and hatch-vcs.
  • The migration is one more reason copier update needs --trust, not a new requirement. The project layer already declares _jinja_extensions, including the file-path _extensions/context.py, and _tasks, so Copier's unsafe check refuses an update of it without --trust. Versioning also lists running copier update across any declared migration as a step that refuses to start without --trust. Layers that Boilerplate bundles are copy-only (ADR-015), so only a project rendered from a git-backed project layer meets the migration.
  • The migration is the reason the change is not breaking. With it, adding build_backend is "adding a new template variable (with a sensible default)" under Versioning; without it, the change is the incompatible default change the Context describes. The migration reads and writes the answers file, which is Copier's file layout and not a Copier API, so the template version that ships it MUST pass a test that updates a hatchling project and asserts that its backend is unchanged.
  • Boilerplate's own pyproject.toml follows the same default. The repository is a pure-Python package with a static version and one src/boilerplate, the shape for which uv_build is the pick.

docs.title: Verification (2026-10-20)
docs.text:
The sources below were read on 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-20, and the trials ran in scratch projects under uv 0.13.3 and Copier 9.18.1. Repository facts in the Context come from the files they name.

  • uv. Documentation: "a great choice for most Python projects", pure Python only, hatchling for build scripts, and the bound >=0.13.3,<0.14 as the example (build backend). uv init declares uv_build for plain apps since 0.12.0 (changelog 0.12.x); uv 0.13.3 writes uv_build>=0.13.3,<0.14.0 into a new project. The minor-for-breaking policy is in versioning. uv_build rejects a non-empty dynamic list in crates/uv-build-backend/src/metadata.rs (source), and a trial with uv 0.13.3 reproduced the message. The out-of-range behavior in point 6 comes from uv 0.13.3 against <0.13 (bundled copy, warning) and uv 0.12.15 against a floor above its version (index fetch).
  • File selection. In a trial with a git-ignored file inside the package and one in a generated subdirectory, uv_build shipped both and hatchling shipped neither.
  • hatchling. 1.27.0 is the first release that writes License-Expression; 1.26.3 writes Metadata 2.3 with the old License: field and no License-Expression (hatchling history; wheel inspected for both). The PyPA tutorial's hatchling >= 1.26 is therefore short of PEP 639 output by default.
  • PyPA tutorial tabs. hatchling >= 1.26, setuptools >= 77.0.3, flit_core >=3.12.0,<5, pdm-backend >= 2.4.0 (build-backend-tabs.rst).
  • setuptools. PEP 639 in the 77.0.0 notes, and PyPI lists 77.0.1 and 77.0.3 but not 77.0.0; PEP 660 in 64.0.0 (NEWS, PyPI JSON). A trial wheel omitted .txt and dotfile data that no package-data entry listed.
  • flit-core. flit_core >=3.11,<5 and PEP 639 from 3.11 (pyproject.toml docs).
  • pdm-backend. Version 2.4.0 writes License-Expression and License-File; 2.4.5 and 2.5.0 write them as well (wheels inspected). The 2.4.6 changelog entry "Add license file metadata" edits pdm-backend's own pyproject.toml and does not change the built metadata. The PDM documentation is at backend.pdm-project.org.
  • poetry-core. [project] support in 2.0.0, PEP 639 in 2.2.0, >=2.0.0,<3.0.0 in the docs, and build scripts "still considered unstable" (CHANGELOG, extension modules).
  • Compiled backends. maturin: PEP 639 in 1.9.0 and the License-Expression fix in 1.9.2 (Changelog). scikit-build-core: PEP 639 in 0.11.0 (changelog). meson-python: PEP 639 in 0.18.0 (CHANGELOG). uv init offers maturin and scikit-build-core and rejects meson-python (uv init). numpy and scipy build with meson-python, which their pyproject.toml files declare.
  • Bounds in each backend's own scaffold. hatch new writes an unbounded hatchling; flit init writes flit_core >=3.11,<5; poetry new writes a range from the installed poetry-core.
  • Render trial. A scratch copy of the project template was rendered with each choice. Each render passed validate-pyproject and ran uv lock, uv sync, pytest and uv build under uv 0.13.3. The hatchling render differs from the output of earlier template versions on the requires line only.
  • Update trial. On a toy template with a build_backend question added after the project's first render, copier update --defaults moved a hatchling project to uv_build; with the before-stage migration it stayed on hatchling, and --data build_backend=hatchling kept it as well.
  • Omitted backends. whey had four sdists in the Quansight Labs sample (PEP 517 build system popularity); py-build-cmake and enscons download figures come from pypistats, and their projects are py-build-cmake and enscons.
  • Copier. _copier_operation is documented for exclude and _tasks only (creating a template).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The update trial used a toy template with the answers file .copier-answers.yml. The project template's own answers file, .copier-answers.project.yml, was not exercised, which is the reason point 7 requires an update test in the template's suite.
  • No Docker image was built. The behavior of the streamlit image under the uv:0.13 tag and the >=0.13,<0.14 range follows from the uv documentation and the 0.12.15 trial.
  • The editable and rebuild behavior of maturin, scikit-build-core and meson-python comes from their documentation; no compiler was available to run them.
  • Whether Dependabot's uv ecosystem updates a [build-system] requirement in a generated project was not tested.
  • The newest usage census (Quansight Labs, "PEP 517 build system popularity", published 2025-02-11) reports no uv_build count; it was read through its markdown source and its figures were not re-checked. The download counts in the options are monthly totals, and they serve for the order of magnitude only.

docs.title: Relationship to other ADRs
docs.text:
• ADR-001 — uv's own backend and hatchling are adopted tools; Boilerplate adds only the choice between them.
  • ADR-003 and ADR-007 — the before migration of point 7 is a first-party migration, the kind that ADR-007 makes the mechanism for structural change and that ADR-003 puts on the task and extension trust surface.
  • ADR-015 — the migration edits the per-layer answers file .copier-answers.project.yml, which that ADR makes the distribution contract, and Copier's own _migrations mechanism runs it.

docs.title: The Development Environment Landscape
docs.text:
The reference taxonomy of what a Python development environment comprises. Boilerplate's design vocabulary calls each recurring role in this taxonomy a slot. This document catalogues the landscape; the §How Boilerplate maps onto the landscape section records which slots Boilerplate opines on.

Provenance. Transcribed from the project author's Python Development Environment mind map, committed alongside this document as the XMind source. This transcription is the repo-canonical text form. Category definitions are the author's; example tools are illustrative, not exhaustive, and not endorsements.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Tools, libraries, and configurations that enable scalable and maintainable Python application development, enhancing productivity, code quality, reliability, and maintainability.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
The context in which Python code runs, including the interpreter, libraries, and configurations. Effective environments ensure isolated and reproducible builds, reducing conflicts between dependencies. (In this taxonomy, Environment names the runtime context specifically — a narrower sense than the glossary's domain-level term.)

  • Python Interpreter — software that reads and executes Python code. Examples: CPython, PyPy, IronPython, Jython, GraalPy, MicroPython, Stackless Python.
  • Environment Management — tools for isolating project dependencies, preventing conflicts, and ensuring consistent builds. Examples: venv, conda, uv.

docs.title: Package/Dependency Management
docs.text: Software that simplifies the installation, upgrading, and removal of Python libraries, ensuring projects have the correct versions of all required packages. Examples: pip, poetry, conda, pip-tools, pipenv, uv.

docs.title: Development Tools
docs.text:
Software and utilities that automate repetitive tasks, profile performance, and facilitate experimentation and prototyping.

  • Interactive Development Environments — platforms combining code, visualizations, and explanatory text for experimentation and collaboration.
    • Notebook Environments — Jupyter Notebook, Google Colab, Deepnote.
    • Remote Development Environments — workspaces accessible via a network or abstracted from the primary local machine. Examples: GitHub Codespaces, Microsoft DevBox, Dev Containers.
    • Interactive Shells — advanced REPLs. Example: IPython.
  • Debugging Tools — identifying and resolving code issues. Examples: pdb, ipdb, debugpy.
  • Build & Automation
    • Build Tools — compile, package, and distribute projects into installable formats. Examples: setuptools, hatch, wheel.
    • Task Runners — automate repetitive development tasks for consistent workflows. Examples: invoke, nox.
  • Performance Profiling — identify bottlenecks and optimize execution. Examples: cProfile, line_profiler, timeit, memory_profiler, py-spy, gprof2dot.

docs.title: Code Management Tools
docs.text:
Tools and utilities that streamline collaboration, improve code quality, and track changes throughout the software development lifecycle.

  • Version Control Systems — track changes to source code over time, enabling collaboration, branching, merging, and reverting. Examples: Git, Mercurial.
  • Code Review Workflows — processes for evaluating proposed changes (pull/merge requests) to ensure quality and share knowledge. Examples: GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab, Bitbucket.
  • Collaboration Tools — planning, task coordination, and discussion. Examples: Azure DevOps Boards, GitHub Projects, GitLab Issues, Trello/Jira, Slack/Teams.

docs.title: IDEs & Editors
docs.text: Applications providing a suite of development features — syntax highlighting, refactoring, debugging, version-control integration — to streamline coding workflows. Examples: PyCharm, Visual Studio Code, Spyder, Jupyter Notebook, Thonny.

docs.title: Code Quality Tools
docs.text:
Software that ensures Python code adheres to style guidelines, avoids errors, and remains maintainable.

  • Linters — inspect code without running it to identify style issues, errors, or potential bugs. Examples: Flake8, Pylint, Ruff.
  • Code Formatters — reformat source code to a consistent style. Examples: Black, YAPF, Ruff.
  • Type Checkers — validate code against type annotations, catching errors early. Examples: mypy, Pyright.
  • Testing Frameworks — create, organize, and execute automated tests.
    • Core Frameworks — pytest, unittest.
    • Environment Management for tests — tox, nox.
    • Mocking — unittest.mock, pytest-mock.
    • Code Coverage — coverage, pytest-cov.

docs.title: Deployment Tools
docs.text:
Technologies for packaging and deploying Python applications, automating processes and enhancing scalability.

  • Containerization — Containers (Docker, Rancher Desktop) and Container Orchestration (Kubernetes, Rancher).
  • Serverless — AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions.
  • CI/CD — continuous integration and deployment platforms. Examples: GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines, Jenkins, TeamCity.
  • Infrastructure as Code — Terraform, Ansible.
  • Platform as a Service — Heroku, Google App Engine, Azure App Service.

docs.title: Security Tools
docs.text:
Tools that enhance the security and integrity of Python applications.

  • Static Analysis — Bandit, Semgrep.
  • Dependency Scanning — Safety, Dependabot, Snyk.
  • Secrets Management — Doppler, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault.
  • Monitoring and Observability — New Relic, Datadog, Sentry, Prometheus, Grafana.

docs.title: Documentation Tools
docs.text:
Tools and standards for creating and maintaining project documentation.

  • Docstring Standards — reStructuredText, Google style, NumPy style.
  • Documentation Generators — Sphinx, MkDocs.

docs.title: Data and Visualization Tools
docs.text:
Tools for manipulating, analyzing, and visualizing data.

  • Data Analysis — pandas, numpy.
  • Visualization — matplotlib, seaborn, Plotly.

docs.title: Learning and Experimentation
docs.text: Interactive platforms and hosted environments for learning Python, prototyping, and experimenting. Examples: Jupyter Notebook, Google Colab.

docs.title: How Boilerplate maps onto the landscape
docs.text:
Each first-party template fills the slots its ecosystem's dev loop uses — the roles a developer exercises on every pass through it — with one opinionated, preconfigured pick each, declared through the profile the template requires. The Python picks:

Slot Pick Environment Management + Package/Dependency Management uv Linters + Code Formatters Ruff Type Checkers Pyright Testing Frameworks (core, mocking, coverage) pytest, pytest-mock, pytest-cov Build Tools uv_build, with hatchling as the override (ADR-017) IDEs & Editors VS Code Version Control Systems Git

Two rules give the mapping its shape:

  • Templates declare their slots and fill them. A template's required profile names the tool per slot, including any secondary toolchain its kind of project needs (the streamlit template needs Docker and Bash; on Windows, WSL2); the environment installs and verifies what the profile declares; the template pre-wires each tool's per-project configuration — Ruff's rule set, Pyright's strictness, pytest's options, the .vscode/ workspace settings — and scaffolds adjacent slots such as CI/CD and documentation generation as gating scaffolding the user opts into.
  • Slots no first-party template requires are out of scope by design. The remaining landscape (profiling, serverless, IaC, PaaS, data tooling, …) is a scope boundary: "should Boilerplate also do X?" is answered by whether some first-party template's kind of project needs X on its golden path. Containerization enters through the streamlit template's required profile.

The development environment built from these picks is itself a first-class, managed surface — installation, verification, update, and drift detection across its lifecycle — per 01-overview.md §Environment lifecycle is managed and the provisioning design in §08 / ADR-009.

docs.title: Development environment
docs.text: Boilerplate projects include a complete, modern Python development environment. This section documents that Development Environment and its parts: the Toolchain, the dev loop, the Project Layout, and their Configuration.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text: Boilerplate fills each slot the dev loop uses with one preconfigured, overridable tool rather than a menu, and the toolchain lists the picks. They are set up on your machine, in each project and in your editor — see A whole environment, one pick per slot; the landscape holds the full taxonomy.

docs.title: uv
docs.text: Dependency & environment manager. An extremely fast package and project manager (written in Rust) that installs and pins Python, manages your virtual environment, and keeps installs reproducible from pyproject.toml — day to day, uv sync, uv add <pkg>, uv remove <pkg>. Official docs

docs.title: Ruff
docs.text: Linter & formatter. One fast tool (also Rust) for both jobs — enforces PEP 8, docstrings, and naming, auto-fixes what it can, and formats on save, so style stays out of your way. Official docs

docs.title: Pyright
docs.text: Type checker. Catches type errors as you type — live in VS Code via Pylance — so mistakes surface early instead of at runtime. On GitHub

docs.title: Pytest
docs.text: Test runner. Discovers and runs your tests from the command line or the VS Code Test Explorer, with fixtures, parametrization, and coverage already wired in. Official docs

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text: Editor. Your workspace, pre-wired so the rest of the toolchain just works — format-on-save, live type hints, and test discovery out of the box. Setup guide Official docs

docs.title: Git
docs.text: Version control. Tracks your project's history, makes branching and experimentation safe, and syncs with remotes like GitHub. Official docs

docs.title: The dev loop
docs.text: The dev loop is the cycle you repeat inside a project, which is test-driven development's red-green-refactor: write a failing test, make it pass with the least code, then refactor with the tests still green. Then run the checks, commit, and start the next turn. Steps 1 and 2 get a project ready; steps 3 and 4 are the loop.

docs.title: 1. Start or clone a project
docs.text:
New project:

boilerplate new <template>

Add dependencies as you go — uv add <pkg>, or uv add --dev <pkg> for a development-only dependency.

Existing project:

  1. Clone the project:

    git clone <repo>

  2. Synchronize the dependencies:

    uv sync

    This installs or updates dependencies based on your pyproject.toml.

    To upgrade dependencies:

    uv sync --upgrade

docs.title: 2. Open VS Code
docs.text:
code .

Launch a fully configured editor with linting, auto-formatting, type checks, etc.

Warning

Opening a cloned project before uv sync can leave VS Code without a detected interpreter — see the fix.

docs.title: 3. Red, green, refactor
docs.text:
• Pytest runs your tests, via the command line or the VS Code Test Explorer. Write a test that fails (red), make it pass with the least code (green), then refactor while it stays green:

    uv run pytest

The checks run alongside:

  • Ruff handles styling and lint checks in real time and formats on save — or run it yourself:

    uv run ruff format .
uv run ruff check --fix .

  • Pyright highlights type issues as you code — or run it yourself:

    uv run pyright

docs.title: 4. Commit and repeat
docs.text:
Commit each turn that passes its tests and checks, then start the next one. Many commits make one pull request.

git commit

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text:
A consistent project layout helps everyone understand the codebase at a glance — see Project structure for the generated tree.

  • .vscode/: Local editor settings and recommended extensions ensure a consistent VS Code experience
  • src/: Houses production code. Separating it from tests and configuration files prevents naming conflicts and maintains clarity
  • src/your_package/: Contains the main application code, including sub-packages and modules
  • tests/: Mirrors the structure of your main package with corresponding test files
  • .gitignore: Lists files and directories (e.g., virtual environments, build artifacts, temporary files, sensitive data) that Git should ignore
  • README.md: Provides an overview of your project's purpose, setup, and usage

docs.title: What boilerplate configures for you
docs.text:
Generated projects arrive with the toolchain pre-wired. Beginners can ignore the specifics and just code; the exact configuration is here when you want it.

The shipped configuration (click to expand)
  • Ruff ([tool.ruff]) — fix = true and a broad rule set (~26 categories: pyflakes, pycodestyle, isort, pydocstyle with the Google convention, annotations, bugbear, pathlib, pyupgrade, and more), plus docstring code formatting. tests/ and __init__.py get sensible per-file ignores.
  • Pyright ([tool.pyright]) — typeCheckingMode = "strict" over src/ (tests relaxed). Type-checking runs live via Pylance in VS Code and from the CLI with uv run pyright; pyright ships in the dev group.
  • pytest ([tool.pytest.ini_options]) — log_cli = true, with pytest-cov and pytest-mock in the dev group.
  • VS Code (.vscode/) — Ruff as the default formatter for Python and notebooks, format-on-save, and pytest discovery enabled. The interpreter isn't pinned; the Python extension auto-detects .venv in the workspace root.

The authoritative configuration is the generated pyproject.toml and .vscode/ — these summaries point you at it, not away from it. The pyproject.toml guide explains the file itself.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• VS Code — interpreter selection, extensions, and troubleshooting for the generated .vscode/ setup.
  • Developer platform architecture — the reference model this environment implements.

docs.title: VS Code configuration
docs.text:
Boilerplate projects ship a .vscode/ folder so the editor is ready the moment you open the project — linting, formatting, type hints, and test discovery all work with no manual setup.

.vscode/
├─ extensions.json
└─ settings.json

New to VS Code? After generating or cloning a project, open the folder and accept the prompt to install the recommended extensions.

docs.title: Recommended extensions
docs.text:
When you open a generated project, VS Code reads .vscode/extensions.json and offers to install these. That file is the authoritative list; this page explains what each one is for:

  • Python (ms-python.python) — the core Python experience: run and debug code, pick the interpreter, and Pylance, which provides IntelliSense, go-to-definition, and live type checking as you type.
  • Jupyter (ms-toolsai.jupyter) — open and run .ipynb notebooks inside VS Code.
  • Ruff (charliermarsh.ruff) — linting and formatting, wired in as the default formatter for Python and notebooks.
  • Even Better TOML (tamasfe.even-better-toml) — syntax highlighting and validation for pyproject.toml and other TOML files.
  • Prettier (esbenp.prettier-vscode) — formatting for non-Python files (JSON, Markdown, YAML).

docs.title: Workspace settings
docs.text:
.vscode/settings.json connects the editor to the project's tools:

  • Ruff is the default formatter for Python and notebooks, with format-on-save enabled.
  • pytest discovery is on, so tests appear in the Testing sidebar.
  • Pylance runs in workspace mode with auto-import suggestions, and honors the [tool.pyright] settings in pyproject.toml (strict over src/) — so the type errors you see inline match what the configured checks enforce.
  • Debugging — set a breakpoint and press F5 to launch the debugger with the workspace interpreter.

The interpreter path isn't set in settings.json — the Python extension auto-detects .venv in the workspace root, and that works the same on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

docs.title: Troubleshooting: the interpreter isn't detected
docs.text:
Most common right after generating or cloning a project, before the virtual environment exists:

  1. Run uv sync to create .venv.
  2. Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or Cmd+Shift+P on macOS) → Python: Select Interpreter.
  3. Choose the .venv interpreter in your project folder.

If an extension doesn't activate, reload the window: Command Palette → Developer: Reload Window.

docs.title: Troubleshooting: Ruff not formatting automatically
docs.text:
Check VS Code settings include:

{
  "[python]": {
    "editor.defaultFormatter": "charliermarsh.ruff"
  }
}

Tip

Still not formatting? Command Palette → Developer: Reload Window.

docs.title: Troubleshooting: tests not discovered
docs.text:
• Cause: The test framework is not enabled or the environment is not activated.
  • Solution:
    1. Run uv sync so .venv exists, then select it (Python: Select Interpreter).
    2. In VS Code, open the Command Palette and run "Python: Discover Tests".
    3. Select pytest as the test framework.
  • Verify:
    • Tests appear in the VS Code Test Explorer.
    • Running uv run pytest in the terminal should show all tests passing.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: Other symptoms (lint errors, template rendering errors)? See Troubleshooting. Back to the Development Environment overview.

docs.title: CI Pipeline
docs.text: How a change travels from your working tree to develop, what runs at each step, and why the pipeline is shaped the way it is. The pipeline lives in .github/workflows/ci.yml; a separate workflow builds the downloadable offline docs bundle.

docs.title: The whole flow
docs.text:
A change moves from local checks to a draft pull request, then to one billed run once the pull request is ready, through the check gate, and on to a push to develop that runs the workflow again.

flowchart TD
    accTitle: How a change travels from local development to develop
    accDescr: Local development, where scripts/check.py mirrors the check job, leads to a draft pull request on which every job skips, and gh pr ready starts one billed run. In that run the changes job sends a docs-only change to skipped code jobs, a code change to the lint, shellcheck, typecheck, package, test and tests-go-red jobs, and a composition-path change to the scenarios job, while the docs build always runs and commit-lint runs on pull_request events only. All of these feed the check job, the single pass/fail signal, and once check is green and the PR is squash merged, the push to develop re-runs the same workflow with the push matrix.
    dev["Local development<br>scripts/check.py mirrors the check job"] --> draft["Draft PR<br>every job skips: free iteration"]
    draft -- "gh pr ready" --> run
    subgraph run["One billed run per event"]
        direction TB
        changes{"changes job<br>anything outside docs touched?"}
        changes -- "docs-only" --> skip["code jobs skip"]
        changes -- "code" --> code["lint / shellcheck / typecheck / package<br>test: the matrix policy below<br>tests-go-red: pull_request events only"]
        changes -- "composition paths" --> scen["scenarios<br>the matrix policy below"]
        docsjob["docs build<br>always runs, no needs"]
        lint["commit-lint<br>pull_request events only"]
        lint --> gate
        code --> gate["check<br>the single pass/fail signal"]
        scen --> gate
        skip --> gate
        docsjob --> gate
    end
    run -- "check green, squash merge" --> push["Push to develop<br>same workflow re-runs with the push matrix"]
    push -.-> free["Public repo: Actions minutes free"]
Hold "Alt" / "Option" to enable pan & zoom

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text:
• push to main or develop.
  • pull_request targeting main or develop, with ready_for_review added to the default activity types — without it, a draft flipped to ready would never get a CI run.
  • Superseded runs are cancelled (concurrency with cancel-in-progress): PRs group per ref, pushes group per branch.

docs.title: The dispatcher: changes
docs.text:
The first job diffs the run's commit range and classifies every changed file as docs (docs/, *.md, mkdocs.yml) or code (anything else). The six code jobs run only when something outside docs changed. It also flags composition when a changed file matches one of these paths; the scenarios job runs only then.

Path Why it counts src/boilerplate/ The scenarios drive the CLI, which reaches every package there tests/integration/boilerplate/composition/ The scenarios themselves tests/boilerplate/templates/ The template fixtures the scenarios build on tests/fixtures/family/ The made-up template family uv.lock The scenarios run against the locked dependency versions .github/workflows/ci.yml The workflow itself Event BASE HEAD pull_request PR base SHA PR head SHA push github.event.before (branch tip before the push) github.sha (tip after)

When BASE is unusable — empty, the zero SHA of a branch-creation push, or an object the clone no longer has after a force-push — the dispatcher falls back to running everything, the scenarios included. The failure mode of the fallback is a few wasted minutes, never a merge that skips validation. On develop and main the fallback is rare by construction: branch rules forbid non-fast-forward pushes.

docs.title: Draft PRs cost nothing
docs.text: changes, docs, and check each carry the guard github.event_name != 'pull_request' || !github.event.pull_request.draft; commit-lint carries the same draft term inside its PR-only condition. Every other job needs: changes, so when changes skips, they all skip transitively. check skips too — a draft never shows a vacuously green check. Iterate on drafts freely; flip ready when the local check passes.

docs.title: Test matrix policy
docs.text:
Repository Event test legs scenarios legs Public pull_request, push ubuntu, windows, macos × 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 the same nine Private pull_request ubuntu × 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 ubuntu × 3.14 Private push ubuntu, windows, macos × 3.14, plus ubuntu × 3.12 and 3.13 ubuntu × 3.14

The full cross product runs wherever Actions minutes are free, and a public repository's standard runners cost nothing. While the repository is private, minutes are metered and Windows bills 2× and macOS 10×, so PRs run every supported Python on Linux and pushes to develop and main run every OS on the newest Python; development and the local check already exercise Windows. The workflow reads the visibility from the event (github.event.repository.private), so the switch needs no edit at the flip. Python 3.15 joins once it is final and every dependency ships a wheel for it; today pywin32 does not.

docs.title: Composition scenarios
docs.text: The scenarios rerun the composition design's evidence against real Copier and git, and a full run takes minutes. The test job deselects them (-m "not scenario"); the scenarios job runs them under the matrix policy above, and only when the dispatcher flags composition. A docs-only change never pays for them. check waits on it like any other job.

docs.title: New tests go red
docs.text: A PR that changes src/ and adds tests must show at least one added test failing against the base commit's src/ — otherwise none of them ever went red and the job fails, naming them. It runs on pull_request events only: a push has no base commit to diff added tests against. Script: scripts/new_tests_go_red.py.

docs.title: Commit messages
docs.text:
Pull requests squash-merge, so the PR title becomes the subject of the one commit that lands on develop, and release-please reads that subject. .github/workflows/pr-title.yml checks the title with scripts/commit_lint.py --message on every push and every edit to the PR, drafts included. It runs apart from this workflow, so editing a title or description never starts a billed CI run, and the develop ruleset requires its PR title check beside check.

Each commit on the branch must also be a conventional commit whose first line is at most 72 characters, so the history a reviewer reads follows the same rules. The commit-lint job checks the whole PR range and is a need of check, so a bad message blocks the merge. It runs on pull_request events only (a push has no PR range) and skips on drafts; check treats that skip as a pass. Script: scripts/commit_lint.py.

docs.title: The docs job
docs.text: The strict docs build (both the online config and the DOCS_OFFLINE release-bundle config) has no needs and ignores the path filter: mkdocstrings and autorefs build API pages from source, so a code-only change can break the docs build. Its only guard is the draft skip. It is a single cheap ubuntu runner.

docs.title: The check job
docs.text: check is the one status check that matters: it passes when no needed job failed or was cancelled, so jobs skipped by the path filter, or by event (commit-lint and tests-go-red on pushes), don't break it. Configure required checks against check alone, never against individual jobs. The one other required check is PR title, from its own workflow (see Commit messages).

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text: Every job sets timeout-minutes (5–45 by job). The GitHub default is 360, which would let a single job that stops responding use up hours of runner time — on a 2× or 10× runner, a large slice of a month's included minutes.

docs.title: The local check
docs.text:
Run before every push:

uv run python scripts/check.py

It mirrors CI's billable check — ruff check --no-fix, ruff format --check, the commit-range lint, pyright, the pytest suite without the scenarios, doctests, and both strict docs builds. It runs the scenarios too when a composition path differs from the merge base with origin/develop, or when it cannot find that merge base, and prints which it chose and why. A failure caught locally costs seconds; the same failure in CI costs a full billed run plus the rerun after the fix.

Next: Versioning & Compatibility — how releases are numbered and what compatibility they promise.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Please review our Security policy and Code of Conduct before contributing.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text: Follow Development environment setup in the repository root's CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Code quality
docs.text: Run the local check before pushing; Development environment setup has the command, and Running linting and type checking has the individual ruff, pyright and pytest commands. The check mirrors CI's lint, typecheck, test and docs jobs; the package smoke test, ShellCheck and the new-tests-go-red check run only in CI. The pipeline these checks feed into is documented in CI Pipeline.

docs.title: Mutation score ratchet
docs.text: A separate workflow, Mutation score, runs mutmut, a mutation-testing tool, once a month against the pure algorithmic core (composition, common, models, types, repository, settings, catalog, integrations — not the CLI or the Jinja templates) and checks the result against tests/mutation-baseline.json with scripts/mutation_ratchet.py: a ratchet that lets a package's score rise but never fall, so a drop fails the run. Trigger it manually from the Actions tab (workflow_dispatch) for a cheap trial on one package by filling in the paths input, e.g. src/boilerplate/common/. The workflow never opens a PR or pushes; raising the baseline after a genuine improvement is a human step — download the run's mutation-scores.json artifact and copy its contents over tests/mutation-baseline.json in an ordinary PR.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Write tests for new features
  • Use descriptive test names
  • Include integration tests for CLI commands

When you add a test alongside a src/ change, make it fail against the old code first, then land the fix — the standard red-green cycle. CI enforces this: see New tests go red for the mechanics. Renaming a test function in place (same file, new name) looks like adding a new one to that check, so give the renamed test a fresh red run too — moving or renaming the whole file is handled automatically.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Update relevant documentation
  • Add docstrings to new functions/classes
  • Include usage examples

docs.title: Submitting changes
docs.text:
Follow the Pull request process.

When you open the pull request:

  • Write each commit as a conventional commit (type: description) — the required check job validates every commit in the PR against conventional-commit types. Pull requests squash-merge, so the PR title becomes the commit on develop: write it the same way, and the required PR title check validates it.
  • Explain the changes.
  • Reference any related issues.

docs.title: Code guidelines
docs.text: See Code standards.

docs.title: Breaking changes and versioning
docs.text:
When contributing breaking changes, follow Boilerplate's versioning and deprecation policies:

  • CLI changes: Follow the Versioning & Compatibility Policy — deprecate for at least one minor version before removal
  • Template changes: Follow Versioning and migration — provide automated migration via Copier scripts
  • Approval & deprecation: See the Versioning & Compatibility Policy § Breaking-Change Approval for the approval process and deprecation guidelines

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: See the Design specifications for the architecture.

docs.title: Reporting bugs and requesting features
docs.text: Search existing GitHub issues first, then open a new one — for a bug, include a clear description, steps to reproduce, and expected vs. actual behavior; for a feature, describe the use case and motivation.

docs.title: Reporting a security vulnerability
docs.text:
See the Security policy — do not open a public issue.

Next: CI Pipeline — what runs when you push and open your PR.

docs.title: Supported Versions
docs.text:
Boilerplate is currently pre-1.0 and under active development. Security fixes are applied to the latest version on the develop branch only.

Version Supported < 1.0 ✅ (latest only)

docs.title: Reporting a Vulnerability
docs.text:
Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues.

Report privately using GitHub's private vulnerability reporting: open the repository's Security tab and choose Report a vulnerability. This creates a private advisory visible only to the maintainers.

Please include:

  • A description of the vulnerability.
  • Steps to reproduce or a proof of concept.
  • The potential impact.

We appreciate your help in keeping Boilerplate secure.

Back to Contribute.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This is the umbrella policy for how Boilerplate is versioned and how it manages backward-incompatible change across the CLI, configuration/profiles, and the Python API. Template-specific versioning and migrations live in Versioning and migration.

Principle: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 — MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A breaking change requires a major bump paired with a migration path.

Pre-1.0 (0.x) scope. Every stability guarantee here applies from 1.0. During 0.x (initial development, per SemVer §4) the only stable commitment is the PyPI distribution name; CLI commands, options, exit codes, error codes, output formats, and template variables MAY change in any 0.x release without a major bump. The first public tag (0.3.0) does not freeze these surfaces.

docs.title: Two breaking-change paths
docs.text:
Boilerplate manages breaking changes along two paths, because the two surfaces upgrade differently:

  • Template changes — automated. Copier's three-way merge applies migration scripts on copier update, so a template MAY introduce a breaking change without a deprecation period when it ships an automated migration.
  • CLI / Python-API changes — manual. Scripts and library callers do not auto-upgrade, so these require a deprecation period (see Deprecation Process) before removal.

docs.title: When to choose each path
docs.text: Scenario Path Reasoning Renaming template variables Template (Copier migration) Copier transforms answers/files automatically Moving/reorganizing template files Template (Copier migration) Migration scripts preserve user changes via merge Removing a CLI option CLI (deprecate → remove) Used in user scripts; cannot auto-migrate Changing a profile.toml field Depends Layout change → template migration; semantics change → CLI deprecation Removing a public Python API CLI (deprecate → remove) Library consumers write against it; needs a warning first

docs.title: What qualifies as breaking
docs.text:
Breaking (major version):

  • Removing or changing the behavior of a CLI command or option
  • Changing the default value of an option incompatibly
  • Changing exit codes for error conditions
  • Removing or changing the format of a profile.toml field
  • Removing a public Python API method or class
  • Removing template variables or restructuring generated file layout

Not breaking (minor / patch):

  • Adding a new command, option, config field, or template variable (with a sensible default)
  • Adding a new command alias
  • Bug fixes, performance improvements, documentation
  • Deprecating a feature (with a warning)

docs.title: Deprecation process
docs.text:
Applies to the manual (CLI / API / config) path. From 1.0, never remove a feature without at least one minor version of deprecation notice.

  1. Warn (minor release). Keep the feature working but emit a warning naming the feature, the removal version, and the replacement:

    ⚠️  'boilerplate <old>' is deprecated and will be removed in v2.0.0. Use 'boilerplate <new>' instead.
    See: <release-notes-url>

  2. Document. Show both the current and deprecated approaches in the docs; mark the deprecation in the changelog.

  3. Remove (major release). Remove the feature; the error message MUST reference the release notes entry that announced the removal.

Minimum window: at least one minor version with the warning in place before removal; 2–3 minor versions preferred. A good deprecation message states what is deprecated, when it is removed, what to use instead, and where to learn more.

Template breaking changes accompanied by a Copier migration do not require this period — see Two Breaking-Change Paths.

docs.title: Breaking-change approval
docs.text:
Every breaking change requires: (1) a proposal stating the rationale, (2) discussion/feedback, (3) a migration path (automated for templates, documented for CLI/API), (4) deprecation in a prior minor version where applicable, and (5) the maintainer's approval. Proposal skeleton:

## Breaking Change Proposal
**Version**: vX.0.0   **Component**: CLI / Template / Both
**Change**: <brief description>

### Rationale       — why is this necessary?
### Impact          — who/what breaks; estimated share of users; affected integrations
### Migration Path  — how users migrate (commands or migration-script outline)
### Alternatives    — what was considered and rejected
### Timeline        — deprecation release → removal release

docs.title: Compatibility test suite
docs.text: Every release should keep a backward-compatibility suite that pins the surfaces above, plus a CI check that flags accidental breaks on each pull request. A compatibility suite is planned — see Roadmap § Backlog.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
CHANGELOG.md is generated by release-please from conventional commits (grouped by commit type — Features, Bug Fixes, …); edit the prose on the release PR before merging (see RELEASING.md). Mark incompatible entries BREAKING (a ! commit or BREAKING CHANGE: footer does this automatically). Worked example of a good release entry:

## [2.0.0] - 2026-08-01

### Added
- New `compose` command for template composition

### Changed
- **BREAKING:** renamed a command (old name removed)

### Deprecated
- A flag superseded by a clearer alias

### Removed
- **BREAKING:** a command removed after its deprecation window

### Fixed
- Template-resolution bug

### Security
- Bumped a dependency to address a CVE

A CLI breaking change is communicated through its changelog BREAKING entry and the release PR's release notes — no separate migration guide. A template breaking change publishes one using the Migration Guide Template.

docs.title: CLI stability surface
docs.text:
From 1.0, the stable CLI surface is: published commands and their core options, exit codes for error conditions, the environment profile format, and the machine-parseable output of commands documented as parseable. Internal Python modules (names prefixed _), error-message text, log format, and cache/temp-file layout are not stable and may change in any release.

The authoritative description of the current command surface is the CLI Reference (generated from the shipped CLI), mapped against the target in Implementation Status; the Design Spec — CLI Reference describes the target contract.

docs.title: Intentions
docs.text: Intentions decompose a Product into testable outcomes. Each Intention is defined in its own INT-XXX.yaml file in this directory.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text: The Intent-Driven Development (IDD) plugin (grillergeek-plugins/idd-framework) prescribes a thin Intention schema. See intention-template.md in the plugin's references for the canonical definition.

docs.title: IDD-prescribed core (required)
docs.text:
Field Notes id Unique identifier scoped to Product (e.g., INT-001) product Parent Product ID (e.g., PROD-001) statement What the product should accomplish — outcome-oriented rationale Why this Intention matters to the Product priority critical \| high \| medium \| low owner Accountable individual status draft \| defined \| in-progress \| fulfilled \| deferred

Optional IDD-prescribed:

Field Notes dependencies Other Intention IDs that must be fulfilled first expectations Expectation IDs that belong to this Intention (populated as Expectations are created)

docs.title: Project extensions
docs.text:
INT files in this repository carry the following non-prescribed extensions:

Field Purpose outcome Prose description of the user-visible end state — bridges statement (terse outcome) to acceptance_criteria (measurable). acceptance_criteria Inline pass/fail or measurable criteria that substitute for separate Expectation files. Functionally equivalent to Expectation.validation_criteria from IDD. not_included Explicit scope boundaries — what this Intention does NOT cover. delivery_phases (INT-009 only) Phased rollout where the Intention can be partially delivered.

These extensions are intentional. They're consistent across all 13 INTs in this directory and provide more concrete acceptance signal than IDD's stock schema does on its own. When IDD's expectations workflow is adopted formally, acceptance_criteria will migrate to per-Expectation files.

docs.title: Status convention
docs.text:
Status Meaning draft In flux; statement may change defined Articulated; ready to enter delivery in-progress Implementation underway fulfilled Acceptance criteria met; integrated deferred Acknowledged but intentionally out of scope for the current cycle

Release timing — when an Intention transitions from defined to in-progress to fulfilled — is tracked in GitHub issues, not in these files. The Intention's status field reflects the latest known state of the work, not a release-phase label.

docs.title: How this register is used
docs.text: This directory is a requirements register, not a lifecycle. The design docs in docs/design/ came first and remain the target-state spine; the Product and Intention files were layered on in IDD's schema to state the outcomes and acceptance signal that spine serves. Execution runs through GitHub issues (see docs/agents/issue-tracker.md), each citing the Intention it serves; planning for efforts too large for one session runs as decision-ticket maps on the same tracker (the wayfinder:* labels). IDD's Expectation and Spec layers are not used: an issue's acceptance criteria and the design docs' MUST clauses carry what a Spec would, and adversarial review runs before any multi-file implementation slice. The tripwire that reopens this choice: agent-implemented slices shipping scope drift that issue-level criteria plus review fail to catch. That is the evidence the Spec layer would earn its cost.

docs.title: Source of truth
docs.text: These files are the source of truth for what each Intention covers. The intentions_index block in PROD-001.yaml is a snapshot for at-a-glance scope and may drift; this directory wins.

Boilerplate pairs a Python development environment, one tool for each job, with templates that build on one another to stamp out projects. Built on Copier.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:

docs.title: Composer
docs.text: Layers and merges template configurations - domain operation.

docs.title: compose(resolution, *, include_states=False, include_deltas=False)
docs.text:
Compose resolved templates into an ordered, layered Composition.

Walks resolution.execution_sequence, extracts each template's complete copier config, and merges cumulatively: later layers override question values; coordination keys (_tasks, _secret_questions, _jinja_extensions, _min_copier_version) merge per CopierConfigMerger; layer-local underscore keys are dropped from final but kept in their own layer's values. Sequence entries missing from resolution.templates are skipped. Pure computation — no I/O, no rendering.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default resolution Resolution

Resolved template set with a dependency-ordered execution_sequence.

required include_states bool

Populate CompositionLayer.state_after with the full merged state after each layer.

False include_deltas bool

Populate CompositionLayer.delta with changes versus the previous layer's state (always a dict, {} when unchanged; _tasks never appears — it is excluded from layer values).

False

Returns:

Type Description Composition

Dependency graph, execution sequence, per-layer values (cumulative questions plus that layer's own directives, _tasks excluded), and the final merged schema used for rendering.

docs.title: Resolver
docs.text:
Resolves template dependencies from a catalog.

Methods in this class are pure with respect to inputs and the provided registry; no side effects beyond logging. Resolution walks the meta.extends chain, validates references exist in the registry, and returns a complete mapping of template specifiers to their direct dependency specifiers along with a map of specifier to TemplateInfo.

Contract:

  • Input template_ref may be name or name@version.
  • Registry must implement lookups for both latest and versioned resolution.
  • No cycle detection is performed here (handled by the graph layer).
  • Dependency lists preserve the order specified in meta.extends.

docs.title: MigrationStatus
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

How an operation recorded in .boilerplate/migrations.yml stands.

Each record is appended once, when its operation ends; the state of a run cut off before then is kept in the restore marker, not in the log. Exit codes: SUCCESS, ADOPTED and CREATED are 0, CONFLICT is 4 and FAILED is 1.

docs.title: RestoreMarker
docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel

What a run cut off between its copy back and its record needs to be finished.

The marker is written before the copy back changes a file and removed after the run appends its record, so a marker found when a command starts belongs to a run that was cut off in between. It lives in the git directory, apart from the staging folder that the stale cleanup removes.

Each layer of the walk, in walk order, with the version the walk was moving it to; never empty, and one layer for an add.

The layers whose steps a paused walk finished, in walk order, the paused layer excluded; empty for a complete run.

docs.title: Merging and precedence rules
docs.text:
Authoritative specification

The authoritative design specification for merge strategies and composition is Composition engine. This page provides supplementary implementation-level reference. For the file-level three-way merge, conflict-pause, and safe-orphan semantics designed for the future update command, see ADR-007.

How configuration values are combined across template layers, with clear rules and deterministic outcomes.

docs.title: A two-layer merge
docs.text:
A base template and an app template that extends it, each with its own copier.yml:

# base template — copier.yml
python_version:
    default: "3.12"
license:
    default: "Apache-2.0"
_tasks:
    - "uv sync"

# app template — copier.yml (its boilerplate.yml declares extends: [base])
python_version:
    default: "3.13"
_tasks:
    - "git init"

Composing the app template produces a single questionnaire: python_version defaults to 3.13 (the later layer overrides), license survives from the base, and _tasks accumulates to ["uv sync", "git init"]. The rules below generalize this.

docs.title: What gets merged
docs.text:
boilerplate new asks the merged questionnaire once, over every layer's questions, and a question default can use a filter from any layer's _jinja_extensions. Each layer then renders through its own Copier Worker invocation, applied in composition order, under its scoped view: the questions and importable _jinja_extensions of that layer and its ancestors, answered from that one pass. A layer's files and questions can use only what its own layer or an ancestor declares; a sibling's or a descendant's questions, filters and hooks are not visible to it. A file-path extension an ancestor declares (_extensions/file.py:Class) loads from that ancestor for each descendant that renders, and a layer's .copier-answers.<layer>.yml records its scoped view's answers only.

  • Non-underscore keys (questions): merged across layers to form a single questionnaire.

    • dicts: later layer keys override earlier ones (shallow override).
    • lists: de-duplicated concat in order (first-seen wins).
    • scalars: later value overrides earlier value.

  • Underscore-prefixed keys (directives): not merged, except a small allowlist below. All other underscore keys are treated as layer-local and skipped.

docs.title: File overlay
docs.text: Each layer renders into the same destination through its own Copier Worker invocation, in composition order. Only the first layer's write respects --force; every later layer always overwrites, so a file that two layers both ship at the same path ends up with the last layer's content — there is no three-way diff or per-line merge. A layer that adds files at new paths never touches an earlier layer's files. boilerplate new ignores every template's _skip_if_exists list, so --force overwrites every file; where the lists apply is specified in the Per-Layer Render Loop.

docs.title: Allowlisted directive keys and strategies
docs.text:
• _min_copier_version: highest PEP 440 version (intersection by max).
  • _tasks: accumulate in order (lists concatenate, scalars append).
  • _secret_questions: accumulate in order.
  • _jinja_extensions: union with original order preserved (dedupe).

Everything else starting with _ is layer-local. These are discovered dynamically from copier.Template attributes at runtime and excluded from merging.

docs.title: Determinism and conflict handling
docs.text:
• Key order: keys are processed in first-seen order across layers.
  • Type safety: incompatible types for the same question raise a merge conflict.

docs.title: Debugging merges
docs.text: Run boilerplate compose <template> --sections layers,deltas to see each layer's contribution and what changed between them.

docs.title: Developer platform architecture
docs.text:
This page is the reference model behind Boilerplate: a toolchain of one tool per slot, picked from a tool landscape, built into the development environment and carried by the starter templates; golden paths run on it, and guardrails check the work. Each element has a single responsibility, from cataloging available tools to enforcing standards automatically.

In platform-engineering terms, an internal developer platform (IDP) is the self-service layer an organization runs for its own developers — templates plus CI/CD, provisioning, deployment, and operations, usually behind a portal. Boilerplate is open-source tooling for the scaffolding-and-environment slice of that: the toolchain, development environment, starter templates, and dev-time guardrails, with the golden path pre-built — where most platform tools hand you the machinery and leave the path to you. Deployment and operations are out of scope.

Scope

The reference implementation documented here is Boilerplate's own: Python-focused, with one toolchain. It is one worked example, not a general prescription for other contexts.

            P["Toolchain\nOne pick per slot"]
        end

The landscape describes available options; the toolchain and path prescribe specific choices; the environment and templates automate setup; guardrails automate verification.

docs.title: The tool landscape
docs.text:
The tool landscape is the descriptive catalog of tools, technologies, and practices available in a domain.

It sits outside the platform itself — it's the knowledge base platform decisions draw from — and answers what tools and categories exist?

Boilerplate maintains this as The Development Environment Landscape, a taxonomy covering language runtimes, dependency management, code quality, testing, and CI/CD tooling.

Category names in the toolchain below are drawn from it.

docs.title: The toolchain
docs.text:
The toolchain is the subset of the landscape Boilerplate commits to supporting, sometimes called a curated stack. It answers what do we use?

The Environment guide documents how each pick is configured and used day to day.

docs.title: Boilerplate reference implementation: Toolchain
docs.text:
Category Standard Rationale Python interpreter Python 3.12+ Modern syntax (match statement, current type-hint features), active security support Environment & package/dependency management uv Fast dependency resolution and installs, pip-compatible, integrated venv management Linters & code formatters ruff Combines linting and formatting in one tool, replaces flake8/black/isort, minimal config Type checkers pyright (strict mode) Native VS Code integration via Pylance; strict mode catches more than default mode Testing frameworks pytest + pytest-cov Fixture-based testing with a large plugin ecosystem; coverage via pytest --cov Build tools uv build (uv_build backend; hatchling as the override) Standards-compliant (PEP 517/660/639); uv_build is uv's own backend for pure-Python code, hatchling covers build hooks and a version from git tags Version control Git Branching and merging underpin template composition and CI workflows CI/CD GitHub Actions (recommended) Boilerplate's own gate runs on it Documentation generators MkDocs Material Markdown-native authoring, built-in navigation and search IDEs & editors VS Code Extension ecosystem (Pylance, Ruff, pytest), remote development support

Planned

Generated projects don't scaffold CI config or a deploy-time and runtime guardrail layer: wire the three quality-check commands into your own CI provider's workflow. See the backlog.

Templates scaffold the interpreter, dependency-management, lint/format, type-checking, testing, and build rows. The CI/CD and documentation rows are recommended picks you wire yourself.

For detailed configuration and usage, see:

  • Environment overview
  • uv guide
  • Ruff guide
  • Pyright guide
  • pytest guide

docs.title: The golden path
docs.text:
A golden path is a workflow whose decisions are already thought out for you (glossary). Golden paths nest: each starter template is a golden path to a starting point, and the dev loop is the golden path for the work that follows. The path below strings them together for a general Python project: a template's path to a starting point, the dev loop, then pull requests, CI and release. Deploy and operate appear for context; they are outside Boilerplate's scope. The term is Spotify's; Netflix calls the same idea the paved road. It answers how do we work?

The path is not mandatory — developers may diverge when circumstances warrant — but it's the most-supported, lowest-friction route, and platform investment (documentation, templates, CI automation) centers on it.

docs.title: From new project to production
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Golden path from new project to production
    accDescr: Four groups in order. Start: create the project, then set up its environment. Dev loop: red, write a failing test; green, make it pass; refactor; then run the checks and commit, and the next change starts the loop again. Pull request, CI and release: many commits are pushed as a pull request, CI builds and checks it, it merges, and many merges make a release. Outside Boilerplate's scope: deploy, then operate. The next change, or a CI failure, starts another turn of the dev loop.
    subgraph start["Start"]
        direction TB
        A[Create the project] --> B[Set up the environment]
    end
    subgraph loop["Dev loop"]
        direction TB
        C["Red: write a failing test"]
        D["Green: make it pass"]
        E[Refactor]
        F[Run the checks and commit]
        C --> D --> E --> F
        F -->|next change or CI failure| C
    end
    subgraph ship["Pull request, CI and release"]
        direction TB
        G[Push a pull request] --> H[CI builds and checks]
        H --> I[Merge]
        I -->|many merges| J[Release]
    end
    subgraph ops["Outside Boilerplate's scope"]
        direction TB
        K[Deploy] --> L[Operate and monitor]
    end
    start --> loop
    loop -->|many commits| ship
    ship --> ops
