docs.title: Template authoring
docs.text: Create custom templates for Boilerplate. Templates are directories with two config files: boilerplate.yml (metadata for Boilerplate) and copier.yml (questions and rendering for Copier).

docs.title: Template structure
docs.text:
my-template/
├── boilerplate.yml        # Boilerplate metadata (name, version, extends)
├── copier.yml             # Copier questions, defaults, and tasks
├── README.md.jinja        # Jinja2 template files use .jinja suffix
├── pyproject.toml.jinja
├── _scripts/
│   └── post_generation.py # Referenced by _tasks below
└── src/
    └── {{package_name}}/
        └── __init__.py.jinja

docs.title: Boilerplate metadata — boilerplate.yml
docs.text:
This file tells Boilerplate how to discover, version, and compose your template.

# boilerplate.yml
schema_version: "1"       # Metadata schema version

name: my-template          # Used in `boilerplate new my-template`
version: 1.0.0             # PEP 440 — bump when template content changes
description: Short description of what this template scaffolds.

# extends: []              # Optional — list parent templates to inherit from.
#                          # Example: extends: [project]
Field Required Description schema_version No Schema version of boilerplate.yml. Defaults to "1.0"; "1" is the same version. name Yes Template identifier, used in CLI commands. version Yes PEP 440 version string (boilerplate validate enforces this). description No One-line description shown in boilerplate list. Defaults to "". extends No Parent templates this template layers on top of.

docs.title: Copier configuration — copier.yml
docs.text:
This file defines user-facing questions and rendering settings. It follows Copier's configuration format.

# copier.yml
_templates_suffix: .jinja

project_name:
  type: str
  help: "The (human-readable) name of the project (e.g. My Project)"
  default: "{{ _folder_name }}"

package_name:
  default: "{{ project_name | replace('-', '_') }}"
  when: false   # Computed, not prompted

description:
  type: str
  help: "A brief description of the project"
  default: "A new Python project."

_tasks:
  - command: ["{{ _copier_python }}", _scripts/post_generation.py]
    when: "{{ _copier_operation == 'copy' }}"

The when guard limits the task to creation: the script removes itself after it runs, and Copier does not restore a file the project deleted, so the task must not run again on update.

docs.title: Key Copier directives
docs.text: Directive Purpose _templates_suffix File extension for Jinja2 templates (.jinja) _exclude Glob patterns to exclude from output _jinja_extensions Custom Jinja2 extensions to load _tasks Post-generation commands, run from the generated project root; scripts they call must ship in the template when: false Hide a question (computed value)

docs.title: Template composition
docs.text:
Templates can inherit from other templates using extends in boilerplate.yml. See the Composition guide for merge rules, layer order, and diagnostics commands.

When authoring a child template, its copier.yml only needs to declare what it overrides or adds — not the full parent config:

# streamlit/copier.yml
dependencies:
  default: ["streamlit", "pydantic>=2"]

Declare _answers_file: .copier-answers.<layer>.yml in copier.yml and ship an answers-file stub — a template file literally named {{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}.jinja rendering _copier_answers (see project's stub for the reference pattern). Copier writes an answers file only by rendering that stub; the directive alone is inert, and boilerplate validate warns when a composition-intended template (one declaring _answers_file or extends) ships without it. See the Composition guide § Layer order for what each layer's answers file records.

docs.title: Template files
docs.text:
Use Jinja2 syntax with the .jinja suffix:

# src/{{package_name}}/__init__.py.jinja
"""{{ project_name }} — {{ description }}."""

__version__ = "0.1.0"

Directory names can also use Jinja2 variables: {{package_name}}/ expands to the value of the package_name question.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Two config files: boilerplate.yml for Boilerplate, copier.yml for Copier. Keep them separate — don't mix concerns.
  • Restate Copier's defaults in _exclude. A declared _exclude replaces Copier's built-in list (.git, copier.yml, __pycache__, …) instead of extending it. Copy the bundled templates' block, which also excludes boilerplate.yml; otherwise a copier update from a git clone copies the clone's .git over the project's.
  • Sensible defaults for all questions so --non-interactive works.
  • Use extends to layer on base templates rather than duplicating files.
  • Version your templates with PEP 440 versions (plain X.Y.Z works). The version moves once per release, not once per change — see when to bump.
  • Point the CLI at your template: custom templates live outside the bundled templates directory, so point the CLI at the directory containing my-template/ with --templates-dir (works on new, list, graph, and compose; it adds to the search path, so bundled parents stay resolvable for extends) or set it persistently via BOILERPLATE_EXTRA_TEMPLATE_DIRS.
  • Test rendering with boilerplate new my-template test-output --force --templates-dir <parent-dir>.
  • Inspect composition with boilerplate compose and boilerplate graph before publishing multi-layer templates.

docs.title: Keeping a project's work
docs.text: A project generated from your template is a git repository, and copier update reads it as one: it refuses a dirty tree, diffs against the index, and merges through it. Anything outside that index is invisible to the merge. Three habits follow; the rules themselves are in Template versioning.

docs.title: Rename through a staged move
docs.text:
Copier deletes every path your new version stops rendering, by name, without comparing content — so a project that edited the old file loses the edit, at exit 0, with nothing in the working tree to show it. A before-stage migration that moves and stages the file turns that deletion into a conflict carrying both versions:

# copier.yml
_migrations:
  - when: "{{ _stage == 'before' }}"
    command:
      - "{{ _copier_python }}"
      - -c
      - |
        import pathlib
        import subprocess

        old = pathlib.Path("tests/smoke_test.py")
        new = old.with_name("test_smoke.py")
        if old.exists() and not new.exists():
            subprocess.run(["git", "mv", str(old), str(new)], check=True)

The entry declares no version, so Copier runs it on every update; the state check makes it a no-op once the old name is gone. Ship it in the same change as the rename, with a test that drives a real copier update from the previous tag — tests/boilerplate/templates/test_streamlit_update_migration.py in this repository is the worked example.

docs.title: Render nothing your .gitignore matches
docs.text: An ignored file never enters the index, so the merge cannot see it: no conflict marker, no .rej file, nothing in history to recover. The reverse holds too — do not ignore a file your README tells the user to commit.

docs.title: Say who owns each file
docs.text: A file your template keeps changing is template-owned: a project that edits it risks a conflict whenever a release touches the same lines, and on a file small enough that one diff hunk spans it, any release at all. A file the project should own after the first render belongs in _skip_if_exists; what the list does, and where it applies, is specified in the Per-Layer Render Loop. Choose per file and say which; silence means template-owned. A file meant to be deleted (a sample module) stays template-owned; project-owned is for the files users are expected to keep and rewrite instead, like the README or the entry point. Both bundled templates' copier.yml declare that split.

docs.title: Bundled examples
docs.text:
The bundled templates serve as working examples:

  • project — the general-purpose Python template (project template source)
  • streamlit — a template for Streamlit apps, built on project (streamlit template source)

Run boilerplate list to see all available templates.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: See the Composition guide for merge semantics, or the Templates Hub to browse bundled templates.

docs.title: Template composition
docs.text: Composition lets one template build on another through an extends list in its boilerplate.yml. It reduces duplication and keeps shared conventions centralized.

docs.title: Extending a template
docs.text:
boilerplate.yml excerpt from the Streamlit template:

name: streamlit
version: 0.2.0
description: A Streamlit app, built on the general-purpose template.
extends:
  - project

Rules:

  1. A parent must be discoverable by name via boilerplate list.
  2. Multiple parents are supported. Siblings are processed in extends declaration order, deterministically; later-declared siblings render later and take precedence on conflicts.

Before you extend

  • Lists merge by union only — inherited entries can't be removed or reordered, so design list-type questions to be purely additive.
  • Dict questions overlay shallowly — a child overriding one key inside a nested structure replaces the whole structure at that level, not just that key — keep nested config shallow or split it into flat keys.
  • File conflicts aren't diagnosed — if a child writes a path the parent also writes, the child's version wins silently, with no warning — diff the output after generation.

Planned

Version-pinned extends constraints (parent@>=1.2) and file-conflict reporting (compose --conflicts) are tracked on the roadmap backlog.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Term Meaning Base template A template that does not declare parents, e.g., project. Derived template A template that declares one or more parents via extends, e.g., streamlit. Layer One template's contribution at a node of the dependency graph: name@version plus its path; see the glossary entry. Layer order The order the layers apply (dependencies first, target last). Dependency graph Nodes, edges, and the layer order describing template dependencies. Merged configuration The merged configuration after all layers; a questions-only view is also available. Delta Per-layer change set: subset of keys this layer adds or overrides relative to previous state.

Concept → class: a layer is CompositionLayer and its changes are CompositionLayer.delta; the sequence and graph are Composition.sequence and CompositionGraph; the merged configuration is Composition.final, with Composition.merged_questions_schema as the questions-only view; templates are TemplateInfo with parents in TemplateMeta.extends. Field-level detail: Data models § Composition Domain Models.

docs.title: Layer order
docs.text:
Layering supports multiple parents (a dependency graph) and always executes linearized, dependencies first and the target template last; sibling ordering and conflict precedence follow the rules under Extending a template above.

Run:

uv run boilerplate graph streamlit

Output (abridged):

#   Layer       Version   Path
1   project     0.3.0     .../templates/project
2   streamlit   0.2.0     .../templates/streamlit

Layers apply in this order: each layer's question schema and internal directives (_jinja_extensions, _tasks) merge into the accumulated result. See CLI examples § Inspect a template graph for the full --format json payload.

A layer's copier.yml declares its own questions and the parent questions it overrides; its ancestors' questions supply every other answer its files and paths use. streamlit declares container_registry and overrides dependencies and sample_module, and its files render project_name, project_slug, package_name, description, author_name, author_email and package_index_url from project's declarations without restating them. Each layer's own .copier-answers.<layer>.yml records the answers to that layer's own questions and its ancestors', and nothing of a sibling or a descendant: project's file lacks container_registry, streamlit's has both. boilerplate new asks the merged questionnaire once, so you answer each question a single time. See the Authoring guide for the _answers_file how-to. Because each file is Copier's own, you can also compose and update with plain Copier.

docs.title: Merge & delta semantics
docs.text:
Show the full composition:

uv run boilerplate compose streamlit --all --format yaml

Merge strategies are a fixed set — per question type under What gets merged, per directive key under Allowlisted directive keys — with no way to declare a per-field strategy. Incompatible types for the same question raise BP_RESOLVE_MERGE_CONFLICT; see Determinism and conflict handling.

docs.title: Diagnostics toolkit
docs.text: Command Purpose Typical Use boilerplate list Discover available templates Verify parent existence boilerplate graph streamlit View ordered layers Confirm inheritance chain boilerplate compose streamlit --stats High-level metrics (layers, keys) Sanity check complexity boilerplate compose streamlit --sections deltas Show per-layer differences Author focus when extending boilerplate compose <tpl> --all --format yaml Full introspection Deep troubleshooting

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Goal: Add a Streamlit UI to any standard project without duplicating base scaffolding.

What the streamlit layer contributes:

Category Added Value Runtime Dependencies streamlit, pydantic>=2 App Entry Point app.py, reading the project's own uv.lock and rendering it as a stack inventory Domain Structure models/, services/, and adapters/ packages encouraging separation Containerization Dockerfile, container scripts (build/push) Developer Experience VS Code launch.json for F5 debugging Tests A unit test module per layer (test_locked_package.py, test_stack_filter.py, test_lockfile.py, test_inventory.py) plus an integration test (tests/integration/{{ package_name }}/test_app.py.jinja)

Because the schema changes are contained (dependencies and sample_module overrides plus the new container_registry prompt), all other prompts remain aligned with the base template—no redundant customization logic.

Observed example specifics for the Streamlit chain:

Aspect Observed Explanation dependencies list Default replaced with two entries Base declares dependencies with an empty default; the child question dict shallow-overrides it, so default becomes the child's list while type and help are inherited Absent questions Inherited unchanged Values simply flow through cumulative state _tasks Single task from base only Child adds none; accumulation == base list _jinja_extensions Three entries (all from base) Child declares two, both duplicates of base entries, so union == base list

Delta for streamlit layer (excerpt):

dependencies:
  default:
    - streamlit
    - pydantic>=2

Interpretation: the streamlit layer overrides the dependencies and sample_module defaults and adds one new question, container_registry (type str, default ghcr.io). (_tasks never appears in deltas or per-layer values; inspect the accumulated task list in the merged configuration, e.g. --sections final.)

File system overlay (illustrative):

Origin Files (examples) project pyproject.toml.jinja, README.md.jinja, src/{{ package_name }}/__init__.py.jinja, base test scaffold streamlit README.md.jinja (overrides project's), src/{{ package_name }}/app.py.jinja, src/{{ package_name }}/adapters/lockfile.py.jinja, src/{{ package_name }}/models/locked_package.py.jinja, src/{{ package_name }}/services/inventory.py.jinja, Dockerfile.jinja, .vscode/launch.json.jinja, integration test

File overlay follows last-layer-wins semantics; the streamlit layer overrides two project paths, README.md.jinja and .gitattributes, so those render from the streamlit layer; every other streamlit path is new.

docs.title: Author checklist
docs.text:
Recommended workflow:

  1. Start from base: design only the deltas you truly need.
  2. After edits, run compose --sections deltas to ensure minimal surface area.
  3. If you added conflicting files, explicitly note the rationale in your template README.

Before publishing:

☐ Parent template listed by `boilerplate list`
☐ Only required deltas introduced (verify with --sections deltas)
☐ New files do not duplicate or fork base files without reason
☐ Dependencies kept minimal and scoped to added functionality
☐ Launch/debug assets only when necessary

Return to the Templates Hub · See the Authoring guide · Next: Compose and update with plain Copier

docs.title: Migration guide template
docs.text:
Use this template when documenting breaking changes in Boilerplate templates. Boilerplate leverages Copier's automated template update mechanism to handle migrations. Migration guides focus on what the automation does, edge cases requiring manual intervention, and validation procedures.

Important

This template is for template migrations (projects updating to new template versions via copier update). CLI breaking changes have no migration guide — they're communicated through the changelog's BREAKING entry and the release notes; see Versioning & Compatibility Policy § Two Breaking-Change Paths.

Reference: Versioning and migration

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
# Migration guide: <feature or tool> v<OLD_VERSION> → v<NEW_VERSION>

## What's changing

[1–2 sentence summary of the breaking change and why it was necessary.]

### Example

Before (v<OLD_VERSION>):
```python
# Old way
from boilerplate import render_template
result = render_template("my-template", answers={...})
```

After (v<NEW_VERSION>):
```python
# New way
from boilerplate import Composer
result = Composer("my-template", answers={...}).render()
```

## Automated migration

Copier handles this migration automatically when you update your project:

```powershell
# Update to latest template version
copier update
```

### What the automation does

The update process will:

1. **Update configuration**: Automatically transform `<old_config>` to `<new_config>` format.
2. **Rename files**: Move `old_structure/` to `new_structure/` preserving your customizations.
3. **Update imports**: Replace deprecated import paths with new ones in `.py` files.
4. **Merge conflicts**: Leave conflict markers in files where your customizations and the template change overlap.

**No manual intervention needed** for these transformations.

### Files affected

| File pattern | Change | Automatic | Manual review needed |
|--------------|--------|-----------|----------------------|
| `pyproject.toml` | Version pins updated | ✓ | No |
| `src/**/*.py` | Import paths updated | ✓ | Verify custom imports |
| `.vscode/settings.json` | New settings added | ✓ | Merge with custom settings |
| `README.md` | Template sections refreshed | ✓ | Preserve custom content |

## Manual intervention (if needed)

### Scenario 1: Custom <component> modifications

**If** you have heavily customized `<component>`, the automated merge may require review:

```powershell
# After running update, check for merge markers
git diff
```

Look for conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`). Resolve by choosing the appropriate sections or merging both.

### Scenario 2: External dependencies on old API

**If** you have external scripts or tools calling the old API:

```python
# Update external scripts from:
old_function(param1, param2)

# To:
new_function(param1=param1, param2=param2)
```

These changes are **outside** the template-managed files and require manual updates.

## Testing and validation

Verify the automated migration succeeded:

```powershell
# Run quality gates
uv run ruff check --no-fix
uv run pyright
uv run pytest
```

**Expected results**:
- ✓ No linting errors
- ✓ No type checking errors  
- ✓ All tests pass
- ✓ Application starts successfully: `uv run python -m <your_app>`

## Rollback procedure

If critical issues arise:

```powershell
# Option 1: Revert the update commit
git revert HEAD
uv sync --locked

# Option 2: Restore from backup (if you created one)
git checkout <branch-before-update>
```

Then open an issue with:
- The error encountered
- Your project structure (especially customizations)
- Output from `boilerplate --version` or `copier --version`

## Troubleshooting

### Merge conflicts during automated update

**Symptom**: Copier leaves conflict markers and exits 0.

**Cause**: Your customizations conflict with template changes.

**Solution**:
```bash
# Review conflicts
git status
# Edit files with markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>)
# Choose appropriate sections
git add <resolved-files>
git commit -m "chore: resolve migration conflicts"
```

### Type errors after migration

**Symptom**: `pyright` reports type mismatches in updated code.

**Cause**: API signature changes not fully applied to custom code.

**Solution**:
```powershell
# Identify failing imports/calls
uv run python -m pyright --verbose
# Update your custom code to match new signatures (see examples above)
```

### Tests fail after update

**Symptom**: Previously passing tests now fail.

**Cause**: Breaking changes in behavior, not just API.

**Solution**:
```powershell
# Review test failures for deprecated patterns
uv run python -m pytest -v
# Update test assertions and mocks to match new behavior
```

## Getting help

- Review the [<Feature> documentation](<link>).
- Search existing GitHub issues: [Link to GitHub search]
- Open a new issue with your error and environment details: [Link to new issue template]

## Summary of changes

| Component | What changed | Why |
|-----------|--------------|-----|
| Config | Property renamed | Improved clarity |
| API | Function signature | Enhanced flexibility |
| CLI | Command structure | Consistency with other tools |

## Timeline

| Version | Status | Support until |
|---------|--------|----------------|
| v1.x | Deprecated | [ISO-8601 date] |
| v2.0 | Current | Ongoing |

---

_Migration guide created: [ISO-8601 date]_

_For latest updates, see the [release notes](link)._

docs.title: Checklist: before publishing a migration guide
docs.text:
• Provide clear rationale for the breaking change.
  • Include at least one before/after code example.
  • Document what the automated migration does (file transformations, renames, updates).
  • List all affected file patterns with automatic vs. manual review indicators.
  • Identify scenarios requiring manual intervention (customizations, external dependencies).
  • Provide validation steps (quality gates, application startup).
  • Explain rollback procedure (git revert, restore from backup).
  • Provide troubleshooting for common automated migration issues (merge conflicts, type errors).
  • Link to detailed documentation for behavior changes.
  • Specify deprecation timeline (when old version ends support).
  • Test the automated migration on a sample project before publishing.
  • Have a Boilerplate maintainer review before merging.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: Return to Versioning and migration for the policy this template documents, and hand the finished guide off through Versioning & compatibility.

docs.title: Compose and update with plain Copier
docs.text: A Boilerplate project is plain Copier output: one .copier-answers.<layer>.yml per layer, each written by Copier. You can compose a project and update its layers with copier alone. This page shows the commands, what they leave out, and which layers can update.

docs.title: Run Copier where Boilerplate is importable
docs.text:
The project template loads extensions from the boilerplate package and from copier-template-extensions, and Copier runs template code only with --trust. Run copier from a checkout of the repository, which has both:

BP=/path/to/boilerplate    # your checkout
uv run --project "$BP" copier --version

The compose commands below use uv run --project "$BP" copier and run from the folder that holds your project, so --project leaves the working directory alone; the update command runs from the project root.

docs.title: Compose streamlit over project
docs.text:
Two copier copy runs build what boilerplate new streamlit builds. Run project first, with the two defaults streamlit overrides:

uv run --project "$BP" copier copy --trust --defaults \
  --data project_name="Probe App" \
  --data description="A probe." \
  --data author_name="Ada Probe" \
  --data author_email=ada@example.com \
  --data 'dependencies=["streamlit","pydantic>=2"]' \
  --data sample_module=false \
  "$BP/src/boilerplate/templates/project" probe-app

Then remove the project's README.md and run streamlit over it, reading project's answers and supplying the two values it never records:

rm probe-app/README.md
uv run --project "$BP" copier copy --trust --defaults --overwrite \
  --data-file probe-app/.copier-answers.project.yml \
  --data project_slug=probe-app \
  --data package_name=probe_app \
  "$BP/src/boilerplate/templates/streamlit" probe-app
Step Why dependencies, sample_module on the first run streamlit overrides both defaults, and project renders pyproject.toml and the sample module from them. rm probe-app/README.md streamlit lists README.md in _skip_if_exists. Copier honors that list over --overwrite; boilerplate new ignores it. project_slug, package_name project computes both from project_name (probe-app, probe_app) and never records them. Without package_name, Copier silently skips every file in a <package_name> folder under src/ and tests/.

project's post-generation tasks run in the first command, before streamlit's files exist. Add --skip-tasks there to run them yourself afterwards.

docs.title: What differs from boilerplate new
docs.text:
The rendered files are identical. Two things differ:

File By hand boilerplate new boilerplate.lock Not written. Written. .copier-answers.streamlit.yml Records only streamlit's own questions: container_registry, dependencies, sample_module. Also records project's questions.

docs.title: Update a git-backed layer
docs.text:
A layer updates with copier update when its answers file records a _commit, which means its template came from a git repository. From the project root, with the working tree committed (Copier refuses a dirty tree):

uv run --project "$BP" copier update --trust --defaults \
  --answers-file .copier-answers.streamlit.yml \
  --data-file .copier-answers.project.yml \
  --data project_slug=probe-app \
  --data package_name=probe_app \
  --vcs-ref <tag>

Copier accepts --data-file once: a second flag stops with Switch --data-file already given. Pass the answers file of the layer's direct parent (project's file, since streamlit extends project). A base layer such as project needs none.

  • A parent's file that boilerplate new wrote also records the parent's own ancestors' answers.
  • A file from a by-hand copier copy, or one an earlier by-hand update trimmed, holds only that parent's own questions. Supply the rest with --data key=value, which wins over the same key in the file.

Pass the two derived names too, as in the compose step: no answers file records them. Without package_name, Copier exits 0 and silently skips every file in a <package_name> folder under src/ and tests/. Use the names your project has.

Omit --vcs-ref to take the latest tag. Update one layer at a time, lower layers first: the layers list in boilerplate.lock is the order, and without a lock you read the templates' extends chains. _src_path in each answers file must be an absolute path or URL.

Two limits come with updating one layer by hand:

  • The answers file shrinks. After the update, the layer's file holds only the questions its own copier.yml declares, so answers inherited from a parent drop out of it. The --data-file supplies them from then on, so pass it on every update: without it, the next update renders the inherited answers empty.
  • A changed line that renders an unrecorded value conflicts. Copier renders the old copy from the answers file alone, so a value the file lacks, such as the computed package_name, renders empty there and your rendered value reads as your edit. A release that changes that line produces an inline conflict (<<<<<<<) in that file and nowhere else. --data and --data-file do not help, because neither reaches the old copy. Resolve the conflict in the file and commit.

docs.title: Bundled layers are copy-only
docs.text:
boilerplate new renders project and streamlit from the template folders inside the installed package. Those folders are not git repository roots, so Copier records no _commit in .copier-answers.project.yml or .copier-answers.streamlit.yml, and copier update stops with "cannot obtain old template references". This holds for the by-hand compose above too, which uses the same folders. A layer you render from a git repository updates; to refresh a bundled layer, run its copier copy command again.

Back to Template composition · Next: Versioning and migration

docs.title: Project template
docs.text: The project template creates a general-purpose Python project, with its tools configured.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Modern toolchain: uv, Ruff, Pyright, Pytest
  • VS Code integration: Pinned settings and recommended extensions
  • Type safety: Full type hint coverage
  • Testing: Pytest with an example module and matching test
  • Notebooks: A starter Jupyter notebook

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
For a project named my-app (package my_app):

my-app/
├── pyproject.toml          # Metadata + tool config (ruff, pyright, pytest)
├── README.md               # Project documentation
├── .gitignore
├── .gitattributes          # LF line endings on every platform
├── .vscode/                # VS Code settings
│   ├── settings.json
│   └── extensions.json
├── notebooks/
│   └── notebook.ipynb      # Starter notebook
├── src/
│   └── my_app/             # Source code
│       ├── __init__.py     # Package version
│       └── module.py       # Example `add(a, b)` function (sample_module, default on)
├── tests/
│   └── my_app/
│       ├── test_module.py  # Tests for the example module (sample_module, default on)
│       └── test_import.py  # Checks the package imports (sample_module off)
├── uv.lock                 # Pinned deps (written by the post-generation tasks)
├── .copier-answers.project.yml  # This layer's answers, for future updates
└── boilerplate.lock        # Each layer's version, source and checksum

README.md and src/<package>/__init__.py are project-owned: the template lists them in _skip_if_exists, which governs what an update does to them.

Post-generation tasks create the virtual environment and uv.lock and initialize a git repository (skipped with --no-tasks). With --no-tasks, the cleanup step also never runs, so _scripts/post_generation.py is left behind in the generated project — it isn't gitignored.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Create new project (template name, then destination)
boilerplate new project ./my-app
cd my-app

# Run tests
uv run pytest

The post-generation tasks already ran uv sync, so the environment is ready. If you passed --no-tasks, run uv sync before the first uv run.

Add dependencies with uv add <pkg> (see Add a dependency); pyproject.toml holds project metadata, entry points and scripts, and the tool configuration described under Configuration.

docs.title: The sample module
docs.text: module.py and its test are a starting point, not scaffolding you must keep. Answer sample_module with no to render without them: boilerplate new project ./my-app --data sample_module=false. tests/<package>/test_import.py renders in their place, so uv run pytest still has a test to run. A template that extends project can set the default to off in its own copier.yml.

docs.title: Choose a build backend
docs.text:
The build backend turns the project into a wheel and an sdist. The build_backend question sets the [build-system] table in pyproject.toml: uv_build by default, hatchling when you answer it that way: boilerplate new project ./my-app --data build_backend=hatchling.

Pick Choose it when Renders uv_build (default) The code is pure Python with a static version and one src/<package>, and uv is your toolchain requires = ["uv_build>=0.13,<0.14"] and nothing else hatchling You need build hooks, plugins, a version from git tags (hatch-vcs), or a custom file layout requires = ["hatchling>=1.27"] and a [tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel] table

The uv_build range names the current uv minor, and the Streamlit template's Dockerfile installs the same minor, so uv runs its bundled backend and fetches nothing from a package index. A newer uv still builds, with a warning on each uv sync until you raise the cap. An older uv fetches uv-build from your default index, so a private package_index_url must mirror it.

uv_build builds from static metadata and ships a git-ignored file that sits inside the package directory. If you need a dynamic version or generated files in the package tree, pick hatchling.

Compiled code (Rust through maturin, C or C++ through scikit-build-core) is a hand edit: replace the [build-system] table, then follow uv's extension module guide. The template scaffolds no Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt. ADR-017 compares nine backends and holds the reasoning behind these two.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: Need a Streamlit UI on top of this? See the Streamlit template. Building your own template? Start with Template authoring. Return to the Templates Hub.

docs.title: Versioning and migration
docs.text: Template versions evolve independently from the CLI. Breaking changes are managed through semantically versioned major bumps paired with automated migration support via Copier's three-way merge system.

docs.title: Version format
docs.text:
Templates use semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), independent from the CLI version:

# boilerplate.yml
version: "0.1.0"  # Template version (independent from CLI)
name: project
extends:
  - base@1.0.0  # exact pin

extends accepts an exact version pin (name@1.0.0) or an unversioned reference (name); range specifiers such as ^1.0 are not accepted; Design — Template system § extends syntax reserves them.

Key: Each template versions itself, not tied to Boilerplate CLI versions.

docs.title: When to bump
docs.text: A template version moves once per release, measured from the last released version of that template. Take the smallest step the whole unreleased change set requires (pre-1.0: MINOR for a breaking change, PATCH otherwise) and land it once. A later unreleased change raises that step if it needs a bigger one; it MUST NOT add another bump. Bumping per change or per pull request produces version numbers no consumer ever saw.

docs.title: Templates vs. projects
docs.text:
Templates (versioned in boilerplate.yml): source code with boilerplate.yml, copier.yml, and template files.

A project generated from a template is not itself versioned; it tracks each composed layer's source, version, and commit in one .copier-answers.<layer>.yml per layer. boilerplate new also writes boilerplate.lock, which records each layer's name, version, source, commit (null for a layer rendered from a plain folder, such as the bundled templates) and template checksum, plus a hash of each answers file. No command reads it yet. The schema is in Design — Data models § BoilerplateLock.

docs.title: Migration-first philosophy
docs.text: Breaking changes in templates are acceptable IF automated migration is provided.

docs.title: Why automated migration?
docs.text:
• Preservation: Projects preserve user customizations during updates
  • Safety: Three-way merge (old template + user changes + new template) minimizes conflicts
  • Visibility: Users see what changed and can make informed decisions
  • Scalability: Enables evolution of templates without cascading manual work

For a worked rename migration, see Template authoring § Rename through a staged move. A layer rendered from a git repository updates with Copier's own copier update; the layers bundled in the package are copy-only. A project built from more than one layer has no shipped update command yet: each layer must render from the composition's merged schema, which only boilerplate update will provide (ADR-007 records that design). Run copier update on a child layer alone, such as streamlit, and it exits 0 while skipping every path under the package directory and dropping the inherited answers from that layer's answers file.

docs.title: Breaking changes (require automated migration)
docs.text:
• Removing template variables (Copier questions)
  • Renaming template variables
  • Changing variable type or validation rules
  • Moving or renaming generated files
  • Restructuring project directory layout
  • Changing template metadata format
  • Changing composition constraints (extends version requirements)

docs.title: Non-breaking changes (minor or patch)
docs.text:
• Adding new template variables (optional, with defaults)
  • Adding new files
  • Improving templates (content updates)
  • Bug fixes to generated files
  • Adding new composition methods
  • Deprecating template variables (with backward compat handler)

docs.title: Pre-1.0 template versioning (0.x)
docs.text:
Templates in early development use 0.x.y versioning. Semantic versioning rules differ for pre-release versions:

Bump Example Semantics Migration PATCH 0.1.0 → 0.1.1 Compatible bug fixes None needed MINOR 0.1.0 → 0.2.0 Breaking changes Copier migration required MAJOR 0.x.0 → 1.0.0 Release-ready; begins stable SemVer Copier migration required

Key: In pre-1.0 versioning, minor bumps signal breaking changes (like major bumps in 1.x+). This reflects that 0.x APIs are unstable and may change frequently.

Example:

# project template (early development)
version: "0.1.0"  # Initial release
---
version: "0.2.0"  # Minor bump = breaking change (migrate Copier)
---
version: "1.0.0"  # Major bump = stable release (migrate Copier)
---
version: "1.1.0"  # Minor bump = new features (no migration needed)

For template authors: If your template is pre-1.0, treat minor version bumps like major version bumps—provide Copier migration scripts for any breaking changes.

docs.title: PATCH version (bug fixes)
docs.text:
# boilerplate.yml (v1.0.1)
version: "1.0.1"  # Patch bump

When to bump PATCH:

  • Fix typo or incorrect content in generated files
  • Fix bug in template logic
  • Update dependencies without breaking changes

No migration needed.

docs.title: MINOR version (new features)
docs.text:
# boilerplate.yml (v1.1.0)
version: "1.1.0"  # Minor bump
extends:
  - base@1.0.0  # exact pin, unchanged

When to bump MINOR:

  • Add new optional template variables
  • Add new template variants
  • Extend composition options

No migration needed (backward compatible).

docs.title: MAJOR version (breaking changes)
docs.text:
# boilerplate.yml (v2.0.0)
version: "2.0.0"  # Major bump
extends:
  - base@2.0.0  # exact pin, major bump

When to bump MAJOR:

  • Remove template variables
  • Rename template variables
  • Restructure project layout
  • Change variable types

Migration is required via Copier's update mechanism.

docs.title: Migration requirements for breaking changes
docs.text: boilerplate update is design-only (ADR-007): no shipped command of this tool runs migrations. Vanilla copier update runs them now for a layer rendered from a git repository, and never for a bundled layer (copy-only); a child layer of a composed project needs the merged schema that command does not have, so its migrations wait for boilerplate update. The bundled layers ship theirs under the rules below; the rules bind template authors either way.

docs.title: Copier migration scripts
docs.text:
Every breaking change ships as one or more entries under _migrations in copier.yml:

template/
├── boilerplate.yml
├── copier.yml       # _migrations lives here
└── template/
    └── ...project files

# copier.yml
_migrations:
  - version: "2.0.0"
    when: "{{ _stage == 'before' }}"
    command:
      - "{{ _copier_python }}"
      - -c
      - |
        # move/rename/rewrite logic, guarded by a state check

Each entry runs a command (a string run through the shell, or a list run directly), optionally gated by version (a PEP 440 version: the entry fires only when the update crosses it, from < version <= to) and when (which stage to run in; defaults to the after stage), with working_directory scoping where the command runs. Typical operations: rename or move a generated file, rewrite import paths or config keys after a rename, create a directory the updated layout needs. See Copier's migrations documentation for the full mechanism, and Template authoring § Rename through a staged move for a complete worked entry.

docs.title: Authoring rules
docs.text:
A migration is fix-up code, not replayed history: an update may cross several versions at once, and every crossed migration runs against one of two trees — the pre-update tree for before-stage entries, the target tree for after-stage ones (the default) — never an intermediate one. Four rules follow, specified in ADR-007:

  1. Jump-safe. Inspect state before acting and stay idempotent — "if the old path exists, move it," never "the tree is at the previous version, so move it."
  2. Carried forward. Keep every historical _migrations entry in every later release, in ascending version order — Copier reads the list only from the version being updated to, and executes it in declaration order rather than sorting by version.
  3. Layer-scoped. Touch only files your own template owns. Copier has no ownership model; a migration that rewrites a file another layer overrode destroys that override silently.
  4. Conflict-aware. Migrations run even when the merge left unresolved conflict markers, so a migration that parses a file must tolerate them — and a non-zero exit fails the whole update.

Three further rules govern what an update costs the project. Copier removes every path the new template version stops rendering — by name, without comparing content — and its merge treats a renamed file as added on both sides. The template, not the tool, is where a project's own work survives that. Both behaviours are Copier internals rather than public API, verified against Copier 9.18.1; tests/boilerplate/templates/test_streamlit_update_migration.py drives a real update and fails if they change.

  1. Rename through a staged move. A template that renames or relocates a rendered path MUST ship a before-stage migration that moves the project's copy to the new name and stages the move (git mv, or a move followed by git add -A -- <old> <new>). Staging is the load-bearing half: Copier snapshots the index before it merges, so a staged move puts the project's content under the new name on the merge's "before updating" side, and the update pauses on a conflict carrying both versions. Without the migration the project's edited copy is deleted at exit 0 — no conflict marker, no .rej file, no message. The worked entry is in Template authoring.
  2. Render nothing the render's own .gitignore matches. A file git ignores never enters the index, so Copier's merge cannot see it: no three-way merge, no conflict marker, no .rej file, and no history to recover it from. A template MUST NOT render a path its own ignore rules match, and MUST NOT ignore a path the render tells the user to commit.
  3. Say who owns each file. For every rendered file, choose between template-owned — the template keeps changing it, so a project that edits it risks a conflict whenever a release touches the same lines, and on a file small enough that one diff hunk spans it, any release at all (ADR-015) — and project-owned, listed in _skip_if_exists (specified in the Per-Layer Render Loop). State the choice where an author will find it; silence means template-owned. A file meant to be deleted (a sample module) stays template-owned; project-owned is for files users are expected to keep and rewrite instead, like a README or an entry point.

docs.title: Copier update process
docs.text:
When a project updates, Copier:

  1. Reads the old template version from that layer's answers file
  2. Refuses to start unless run with --trust, once the update crosses any declared migration — nothing is applied without it
  3. Runs before-stage migrations for every version crossed, against the pre-update tree
  4. Performs three-way merge:
  5. Old template files (v1.x)
  6. User changes (what they customized)
  7. New template files (v2.0.0)
  8. Runs after-stage migrations — the default stage — for every version crossed, against the merged tree
  9. Leaves conflict markers in place for incompatibilities

Conflicts do not stop migrations, and Copier's exit code stays 0 through a conflicted update: the conflict pause is where the update model in ADR-007 picks up.

docs.title: One version stream per repository
docs.text:
Constraint: All templates in a Git repository MUST share a single version stream — one tag series versioning the repository as a whole. A template that versions independently MUST therefore resolve to its own repository.

Rationale: Copier's version mechanics are repository-wide. It finds "latest" by sorting the repository's Git tags (PEP 440), and it records the project's template version from the nearest tag (git describe). Two independently versioned templates sharing a repository would interleave their tags: an update could move one template to the other's release, and a project's answers file could record the wrong template's version. Copier's _subdirectory supports multiple templates in one repository only when they release in lockstep under one tag series — and even then at a cost: Copier reads _subdirectory from the repository's root copier.yml, so serving several templates from one repository means a root config with a dynamic _subdirectory and every template's questions when:-gated in that single file, which stops per-template question schemas from being self-contained artifacts.

The bundled project and streamlit templates version independently inside the Boilerplate repository, so they do not resolve to their own repositories; release-time extraction into per-template repositories is the design in ADR-006, and the catalog-monorepo convention for aggregating independently versioned template repositories as submodules is in Design — Template system § Submodule Federation and Tool Ownership.

docs.title: Composition constraints
docs.text:
Templates declare dependencies via extends:

# boilerplate.yml (streamlit template)
version: "0.2.0"
name: streamlit
extends:
  - project  # unversioned reference: the latest registered project template

A breaking change in a base template, and how it propagates through the templates that extend it, is specified in Design — Project lifecycle § Structural changes to the extends chain and the UpdatePlan/LayerChange fields in Design — Data models.

docs.title: Before adding breaking changes
docs.text:
1. Consider Alternatives
  2. Can the change be non-breaking?

  3. Can it be added as optional new variable?

  4. Plan Migration

  5. Write Copier migration scripts
  6. Test with real projects

  7. Document what changed

  8. Check Dependents

  9. If other templates extend this template, bump their version too
  10. Update their extends constraint
  11. Provide their migration scripts

docs.title: For each breaking change
docs.text:
• Bump MAJOR version (e.g., 1.0.0 → 2.0.0)
  • Add the migration to _migrations in copier.yml
  • Test migration with copier update on sample projects
  • Update referenced templates' extends constraints
  • Document migration in migration guide (see Migration guide template)
  • Update template documentation

docs.title: Example: renaming a template variable
docs.text:
Renaming a template variable (for example, project_name → project_id) bumps the major version, then ships a migration that:

  • Renames the key in the layer's .copier-answers.<layer>.yml
  • Finds and replaces the old variable name across generated files
  • Updates the question definition in copier.yml

See Copier's migrations documentation for the mechanism.

docs.title: Features being removed (deprecation required)
docs.text:
Deprecation applies when removing template features with no automated migration path:

v1.0.0: Feature works normally
v1.1.0: Feature deprecated (still works, warning in docs)
v2.0.0: Feature removed (no migration script exists)

Deprecation period: At least one minor version.

docs.title: Breaking changes (with automated migration)
docs.text:
Template breaking changes accompanied by Copier migrations do not require a deprecation period:

v1.0.0: Old structure (e.g., config.yml at root)
v2.0.0: New structure (config.yml in .boilerplate/)
        + Copier migration script handles the move
        → Users update with copier update (automatic migration)

Rationale: Copier's three-way merge system preserves user customizations during updates.

See Versioning & compatibility policy § When to choose each path for the distinction between template and CLI breaking changes.

docs.title: Migration guide documentation
docs.text:
See Migration guide template for required format. Migration guides document:

  • What template changed
  • Why it changed
  • What migration does automatically
  • What requires manual intervention (if any)
  • Validation procedures

docs.title: Test suite requirements
docs.text:
A migration test does three things:

  • Create a project from the previous template version.
  • Run copier update against the new version.
  • Assert the migration's effect on the resulting tree — renamed or moved files exist at their new paths, and a project edit to the old path survives as a merge conflict rather than a silent deletion.

tests/boilerplate/templates/test_streamlit_update_migration.py drives exactly this against the streamlit layer's smoke-test rename and is the worked example for a new migration test.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
Template, Question, Copier, copier.yml, and boilerplate.yml follow the definitions in design 01's glossary. A "template variable" above is a Question. Migration-specific terms used on this page:

Copier Migration: An entry under _migrations in copier.yml — a command, gated by an optional version and when — that transforms a rendered project during copier update.

Extends: A dependency on a base template, pinned to an exact version (e.g., project@1.0.0) or left unversioned.

Migration-First: The principle that a breaking change is acceptable when an automated Copier migration handles it.

Three-Way Merge: Copier's merge algorithm, combining old template files, the user's customized project files, and new template files into a result that preserves user customizations.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: Authoring a template that will need to version and migrate? Start with the Template authoring guide, draft the change with the Migration guide template, and check whether it also needs a CLI-side deprecation path in the Versioning & compatibility policy. The target machinery this page prepares for — BoilerplateLock and UpdatePlan in Design — Data models, the extends syntax and submodule federation in Design — Template system, structural extends-chain changes in Design — Project lifecycle, and the update orchestration in ADR-007 — is where the rest of the story lives.

docs.title: Streamlit template
docs.text: The Streamlit template creates a Streamlit app, built on the general-purpose template. The app reads its own project's uv.lock and shows the stack it runs on, with container deployment included.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Stack inventory dashboard: locked package count, runtime vs. development vs. transitive dependencies, and the packages the most others depend on — no network, sample data, or fixtures needed at runtime.
  • Layered architecture: models validate, services compute, an adapter reads the lock file, and app.py only renders.
  • A unit test module per layer, plus a Streamlit AppTest that drives the rendered page.
  • VS Code debugger configuration — press F5 to run the app under the debugger.
  • Container deployment: a Dockerfile and build/push scripts that work with whichever registry you answered at generation time.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
my-streamlit-app/
├── pyproject.toml          # Project configuration
├── README.md               # App documentation
├── uv.lock                 # Dependencies
├── Dockerfile              # Multi-stage container definition
├── .dockerignore
├── .copier-answers.project.yml    # The project layer's answers, for future updates
├── .copier-answers.streamlit.yml  # This layer's answers, for future updates
├── boilerplate.lock        # Each layer's version, source and checksum
├── .vscode/
│   ├── settings.json       # Workspace settings (inherited from project)
│   ├── extensions.json     # Recommended extensions (inherited from project)
│   └── launch.json         # Debugger configuration
├── scripts/
│   ├── build-container.sh  # Container build script
│   └── push-container.sh   # Registry push script
├── src/
│   └── my_streamlit_app/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── app.py              # Widgets and layout only
│       ├── adapters/
│       │   ├── __init__.py
│       │   └── lockfile.py     # Reads uv.lock with tomllib, returns validated models
│       ├── models/
│       │   ├── __init__.py
│       │   ├── locked_package.py
│       │   ├── project_info.py
│       │   ├── stack_filter.py
│       │   ├── stack_row.py
│       │   └── stack_summary.py
│       └── services/
│           ├── __init__.py
│           └── inventory.py    # Pure functions: classify, filter, summarize
└── tests/
    ├── my_streamlit_app/
    │   ├── adapters/test_lockfile.py
    │   ├── models/
    │   │   ├── test_locked_package.py
    │   │   └── test_stack_filter.py
    │   ├── services/test_inventory.py
    │   └── test_import.py      # Checks the package imports (from project)
    └── integration/
        └── my_streamlit_app/
            └── test_app.py      # Drives the page with Streamlit's AppTest

The package name derives from the project name. The render also inherits the project template's notebooks/, .vscode/, .gitignore, and tests/<package>/test_import.py; the base layer's sample module stays off, and the import test renders in its place, because this template answers sample_module with no. Each layer records its answers in its own .copier-answers.<layer>.yml.

README.md, src/<package>/app.py and tests/integration/<package>/test_app.py are project-owned: the template lists them in _skip_if_exists, which governs what an update does to them.

A project rendered by an earlier 0.1 release of this layer carries the smoke test as tests_app.py. On update, a before-stage migration moves it to test_app.py with git mv, so the update presents the file as a conflict holding both versions instead of deleting yours. This layer declares only its own questions and takes the rest from project through the composition, so updating it needs the merged schema that boilerplate update will provide (ADR-007 records that design); a plain copier update of a copy of the layer rendered from a git repository exits 0 while skipping every path under the package directory, and Update a git-backed layer shows the flags that update it by hand. The copy bundled in the package cannot update with plain Copier at all (copy-only). Copier requires --trust for an update that runs a migration. With --no-tasks, the inherited cleanup task never runs either, so _scripts/post_generation.py (from the project layer) is left behind and isn't gitignored.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Create new Streamlit app (template name, then destination)
boilerplate new streamlit ./my-data-app
cd my-data-app

# Run the app locally (package name derives from the project name)
uv run streamlit run src/my_data_app/app.py

The inherited post-generation tasks already ran uv sync. If you passed --no-tasks, run uv sync before the first uv run.

For container deployment, see container deployment.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The template follows a layered architecture:

  • Models (models/): Pydantic models that validate the lock file's contents and the UI's widget values.
  • Services (services/): pure functions over the models — no I/O, no Streamlit import.
  • Adapters (adapters/): I/O — reads uv.lock and returns validated models.
  • App (app.py): the Streamlit UI — widgets, layout, and calls into services and the adapter.

Condensed from the template's adapters/lockfile.py, models/locked_package.py, services/inventory.py, and app.py (imports, docstrings, and the adapter's parsing body trimmed — the rendered files are complete):

# adapters/lockfile.py
def read_lockfile(path: Path) -> tuple[ProjectInfo, tuple[LockedPackage, ...]]:
    data = tomllib.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    # ... locate the root package, build ProjectInfo and every LockedPackage
    return project, packages

# models/locked_package.py
class LockedPackage(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)
    name: str
    version: str
    source_kind: str
    dependencies: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# services/inventory.py
def build_rows(
    project: ProjectInfo, packages: Sequence[LockedPackage]
) -> tuple[StackRow, ...]:
    dependent_counts: dict[str, int] = {}
    for package in packages:
        for dependency in package.dependencies:
            dependent_counts[dependency] = dependent_counts.get(dependency, 0) + 1

    rows = [
        StackRow(
            name=package.name,
            version=package.version,
            scope=_scope_of(package.name, project),
            source_kind=package.source_kind,
            dependents=dependent_counts.get(package.name, 0),
        )
        for package in packages
        if package.name != project.name
    ]
    return tuple(sorted(rows, key=lambda row: row.name))

# app.py
project, packages = read_lockfile(LOCKFILE)
rows = build_rows(project, packages)
stack_filter = StackFilter.model_validate({"search": search, "scope": scope, "limit": limit})
st.dataframe([row.model_dump() for row in apply_filter(rows, stack_filter)], hide_index=True)

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: Press F5 in VS Code to launch the Streamlit app with the debugger attached. The .vscode/launch.json is pre-configured.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• test_locked_package.py: PEP 503 name normalization.
  • test_stack_filter.py: widget-value validation — search pattern, scope, and limit bounds.
  • test_lockfile.py: parses a lock file into ProjectInfo and LockedPackage; raises on a missing root package or a missing file.
  • test_inventory.py: classification into runtime, dev, and transitive; dependent counts; filtering; summarizing.
  • test_app.py (integration): drives the rendered page with Streamlit's AppTest — runs without exception, shows the correct locked-package count, and warns on invalid filter input.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: Need container deployment details? See container deployment. Building your own template? Start with Template authoring. Return to the Templates Hub.

docs.title: Deploying Streamlit containers
docs.text: Every render ships a Dockerfile and two scripts — scripts/build-container.sh and scripts/push-container.sh — that build and publish a container image. This section covers each part of the process; every script step also has a manual equivalent.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The scripts run on any Docker host: Linux, macOS or Windows with Docker Desktop, or WSL2 on Windows. Environment setup covers the WSL2 case.

Once an image is built, running it locally always looks the same:

docker run -p 8501:8501 text-highlighter:local

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
• How to prepare your machine for containerized Streamlit deployment.
  • How to build Docker images from your Streamlit project.
  • How to push those images to GitHub Container Registry, Azure Container Registry, or any other registry you're already logged into.

Don't add yourself to the docker group

Running Docker without sudo requires membership in the docker group, which grants root-level access via the Docker socket. The build and push scripts detect whether your session can already reach Docker and fall back to sudo otherwise, so you never need that group membership just to run them.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Environment setup Install Docker and uv, plus the Azure CLI if you push to Azure Container Registry or build against an Azure DevOps package index.

  • Building container images Build an image with the script or manual docker buildx commands; authenticate to a private package index when your project uses one.

  • Pushing container images Publish the image to GitHub Container Registry, Azure Container Registry, or another registry, using the script or manual docker commands.

docs.title: Building container images
docs.text: Build a Docker image from your Streamlit project using either the included script or manual docker buildx commands.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Before you begin:

  • Docker, reachable directly or via sudo — Environment setup covers installing it, including on WSL2.
  • Your project must include:
    • A pyproject.toml file with a [project] name field.
    • A uv.lock file for dependency resolution.

If your project's package index (the package_index_url answer from generation time) is empty, that's everything you need. If it points at a private index, see Private package index below.

docs.title: Build options
docs.text: You can use the provided script to streamline the build process or follow the manual steps below.

docs.title: Use the build script
docs.text:
Run the build script from your project directory:

./scripts/build-container.sh

This script will:

  • Validate the presence of uv.lock (and read pyproject.toml to derive the default image name).
  • Use docker directly if your session can reach the daemon, or sudo docker otherwise.
  • Build the image with docker buildx. When your project has a private package index configured, it authenticates first — see Private package index.
  • Tag the image using the project name with a default :local tag.

If your pyproject.toml includes:

[project]
name = "text-highlighter"

The resulting image will be:

text-highlighter:local

Upon successful completion, you'll see:

✅ Docker image built successfully: text-highlighter:local
ℹ️  To run your container locally:
   docker run -p 8501:8501 text-highlighter:local
📣  Note: If your app runs on a different port, update the -p flag accordingly.

docs.title: Build manually
docs.text:
With no private package index, the script's build step is one command:

docker buildx build --tag text-highlighter:local --load .

Prefix it with sudo if your Docker daemon needs that. Replace text-highlighter:local with your preferred image tag.

docs.title: Private package index
docs.text: When your project's package index needs credentials, the build passes them to uv sync as a Docker secret (id=index) so they never land in an image layer — the Dockerfile's RUN --mount=type=secret,id=index,env=INDEX uv sync --default-index "$INDEX" --keyring-provider subprocess consumes it. Which credentials, and how the script gets them, depends on the index host.

docs.title: Azure DevOps index
docs.text:
When the index host is dev.azure.com or pkgs.visualstudio.com, the script requests a short-lived Azure DevOps token through the Azure CLI and passes it as the secret. You need az installed and available on PATH.

Manual steps:

  1. Authenticate with Azure CLI

    az login

  2. Retrieve a short-lived Azure DevOps token

    TOKEN=$(az account get-access-token \
  --resource 499b84ac-1321-427f-aa17-267ca6975798 \
  --query accessToken -o tsv)

  3. Build the Docker image

    INDEX="https://AzureDevOps:${TOKEN}@<your-feed>/simple/" \
docker buildx build \
  --secret id=index,env=INDEX \
  --tag text-highlighter:local \
  --load .

docs.title: Any other private index
docs.text:
Set INDEX_URL to the index URL with credentials embedded (for example https://user:token@host/simple/) before running the script; the script errors with this instruction if it's unset:

INDEX_URL="https://user:token@host/simple/" ./scripts/build-container.sh

Manually, pass the same value through as the build secret:

env INDEX="$INDEX_URL" docker buildx build \
  --secret id=index,env=INDEX \
  --tag text-highlighter:local \
  --load .

docs.title: Verifying the image
docs.text:
After building, confirm that your image exists:

docker images

To test it locally:

docker run -p 8501:8501 text-highlighter:local

Change the -p value if your application serves on a different port.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: Continue to pushing container images, or return to the container deployment overview.

docs.title: Environment setup
docs.text: Install the tools needed to build and deploy containerized applications from your WSL2 Ubuntu environment. Choose between a fully automated setup script or manual installation.

docs.title: Platform setup (one-time)
docs.text:
If you're setting up WSL2 for the first time, open PowerShell as Administrator and run:

wsl --install

This installs:

  • Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2)
  • Ubuntu (default distribution)
  • Required virtualization components

After installation, restart your machine and launch Ubuntu from the Start Menu to complete setup.

docs.title: Setup options
docs.text:
The build and push scripts use docker directly when your session can already reach the daemon, and fall back to sudo docker otherwise — see the Docker security note for why staying out of the docker group is worth it.

Choose one of the following methods to install the required tools inside your WSL2 Ubuntu environment.

docs.title: Automated setup (recommended)
docs.text:
The setup script ships in the boilerplate repository, not in your generated project — download it first, then run it in your Ubuntu terminal:

curl -O \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TheRealBillSiegler/boilerplate/main/scripts/setup-wsl-env.sh
chmod +x setup-wsl-env.sh
./setup-wsl-env.sh

This installs:

  • Docker CE (from Docker's official APT repository)
  • Azure CLI (from Microsoft's APT repository). The script always installs it; you only need it for Azure Container Registry pushes or an Azure DevOps package index. If neither applies, use the manual setup below and skip the Azure CLI section.
  • uv (from Astral's installer)

Example usage:

sudo docker run hello-world

docs.title: Manual setup
docs.text: If you prefer to install dependencies manually, use the commands below.

docs.title: Docker CE
docs.text:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y ca-certificates curl gnupg lsb-release apt-transport-https

sudo mkdir -m 0755 -p /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg |
sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg

echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) \
signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] \
https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu \
$(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" |
sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y \
  docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin \
  docker-compose-plugin

docs.title: Azure CLI
docs.text:
Only needed for pushing to Azure Container Registry or building against an Azure DevOps package index — skip this section otherwise.

curl -sL https://packages.microsoft.com/keys/microsoft.asc |
gpg --dearmor |
sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/microsoft.gpg > /dev/null

AZ_REPO=$(lsb_release -cs)
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) \
signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/microsoft.gpg] \
https://packages.microsoft.com/repos/azure-cli/ $AZ_REPO main" |
sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/azure-cli.list

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y azure-cli

docs.title: uv
docs.text:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Verify the installation:

uv --version

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: Continue to building container images, or return to the container deployment overview.

docs.title: Pushing container images
docs.text: Push a local Docker image to a registry using the included script or manual docker commands. Authentication depends on which registry you push to.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Before pushing, ensure:

  • You've already built a local Docker image (see Building container images).
  • Docker is reachable, directly or via sudo.

docs.title: Push options
docs.text: You can use the provided script to streamline the push process or push the image manually.

docs.title: Use the push script
docs.text:
Run the script from your project directory:

./scripts/push-container.sh

Options:

  • -i/--image-name — local image (default <project-name>:local).
  • -r/--registry — registry hostname (default the container_registry answer from generation time).
  • -n/--namespace — owner or organization within the registry (default $CONTAINER_NAMESPACE, else empty).
  • -t/--tag — remote tag (default latest).

The remote name is <registry>/<namespace>/<repo>:<tag> when a namespace is set, otherwise <registry>/<repo>:<tag>:

./scripts/push-container.sh \
  --image-name text-highlighter:local \
  --registry ghcr.io \
  --namespace my-org \
  --tag prod

Authentication is chosen from the registry hostname at push time, so the same script keeps working if you change registries later.

docs.title: GitHub Container Registry and Docker Hub
docs.text: --namespace is required — it's the owner or organization the image belongs to; the script exits with an error if it's missing. If REGISTRY_TOKEN is set, the script signs in with it (docker login ghcr.io --username <namespace> --password-stdin); otherwise it assumes you already ran docker login ghcr.io and continues. New packages on GHCR are private until you make them public in the package's settings on GitHub — that switch can't be undone. Docker Hub (docker.io) follows the same rules: --namespace is required and REGISTRY_TOKEN signs you in.

docs.title: Azure Container Registry
docs.text: No namespace needed. The script requires the Azure CLI, checks az account show and runs az login if you're signed out, then acquires a short-lived Microsoft Entra ID access token with az acr login --expose-token and logs Docker in with it.

docs.title: Any other registry
docs.text: The script assumes you're already signed in (docker login <registry>) and continues.

docs.title: Push manually
docs.text:
GitHub Container Registry:

echo "$REGISTRY_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io \
  --username <owner> \
  --password-stdin   # skip if you already ran `docker login ghcr.io`

docker tag text-highlighter:local ghcr.io/<owner>/text-highlighter:latest
docker push ghcr.io/<owner>/text-highlighter:latest

Azure Container Registry:

az login

TOKEN=$(az acr login \
  --name <your-registry> \
  --expose-token \
  --query accessToken -o tsv)

echo "$TOKEN" | docker login <your-registry>.azurecr.io \
  --username 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 \
  --password-stdin

docker tag text-highlighter:local <your-registry>.azurecr.io/text-highlighter:latest
docker push <your-registry>.azurecr.io/text-highlighter:latest

Any other registry:

docker login <registry>   # once, if not already signed in
docker tag text-highlighter:local <registry>/text-highlighter:latest
docker push <registry>/text-highlighter:latest

Prefix any docker command above with sudo if your daemon needs it.

docs.title: Verifying the push
docs.text:
GitHub Container Registry lists the image under the owner's or organization's Packages tab. Azure Container Registry lists it with:

az acr repository show-tags \
  --name <your-registry> \
  --repository text-highlighter

For any other registry, check its own UI or API.
